Sports.title: The Premier League is back: welcome to the new era of post-verdict unreality | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
The internet: an apology. It turns out you were right. It was actually a simulation all along. Now, talk to me about chemtrails again. And yes, maybe Vinícius Júnior has been replaced by a handsome, baffled-looking waxwork.

Welcome to the weirdest weekend of them all. We are now post-judgment, post-statement, postlapsarian. As the Premier League prepares to snap back into what must be described, out of habit, as reality, armed with the knowledge its serial champions have been the authors of a 10-year sham supremacy, the first question is fairly simple. How is it going to feel?

There is no precedent for this. Even the state of total confusion feels brittle given City maintain their complete state of innocence and deny all charges. We await the release of Irrefutable Body of Evidence, the great lost Madonna erotic thriller sequel, presumably recast around a steamy three-year regulatory tribunal scenario.

City’s appeal defence appears to be based around the government giving them money. This may or may not be related to how you control what the high court considers admissible. But it is also implied confirmation that the club is the propaganda tool of an overseas state, that Kyle Walker, for example, has basically been a civil servant all these years. Maybe the United Arab Emirates should have six stars on the national team jersey, one for each title. They even look like asterisks.

Beyond this there is the more basic issue of how to present this spectacle as entertainment. How do you structure a Match of the Day now? What’s the balance in the edit of bus-rage, taunting banner clips, managerial evasiveness content, versus the trivial stuff on the pitch with the balls and goals and men in shorts?

Mainly the Manchester City affair has created an existential problem. The key questions in English football are no longer things such as who will win the league, or will Tottenham get relegated (although this is still an excellent question). They are instead: what is real now? What was real then? What will be real in the future? Will something that seems real now become unreal later?

View image in fullscreen Was Kyle Walker basically a civil servant during his time at City? Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images

The whole experience brings to mind visiting the Yas Marina Formula One track in Abu Dhabi a few years back, a pristine place, all sweeping curves, perfect surfaces, dreamy floral boulevards. At that stage exploring its far reaches, following the curve around the final corner, led to: nothing. Out of sight the hanging baskets stopped dead. The sprinklers cut out. The pavement ended. The next step took you straight into sand and dead space.

Beyond the main stage the Yas track was a set, an imitation of life. And it turns out this is basically what Abu Dhabi was doing to the Premier League in the years 2009 to 2018: creating a product, a simulacrum, a pop-up.

At the end of which we have a blurring of edges, different versions of what could be real eliding into one another, a place where an AI video of Uncle Phil from the Fresh Prince scoring the Özil goal against Ludogorets seems just as real, just as plausible as City’s 6-0 thrashing of Watford in the FA Cup final. Seen through that lens this can feel like an extinction-level problem. Being real is, in the end, all sport actually has.

It feels fitting City’s first date in the new unreality is Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, one of the great Premier League fixtures recast as a kind of ceremonial shame-event, a requiem for a dream. Liverpool have a clearer sense of grievance than most, having been deprived of league titles three times on the final day by a club that was colouring outside the lines.

In many ways the game at Anfield is a perfect snapshot of what we have lost. This should be an entirely pure and gripping sporting contest. Instead the biggest story in top-tier English football is the meaninglessness of top-tier English football. The headline product is gossip, side-eye, legal backstory.

In their next 14 league games City will play three teams who have reserved the right to sue them. How can these occasions be seen as credible acts of sport? Even the banter-culture is out of date. For the past 12 years City at Anfield has been soundtracked by the Steve Gerrard/He slipped on his arse incident, a source of public pain that has defined the late-stage career of Liverpool’s most beloved modern captain. Except, we now know the actual story is the club that finished above them were cheating.

View image in fullscreen Steven Gerrard after that mistake against Chelsea in 2014. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

It turns out this is the first stage of football grief. Poring over the endless counterfactuals. Some are pretty stark. The five league titles won on the last day of the season. The 1-0 FA Cup final victory against Stoke, coached by a man with two contracts, the winning goal scored by a player linked, by close association, with the book-cooking regime.

There is a butterfly effect here of endless interference. What do Inter make of all this? Imagine losing a Champions League final that could have transformed your modern history, by the narrowest margin, to a club that appear to have built their own era out of cheating on their income. Two years later Inter were thrashed by another nation-state team and Simone Inzaghi was shunted off the set. He’s in Saudi now. Just get on the train.

Then there’s the wider structural stuff. City spent nine years flooding the zone with government-backed transfer funds (€1.2bn in those nine years: miles out in front), skewing the money supply in every league in Europe. The extra £20m disbursed at the last moment to drag Kevin De Bruyne out of the Bundesliga. What happens if that doesn’t happen?

At home, Spurs missed the Champions League by one spot four times, always in City’s slipstream. Would Manchester United have signed Rasmus Højlund without that steamrollering model of Erling Haaland-era success?

How to reprocess the deep cultural influence of Pep Guardiola? This was based on Guardiola’s genius as a coach, which is still real, irrespective of the gradient of the playing field. But nothing succeeds like success. Winners get to rewrite history. How does it feel now that Guardiola’s style affected so profoundly the way kids play park football, the way young coaches work, all of it based on sustained blockbusting example?

Even the Football Association’s England DNA pathway was basically a Pep document, predicated on the undeniable evidence of his winning way. The method is still good, the detail unarguable, the tactical blueprint pure. But that 10-year spell in England was also supercharged by cheating.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

We mourn too the legend of the Catalan brain trust, the hours spent studying this pure and monk-like dynamic. Yeah, fine. But also chuck vast amounts of hidden cash at it. Not to mention the hundreds of articles, podcasts, academic studies, fan tributes and personal tomes about purity, legacy, style, the glory that sailed above all other questions.

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola reminds Liverpool fans of his six titles in 2024, but how now do we assess his influence? Photograph: Ian Hodgson/AP

City’s fans are entitled to some space here, a chance to effect their own reckoning up. Elements of that support may have responded over the years with bizarre levels of aggression to any questioning of the process. But it is also normal to believe what you’re told, not least when it includes the profound transformation of the thing you love. How to process a total narrative U-turn?

The City documentary series A Beautiful Obsession is a far more interesting watch now, like The Sixth Sense when you know the ending. The project is cast by its editors as a pure passion play, Pep portrayed as a tunnel-vision obsessive, pictured most often staring at a whiteboard covered in magnets while the world turns beyond his line of vision.

It is impossible now not to see some kind of willed seclusion, Prospero on his island, rough magic starting to fray as reality crashes on to the shores. Episodes one to four are portrayed as a Viking funeral for the age of Pep. But they are now an unwitting farewell to something else too. In his final appearance Pep is shown quoting Kipling, saying triumph and disaster are both impostors. And he’s right. It turns out they were. Most notably the triumph bits.

Just before the end credits we see one of City’s club channel celebrations, with boards plastered in the usual phrases the club seems to feel drawn to. This is how it felt. We see things they’ll never see. Looking back this was always part of the dynamic, the insistence, which is usually just taken as read, that this is all real, that the feelings were feelings, that nobody can fake this away.

It is still the mantra for some. And maybe that’s true. But if so, what did it add up to in the first place? An episode of a TV show? An induced high, a snort of disposable pleasure?

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans celebrate their 2012 Premier League title. They too are entitled to some space here. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/Getty Images

But then, this is also not the end. There is always disasterism in football, the sense the thing happening now is the thing that will always happen. But football’s enduring strength, the one thing that marks it out as indestructible, is its relentlessness. We are in the period of rupture and parallax error. But how long will it last?

Plenty of good can still come from this. The idea that English football is profoundly damaged by this may prove wide of the mark. What is happening here, and this includes the outcome of the appeal, is that rules are being enforced. Andy Burnham may have confused the process with his tone-deaf and weirdly partial comments. But for all the delay and indecision this is still the rule of law in action.

And maybe English football gets to learn something. Maybe the unregulated nature of the league can reset a little. At the very least it seems axiomatic the new regulatory powers should ensure no nation state, or state fund, however you want to semanticise it, gets to own a club again.

There are still 33 rounds of Premier League games to run in the age of whiplash. The current interlude may feel like a football version of those bits in the Terminator films where Sarah Connor drives around in a Jeep looking glazed and distant, prepping for the time of skulls and robot death-rays, disengaged from the meaningless lives of blind and foolish humans.

Football always moves on. Throw flares at a bus, taunt the deceived souls in the away end. But the future is still wide open. Perhaps we can even face it with a little hope in the time of conflict.

Sports.title: Lionesses take control of World Cup playoff tie but unfancied Greece still in fight
Sports.content:
Sarina Wiegman said she wanted to see a bit more from her side after their fairly underwhelming performance against a hugely unfancied Greek side, despite securing a valuable first-leg victory in their Women’s World Cup playoff tie.

Georgia Stanway’s neat finish, Maya Le Tissier’s first England goal and Alessia Russo’s low strike were enough to give England control but a Kallisti Brouksair goal for Greece means that the tie is not definitively over, going into Tuesday’s second leg, and Wiegman acknowledged that England had been “a bit sloppy” at times.

“I think we made it a bit harder [for ourselves],” Wiegman said, while also giving credit to Greece for being “very well-prepared, very well-organised and very disciplined”, before adding: “Of course, I’m happy with the 3-1. I’m not happy with the 1.

“We were – in moments – really good on the ball, and we were, in moments, not so good on the ball and we could have made better decisions, too.

“We want to play really well. Of course, we go out to win, but we want to show more than winning, we want to play really well too.”

Facing a Greek side ranked 59th in the world, who have never qualified for a major tournament, England began as overwhelming favourites and dominated the ball but often appeared to be going through the motions, making hard work of breaking down Greece’s deep defensive shape. It would be too much of a stretch to describe it as a bad performance but, at the same time, England did lack their usual zip, charisma and urgency and their body language suggested they were focused on the job at hand, rather than enjoying themselves.

Perhaps the flat atmosphere was to blame for that. The Hellenic Football Federation had made the tickets free for this fixture but – despite that – only a few thousand turned up and there was scarcely any cheers from the home supporters. Instead, around 500 travelling England fans were generating the majority of the noise.

It meant that the first 45 minutes were largely forgettable and lacking in real quality, aside from a few isolated moments such as a delicious chip from 25 yards out from Lauren James, which drew a gasp of appreciation from the away fans as it hit the net and they thought England had taken the lead. A VAR check showed that James was offside.

View image in fullscreen Georgia Stanway finishes off an England team move to open the scoring in Greece. Photograph: Miloš Bičanski/Getty Images

England were playing with a back three when in possession, pushing Le Tissier very high up the pitch as a right wing-back, and with a back four when out of possession. They were untroubled defensively except for a huge let-off at 0-0 when the Greece striker Ionna Papatheodorou hit the woodwork. She eased past Esme Morgan and Leah Williamson with alarming ease and her shot from range looked to have beaten Hannah Hampton, but struck the bar.

England, who had gone close when Laura Blindkilde Brown shot straight at the goalkeeper, James curled a free-kick wide and Lauren Hemp drilled a low shot narrowly wide across the face of goal, eventually found their breakthrough when Blindkilde Brown played a quick ball to Russo, whose good touch to lay the ball off for Stanway allowed the midfielder to slot in low.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

After the break, Le Tissier powered in a strong finish after clever work from Keira Walsh to open up space, and when Russo tucked a low finish into the bottom corner to make it 3-0 four minutes later, England might have been hoping the floodgates were open. However, some limp defending allowed Rangers’ Brouksair to pull a goal back, firing in a low finish after a hopeful, bouncing, high long ball was not initially dealt with by Morgan.

Quick Guide Women's World Cup qualifying roundup Show The Republic of Ireland cruised to an 8-0 victory in the first leg of their Women’s World Cup qualifying play-off against Kazakhstan in Astana. Kyra Carusa scored twice while further goals from Chloe Mustaki, Emily Murphy, Abbie Larkin, Jamie Finn, Shanade Hopcroft and Jessie Stapleton made Tuesday’s second leg in Cork a formality. Carusa had already grabbed her brace – and Mustaki also hit the target – before the Kazakhstan captain, Yulia Myasnikova, was sent off just beyond the half-hour mark for a foul on Larkin. The decision allowed the visitors to shrug off the absence of Katie McCabe due to injury and stroll to victory, with the outstanding Mustaki providing the assists for both Carusa’s goals as well as the fifth for Larkin shortly before half-time. Scotland defeated Czechia 2-0 in Pardubice, with Caroline Weir and Claire Emslie on target in the second half. Tereza Krejciríkova was sent off for the hosts three minutes from time. A 21st-minute Ezmiralda Franja own goal secured Wales a 1-0 win in Albania. Northern Ireland's World Cup hopes are all but over, however, after a 4-0 first leg home loss by Portugal. Telma Encarnação, Jéssica Silva, a Rebecca Holloway own goal and Fátima Pinto the scorers. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

England went close to adding to their tally, as James curled narrowly wide and the substitute Jess Park’s effort hit the bar, on a night when Erica Meg Parkinson and Grace Fisk were handed senior international debuts, late on.

Assuming they finish the job off on Tuesday in the second leg in Leicester, England would face Slovakia or Ukraine in the second round of the playoffs in the November-December international window. That tie would also be staged over two legs and England would need to win that to secure their spot at next summer’s tournament in Brazil. To be competitive there, though, they know they will need to markedly improve on their cohesion and fluidity with the ball.

Wiegman said: “I have seen some fluid moments too. You just want more. And you want the final balls and the positions in front of the goal [to be] better, and of course we’re working on that, with the amount of time we have. Some things, we’d really want to do better and we’re working really hard to do so. We have an opportunity now to fix that, for Tuesday.”

Sports.title: Managers react to Manchester City’s guilty verdict: ‘Uncertainty is not good for anyone’
Sports.content:
1. Carrick ‘personally’ affected by verdict Michael Carrick has said retrospectively receiving a winner’s medal would not make up for being robbed of emotional moments of glory by Manchester City’s breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules. Manchester United’s manager was part of the squad that lost out on the Premier League title to City on the final day of the 2011-12 season when Sergio Agüero scored a last-minute winner to secure top spot on goal difference. Carrick and his United teammates were left solemn on the touchline at Sunderland while City, who have been found guilty of breaking financial rules during a nine-year-period between 2009 and 2018, celebrated. “The emotion, the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment,” Carrick said. “Whether you’re successful, whether you lose, whether it goes against you, that initial [feeling], the beauty of sport and the beauty of football and the beauty of trying to win trophies here, is a little bit on the journey towards it and then the finale, and does it go for you, does it go against you. “Once that’s done, there’s no getting that back in any direction. The feeling we all crave is coming out on top – that kind of sums it up. Whatever’s done in the past tense is in the past, but in that moment is how you feel in that moment. Certainly as a participant, as a performer, and I’m sure the supporters feel the same, that’s why we love it so much because of the emotion in the moment.” Carrick was also part of United’s staff under Ole Gunnar Solskjær when they finished second, 22 points behind City, in 2021. City continue to plead their innocence and have appealed against the verdict. If they fail to overturn the independent commission’s ruling, they will probably face a serious punishment. “It’s affected me personally in different ways,” Carrick said. “But as the case is ongoing now I don’t know where that stands and how it’s going to end up, so we’ll just have to wait and see. What I will say, the sooner it gets sorted I think for everyone’s benefit is essential.” Will Unwin

2. Iraola understands Liverpool fan anger Andoni Iraola understands the anger among Liverpool supporters towards Manchester City and believes the Premier League needs a resolution to the scandal engulfing English football as swiftly as possible. Iraola avoided condemning City during his first press conference since the club were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules on an industrial scale over nine years. City have lodged an appeal against the findings and Liverpool’s head coach admitted a final, definitive verdict is essential for the good of the game. “I think it should be [concluded quickly],” he said. “There should be a moment when something comes from this, but now is not that moment. Nobody knows what is going to happen and I think this uncertainty is no good for anyone.” While refusing to be drawn on the controversy while the legal process is ongoing, Iraola acknowledged the strength of feeling that will be directed at City by Liverpool fans at Anfield on Sunday. City pipped Liverpool to the Premier League title in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22, the latter two during the fierce rivalry that developed between Jürgen Klopp’s and Pep Guardiola’s teams. Sunday’s reception for the current league leaders promises to be brutal. “We understand and I understand everything that goes above football,” said Iraola. “Every fan will have their own opinion and attitude towards that but it’s not something that I can control. I need to do my job, to give the best game we can give on the sporting side, so everyone of our supporters is happy on Sunday. I think the challenge of the game for us is big.” Liverpool’s task on Sunday, as Iraola referenced, will be complicated by the absence of leading goalscorer Alexander Isak and the in-form Cody Gakpo due to injuries sustained on international duty. The two are not long-term absentees but, with Liverpool facing four games in 10 days, they could miss several matches. He admitted: “It’s a bad thing for us, definitely, because both of them have been prolific at the start of the season but the good thing when you coach Liverpool is you still have very good players available. I trust the players we have ready to go. It’s also a good moment for those players to step up, to add good numbers and good performances while we recover Cody and Alex.” Andy Hunter

3. Kompany ‘really proud’ of City medals Vincent Kompany, the former Manchester City captain, insists he is still “really proud” of his success with the club after it was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The Bayern Munich manager won four Premier League titles and multiple domestic cups during his spell at City from 2008 to 2019. The former Belgium international was a key figure in City’s dominant era under their Abu Dhabi-based owners and is honoured with a statue outside the Etihad Stadium. “I played 11 years for the club. I’ve loved all of the years I played for the club and everything we achieved and [did] on the pitch – that’s something I’m really proud of,” Kompany said. View image in fullscreen A statue of the former Manchester City player Vincent Kompany’s stands outside the Etihad: ‘I’m really proud of everything we achieved.’ Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP Kompany signed for City from Hamburg just weeks before Sheikh Mansour completed a takeover that turned the club from also-rans to serial winners. Asked about the off-pitch issues at his former club, he said: “Everything else, as a player you’re not a part of that and right now as a coach of Bayern Munich I’m not too much occupied with that topic. I’m preparing the game next week and preparing the game we have tomorrow and everything I have as a coach.” Agence France-Presse

4. Arteta will wait for judgment before speaking Mikel Arteta has insisted his conscience is clear about his time as Manchester City’s assistant manager and promised to “talk with clarity” about his former club when their appeal against a guilty verdict on more than 100 Premier League’s charges has been decided. Arteta spent more than three years as Pep Guardiola’s assistant at City before moving to Arsenal in December 2019. The Spaniard, who signed a lucrative new four-year contract this week, moved to the Etihad in July 2016 and was part of Guardiola’s backroom staff as they won titles in 2018 and 2019. The first came during the period in which City breached financial regulations, according to an independent commission. Arteta was reluctant to discuss any potential punishment City could face but was asked whether his conscience was clear from his spell at City and responded: “Yes.” That was as far as he was prepared to venture after being bombarded with questions about City before Arsenal’s game against Leeds on Saturday. Arteta had been due to deliver a statement at the start of his press conference but the plan changed at the last minute. He refused to be drawn on how he felt when he heard the verdict or whether the uncertainty it had created would have a long-term impact on the Premier League’s brand. “I want to think that it doesn’t, but I don’t know,” he said. “Uncertainty is not in our control and our control is to bring everything that we can individually through the club to maintain the position that we have to be the best league in the world.” Arteta added: “The thing is that this has been going for various years. That process is still not finished. So it is very difficult to express how I feel, because it is not resolved. When it is resolved I can talk with clarity and tell you exactly how I feel.” It is understood Arsenal and other Premier League clubs are keen for the situation to be resolved as quickly as possible, although City’s appeal means it could drag on until at least the new year. Arteta also dismissed suggestions Arsenal could be the main beneficiaries should City find themselves relegated, having finished as runners up to them three years in a row before becoming champions last season. “I think we control our accelerator, and believe me, for seven years it’s been full gas in everything that we can do and take in every corner at maximum speed,” he said. Ed Aarons

Sports.title: West Ham’s penalty pain costs them top spot in Championship after QPR draw
Sports.content:
The QPR goalkeeper Pierce Charles made a stunning double save from a Jarrod Bowen penalty in stoppage time to secure a 1-1 draw at West Ham. The 21-year-old, who kept four clean sheets and saved a penalty for Northern Ireland over the international break, pulled off more heroics to deny the Hammers top spot in the Championship.

Bowen had already equalised for West Ham, cancelling out a hugely controversial first-half penalty from Nicolas Madsen. But the Hammers captain saw his spot-kick saved and Charles then somehow pushed the rebound from Arne Engels on to the crossbar.

West Ham were earlier on the wrong end of a dreadful penalty decision after Tomas Soucek was penalised for fouling Paul Smyth. Replays showed the challenge was well outside the area and that the Hammers midfielder got the ball. A VAR review would have definitely overturned referee Ruebyn Ricardo’s decision but with no technology in the Championship it stood, to the dismay of the majority inside the London Stadium.

The West Ham assistant coach Rui Pedro Silva was booked for his complaints, as was Engels for stamping on the penalty spot, but Madsen kept his cool and calmly rolled the ball into the bottom corner.

View image in fullscreen Nicolas Madsen celebrates after rolling home from the spot. Photograph: John Walton/PA

Rangers almost doubled their lead from a West Ham corner, mounting a swift counterattack which left recalled striker Rayan Kolli with a shooting opportunity 15 yards out, but Mads Hermansen made a fine save.

Just as he had done at Millwall last time out with his side 2-0 down, the West Ham manager, Nuno Espírito Santo, made a double substitution at half-time, sending on Pablo Felipe and Edvin Austbø for Soucek and Kyle Walker-Peters. But Rangers almost struck again when Smyth danced past Konstantinos Mavropanos and into the area, only for the Greek defender to make a crucial recovery tackle.

View image in fullscreen A tribute to former West Ham goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko, who died in September, at the game. Photograph: John Walton/PA

Bowen, well marshalled by Rangers left-back Boy Kemper, had been enduring a frustrating evening until he burst into life in the 70th minute. The England international won the ball back with a crunching tackle on Ronnie Edwards, earning himself a bloody nose in the process. Pablo played the ball back to Bowen, who darted into the area and saw his first shot block before snaffling the rebound.

View image in fullscreen Jarrod Bowen after levelling for the Hammers. Photograph: John Walton/PA

West Ham went in search of a winner and Bowen’s scuffed effort looked destined for the net until Charles flung out a hand to push it past a post. Then, as the clock ticked into stoppage time Rangers substitute Amadou Mbengue grabbed a handful of Pablo’s shirt, referee Ricardo pointed to the spot again, but Charles superbly denied Bowen and Engels to earn his side a point.

Sports.title: Chelsea manager Alonso insists Cole Palmer is committed to playing for England
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso has said Cole Palmer is committed to playing for England and revealed Chelsea’s No 10 missed this international break with a problem related to the groin injury that kept him out for much of last season.

Thomas Tuchel did not hide his disappointment with Palmer, who is fit to face Bournemouth on Saturday, after the attacker made himself unavailable for the start of his country’s Nations League campaign last month. Tuchel said the 24-year-old “misses too many opportunities” to play for England and questioned whether Palmer wanted to be part of the squad.

Palmer has won five caps since scoring against Spain in the Euro 2024 final but his latest withdrawal was for genuine reasons. Palmer struggled with persistent groin pain last season, which led to him missing out on a place in Tuchel’s World Cup squad, and felt minor irritation before Chelsea’s defeat by Brentford last month. It still needs careful management, and Alonso is adamant Chelsea’s talisman is intent on playing for England.

“The most important thing for Cole is to be fully fit, that he enjoys his game, that he is feeling OK,” Chelsea’s manager said. “Whenever he is not, like in the Brentford game, we could see that he was struggling. He’s committed but he needs to be fully fit to play. We need him – the club and the national team.”

The recent issue is nowhere as near as bad as when Palmer struggled to shoot properly last season. Resting during the extended break has helped. “Now he’s fine,” Alonso said. “He’s been feeling better this week. We use the first two weeks for him to recover. It’s a little bit from the pubalgia he had.”

Tuchel has plenty of competition in attacking midfield and it remains to be seen whether he picks Palmer for next month’s games against Croatia and Spain. Alonso was asked whether a player can be considered truly world class if they do not play international football. “Things happen naturally,” he said. “When you show for your club that you are a top-level player and you have regularity, normally it is the natural way that you are part of the national team.”

Alonso was nonplussed to hear about the broadcaster Piers Morgan calling Palmer a bottle job for failing to represent England. “I don’t know the comment and I don’t know the guy,” he said.

Palmer has been in fine form for Chelsea this season, scoring four goals. They will need him at his best after three league games without a win. Alonso hopes that Reece James, Moisés Caicedo and Marco Palestra will also return from injury against Bournemouth.

Sports.title: Manchester United’s early wobble makes Tottenham visit a must-win for Carrick
Sports.content:
The noise in the Premier League was focused elsewhere for the last two weeks of the international break, allowing a glorious silence to drift across Manchester United. Without Manchester City’s woes, Michael Carrick may have faced a more difficult time, with plenty to review in regards to the first five games of the season.

United sit solemnly in 12th with only one league win, and misery needs company. The hosts will find just that at Old Trafford on Saturday evening. Tottenham, bottom of the Premier League, visit, with both sides hoping to kickstart their season. Spurs have secured a measly two points after a summer where £300m was spent on Roberto De Zerbi’s rebuild but the architect’s drawings are already at risk of being set alight. For Carrick and United, beating the worst team in the league is close to a necessity as they enter a very difficult run of fixtures.

October is theoretically and practically problematic for United, who have six fixtures this month, with away games against Leeds, Atlético Madrid, Como and Chelsea, who play a variety of styles that need preparing for, making a home game against Spurs a must-win. On paper, the second easiest game of the month is Bournemouth at home. Carrick has plenty of credit in the bank from his work in the second half of last season, and will be afforded as much time as possible to get things right because no one is eager for another mid-season change of manager. United need to be in a better position by the end of October than they started it, which will require significant improvement on the pitch.

For Carrick there are plenty of small margins he can point to. The opening-day defeat at Hull was a grisly performance and worthy of criticism; Ipswich were eventually dispatched, while the derby was a tight and controversial loss, coming between two draws. The truth of the matter is United know they need to be better in both boxes. United have conceded fewer opposition touches in their box than any other team in the league but, on the other hand, they are the only side yet to keep a clean sheet. They can also boast the most touches in opposition boxes but are largely incapable of killing matches off.

United, like Tottenham, are very good at dominating possession, averaging 60% per match, but cannot translate that to goals and points. Even in the victory against Ipswich, United were unable to put a full 90 minutes of composure together, relying on Bruno Fernandes to drag them through against a promoted side. The forwards are yet to synchronise, with Matheus Cunha, the man tasked with leading the line, having only one goal to his name, and even that took a heavy deflection.

No one has more than one assist so far, while only Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo have scored twice or more, the Portuguese getting a hat-trick against Ipswich. Marcus Rashford has shown glimpses of promise on the left but has no goal involvements, giving the impression of a man who requires a confidence boost after returning to the club where he was not wanted for 18 months. Nor is there the option of Benjamin Sesko playing as a more traditional central striker given he is sidelined with injury, while Joshua Zirkzee cannot even class himself as a plan B. But United are prolific compared with Tottenham, whose only league goals came in a 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa just before the international break.

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick has had lots to ponder this season, with only one league win so far. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

Losing to 10-man Manchester City was the most worrying of United’s defeats, showing how far off they look against a Champions League side. Phil Foden’s red card gave United plenty of space but they were unable to take advantage, instead plodding around, short of ideas, barely threatening. United are expert at dominating possession but not games, traits that create hope and frustration in equal measure.

The summer signings of a goalkeeper who cost nothing and three central midfielders is coming under as much scrutiny as Carrick’s tactics. At least Carlos Baleba is poised to finally make his debut after joining from Brighton for £65m in August and Carrick desperately needs him to provide the energy lacking in central areas thus far. Having recovered from an ankle injury, the Cameroonian has what it takes to snuff out the danger that has been leading to the concession of goals.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sesko is not the sole injury concern; Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford were ruled out of playing for England, while Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui’s international breaks ended prematurely. Meanwhile, Matthijs de Ligt has not played competitively for 10 months and Amad Diallo is yet to feature this season.

The run of 12 wins in 17 games after Carrick took interim charge in January showed plenty of individual and collective improvements, but whether certain players can crash through their current ceiling requires clear evidence sooner rather than later. With finances tight, it is imperative that United improve from within. More academy players have spent time with the squad in recent weeks, with Noah Ajayi impressing the coaches Steve Holland and Jonathan Woodgate. It is thought a number of youngsters could make first-team debuts before the season concludes, which would be a display of Carrick’s long-term vision. Results, however, will decide if he gets a chance to implement it in the first place.

United are desperate for a catalyst and if it does not come against Tottenham at the weekend, Carrick will become fearful of Halloween.

Sports.title: The Premier League so far: draws, underperforming xG and other data pointers
Sports.content:
Goals are on the up in the Premier League. The average of 2.70 non-penalty goals per game in 2026-27 is higher than last season and two of the four previous campaigns. Yet we should have been even more royally entertained. Matches have averaged 2.88 non-penalty expected goals, the second most in the past six seasons. Chances have been going to waste.

If the 20 teams converted at the par rate, there would have been almost two extra goals per week. As few as that sounds, the proportion of games drawn is higher than in any past Premier League season. Some tied matches might have been settled had the finishing been up to the mark.

This is an issue across the Premier League. Fourteen clubs have scored fewer goals than expected, whether penalties are included or not, up from 10 last season. While there are eight teams that are within a goal of their underlying numbers and may see an immediate change of fortunes this weekend, the remaining 12 are split 8-4 towards the underachievers.

It is not just season-wide averages that are crumbling but week-by-week performances, too. There were 24 instances of a team scoring at least one goal fewer than their xG implied they should have across the first five match weeks, twice as many as occurred in the opening 50 games last season.

There are numerous possible explanations. Chance quality does not appear to be one of them, as the expected goals per non-penalty shot average only drops once more decimal places are applied than feels healthy.

At first glance, volume of touches in the penalty area has barely shifted either. A Premier League team is averaging 24.8 touches in the opposition box per game, down just 0.6 on last season.

The breakdown by team is more revealing. Four of last season’s top five are having fewer box touches per match, with Aston Villa and Liverpool having seen around a third disappear from their averages.

The one team from the quintet to increase is Manchester United, but they have only played one club that finished in the top 10 last season and five of their eight goals occurred against Championship runners-up Ipswich. A finely tuned attacking machine they are not. United top the Premier League for non-penalty shots, and are joint-second bottom for the average expected goal value.

They have not been helped by their top player for non-penalty xG: Bryan Mbeumo is one of 10 players who have scored at least one goal fewer than underlying numbers imply he should have. As he underachieved by 1.19 last season, this is not especially odd. The issue is how reliant United are upon the 27-year-old. This problem is not exclusive to this combination of club and player either.

The top player for expected goals at almost every Premier League club is having a bigger share of the xG pie than they enjoyed last season. This need not necessarily be a concern, as the figures will drop once playing time and chances are more equally shared within squads.

The most involved players themselves may help explain why goals are down, though. The top players from each club have collectively scored 6.8 non-penalty goals fewer than expected, almost 40% of the shortfall across the division from just 20 players.

Thierno Barry has been the player taking the chance for 49.4% of Everton’s non-penalty expected goals this season, up from 17.7% last term. It’s a massive increase in responsibility for a relatively young player – he has scored twice from chances valued at 3.5 xG.

Alexander Isak has seen a greater leap in share of team expected goals, though injuries meant he did not feature that often last season. There are seeds of growth for him at Liverpool, but he remains relatively new in terms of minutes played for the club. As with more than half of Premier League clubs, Isak is playing under a new man in the dugout.

Isak’s replacement at Newcastle, Yoanne Wissa, underperformed against xG by more than two goals last season, as did Marcus Tavernier at Bournemouth. They may not be the best players for their clubs to funnel their chances through. At least they are preferable to the situation at Tottenham, where centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is their leading player for non-penalty expected goals.

Elsewhere, the players with the most xG for Fulham (Gonzalo García) and Ipswich (Emersonn) are 22 years old and new to English football. Hull’s Oli McBurnie, meanwhile, has never scored more than six goals in a Premier League campaign. Erling Haaland remains a reliable presence in the xG-heavy frontman stakes, but the situation at Manchester City may affect his form.

Excessive reliance on players who can be forgiven for underperforming could prove to be a small-sample statistical quirk that is quickly remedied. Until it is, do not bank on the goal rate reaching the expected goal level in the Premier League.
