“We created chances to score many other goals in these seven games but we didn’t. We are working to improve in the last third, the assists and the finishing,” he said.

“We are fourth in the table for the team who brings the ball into the opponents’ area the most times.

“It is nothing but it shows we can arrive in the area. We are not good enough to score goals so far when we have clear chances.”

Can Carrick or De Zerbi survive ‘El Sackicko’?

With Carrick also under pressure following their poor start, Tottenham’s trip to Manchester has been dubbed ‘El Sackicko’.

De Zerbi saved Tottenham from relegation after arriving late last season, but that final-day survival feat is unlikely to save him from the axe if results don’t improve soon.

“We are Tottenham. United and Tottenham are still big clubs in the Premier League,” he said.

“We have to deserve to work in this club, playing better and making different results.”

What happened the last time Man United played Tottenham

The sides last met in February in a Premier League encounter at Old Trafford with the home side winning 2-0.

Cristian Romero was shown red on the half-hour mark for Spurs before Bryan Mbeumo and Bruno Fernandes netted the United goals.

When did Tottenham last beat Manchester United?

Spurs famously beat United 1-0 in the UEFA Europa League final in May 2025, thanks to Brennan Johnson’s first-half strike.

The match marked Ange Postecoglou’s last game in charge of the club before being sacked for their lowly league finish.

Ruben Amorim paid the same heavy price the following season.

When did Tottenham last win a match at Manchester United?

Spurs piled the pressure on Amorim early in the 2024-2025 season with a 3-0 Premier League win at Old Trafford.

Johnson gave the away team a third-minute lead, before United had Bruno Fernandes sent off on the stroke of half-time.

Dejan Kulusevski and Dominic Solanke completed the scoring in the second half.

Head-to-head – Manchester United vs Tottenham

This will be the 205th meeting between the clubs with United winning 96 matches compared to Tottenham’s 56 victories.

Prediction – Manchester United vs Tottenham

The Opta supercomputer has given United a 54 percent chance of winning, while offering Spurs only a 22 percent chance of emerging victorious.

Manchester United team news

“It’s a bit mixed really through ‌the internationals,” Carrick said. “(Wing back) Patrick Dorgu came off and it looks like he’ll be out probably for a number of weeks.

“(Defender) Noussair Mazraoui came off and took a knock. He’s not quite right yet, we’ll have to ‌see ‌how he is.”

He added that Carlos Baleba was improving, while fellow midfielder Kobbie Mainoo, winger Amad Diallo and forward Marcus Rashford had resumed limited training. Striker Benjamin Sesko remains further away from a return.

Predicted Manchester United starting lineup

Lammens; Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw; Mainoo, Tielemans; Mbeumo, Fernandes, Rashford; Cunha

Tottenham team news

Kulusevski, Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert and Mykhaylo Mudryk all remain sidelined due to injury.



Jan Paul van Hecke has overcome a foot injury, but may miss out after his wife gave birth to twins – the club has said emotional needs will be taken into consideration.

Predicted Tottenham Hotspur starting lineup

Kinsky; Gray, Senesi, Van de Ven, Robertson; Gallagher, Tonali, Fernandes; Savio, Solanke, Marmoush

World.title: UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’, urges dialogue
World.content:
United Nations Special Envoy to Yemen Hans Grundberg says that the country has slid back into “full-scale war” as fighting between the Houthis and internationally recognised government forces continues.

During a meeting at the UN Security Council on Friday to discuss the situation in Yemen, Grundberg said civilians, including women and children, were bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.

“Ongoing instability in the Middle East continues to impact dynamics in Yemen, while developments in Yemen, in turn, reverberate across the region,” he said.

“Regional security, freedom of navigation and the protection of international trade are legitimate concerns that must be addressed. International engagement on Yemen must also be grounded in the realities of Yemen and the needs and aspirations of its people,” Grundberg added.

The envoy stressed that “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now.”

“Ultimately, gains on the battlefield cannot substitute for the negotiations that will be required to settle the conflict,” he said, urging Security Council members to collectively support mediation efforts.

According to the UN, at least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others have been injured since August, with children bearing a disproportionate toll during the ongoing clashes.

‘Dangerous escalation’

The UN representative for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi, told the Security Council that the threat from the Houthis was no longer an “internal Yemeni affair”.



Al-Saadi called on the council to take “decisive, practical measures” to reduce the flow of funding, weapons and technology to the Iranian-backed group and also strengthen cooperation with the Yemeni government.

He thanked Riyadh, which supports the government, for “standing beside the Yemeni people and their government, and for their continued support to state institutions and our economy”.

This comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue, with the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority reporting on Friday that the King Khalid International Airport, north of Riyadh, was subjected to two attacks on Thursday, in which three Saudi citizens were killed.

Gulf states and European countries have condemned the attack on the airport, with Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs calling it “unacceptable”.

During the council meeting, Saudi Arabia’s UN representative, Abdulaziz al-Wasil, said the UN body must address the “dangerous escalation” ongoing in Yemen.

“These rapid developments in Yemen and the continued escalation by the terrorist Houthi militias must be addressed by the Council,” al-Wasil said.

Al-Wasil added that Riyadh will “not allow Yemen to be turned into a staging ground for threats to its security or to the freedom of navigation”.

World.title: How will Spain’s housing crisis affect elections?
World.content:
Snap vote called after Parliament rejects measures to protect tenants and freeze rents.

Rising frustration about housing shortages and surging rents in Spain has led to mass protests.

The demonstrations started last month after the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, who died at age 87 this week.

The Socialist-led government tried to introduce measures to protect tenants and freeze rents, but Parliament rejected them. The conservative opposition says the solution is to ease regulations and build more homes.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has since announced early elections. Analysts say he wants to galvanise support, as he faces pressure on immigration and corruption investigations into his party.

Two recent polls indicate the right-wing People’s Party and far-right Vox are on track for a combined majority.

Can demonstrations against the housing crisis reverse Sanchez’s political fortunes?

Presenter: Sami Zeidan

Guests:

Hana Jalloul – Secretary of international politics and cooperation for the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party and a member of the European Parliament

Daniel Lacalle – Chief economist at Tressis and professor at the IE Business School

Pablo Calderon Martinez – Associate professor in politics and international relations at Northeastern University

World.title: Human rights veteran Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
NewsFeed Human rights veteran Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize

South African jurist Navanethem Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her work to promote peace and international law. The ex-UN rights chief chaired the UN inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza, and served as Nelson Mandela’s defence lawyer.

World.title: Rising fuel costs slashed Delta’s profit outlook despite strong demand
World.content:
Delta Air Lines cut its profit forecast despite heightened demand as fuel costs surge across the air travel sector.

The Atlanta-based air carrier said in its third-quarter earnings report released on Friday that it expects its annual fuel costs to jump by $6bn, as ongoing tensions between the United States and Iran have sent fuel prices surging across the global aviation sector.

Overall, US airlines spent nearly $43bn on fuel in the first eight months of the year, a $13.2bn increase from the same period a year earlier.

On Wall Street, Delta cut its earnings outlook for the year to adjusted earnings per share of $5.10 to $5.60, down from its July forecast of $6.50 to $7.50. The midpoint of the new range is below analysts’ average estimate of $5.46, according to LSEG data.

Delta’s stock tumbled in midday trading as the trading week came to a close. It was down 1.1 percent from Friday’s opening price. While the stock has fallen 4.4 percent over the past five days, it has performed well in 2026, gaining nearly 18 percent since the beginning of the year.

CEO Ed Bastian said the airline had raised prices by roughly 20 percent this year and said those prices could be sustained even if fuel prices decline.

Delta Air Lines is the first of the major US airlines to report earnings and is generally more protected from price fluctuations than its competitors because it owns a refinery in Pennsylvania, which it acquired in 2012.

Despite higher prices, demand remains elevated, with 60 percent of flights in the fourth quarter already booked. Delta also announced several new international routes, including Seattle–Tokyo, Japan and Boston–Venice, Italy, as well as Austin-Paris, France, all beginning next year.



Bastian told the Wall Street Journal that holiday bookings also remain strong and that premium travel is growing, with premium seat revenue jumping 18 percent for the quarter compared with the same period last year.

Broadly speaking, premium flights can be a boon for major airlines, and prices in the segment are rising. Average ticket prices for premium seats across major airlines were up 11 percent compared with the same period last year, according to the Airline Reporting Corporation’s monthly report, which tracks airline ticket transactions.

But lower-income consumers are pulling back. US consumer sentiment is slumping, according to the University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers, which released its Consumer Sentiment Index on Friday.

“Overall, sentiment for lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock portfolios dropped steeply this month, groups that have fewer resources to weather increases in prices,” Joanne Hsu, director of the Surveys of Consumers, said in the release.

Delta’s report comes as the US summer travel season draws to a close, following reports that lower-income travellers would pull back amid rising prices. In May, 51 percent of Americans earning less than $100,000 annually said travel would be one of the first expenses they would cut, according to a report from consulting firm Deloitte.

United Airlines is the next major carrier expected to report earnings, with results slated for after the market close on October 20. Like Delta, United’s stock was down on Wall Street, falling 0.8 percent from Friday’s opening price.

World.title: China Expands Its Military Reach by Building a Base in Laos
World.content:
China has the world’s second biggest military after the United States. The People’s Liberation Army has been expanding rapidly but has taken only limited steps to open bases in other countries: a naval facility in Cambodia and another naval support center in Djibouti, in East Africa.

“Ban Keun is significant because it appears to be China’s first openly acknowledged overseas military facility for air power,” said Ying Yu Lin, an associate professor at Tamkang University in Taipei who studies China’s military. The new facility “sits in the center of the Indochinese peninsula, and could enable the Chinese Communist Party to easily project air power across surrounding areas.”

But for now at least, the Chinese air force presence at Ban Keun is too small and isolated to have tangible military consequences, said Drew Thompson, a former Pentagon official.

“Laos is landlocked, so a base there doesn’t give the Lao or Chinese air force unfettered access to the Indian Ocean or Gulf of Thailand,” said Mr. Thompson, who is now a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. “The threat of a joint Lao-China air force base is primarily political rather than military because it was established without consultation” with Laos’ neighbors.

World.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel to the US and globally.

Trump said the proposed release of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel, in tranches, would see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Ukraine's president criticised the decision, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war between the two countries.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.

He added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have seen attacks by Ukraine.

Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.

The BBC has asked the White House for clarity on what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.

Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.

That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."

An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.

Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, and introduced a ban on diesel exports.

According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.

Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.

But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".

"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.

World.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
World.content:
The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.

The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".

World.title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
World.content:
US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter.

Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that the December execution would go forward as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it".

Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved the live stream plans but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.

Hasan killed 13 unarmed US soldiers at a base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. The firing squad execution would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute former US Army major Nidal Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad in the attack on the Fort Hood base.

Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth explained.

Trump, as he left the White House on Friday, was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists.

"He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people, and he's totally nuts," Trump said. "So I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

The BBC has contacted the Pentagon for more information about the livestream determination.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11". Asked about how his Catholic faith impacted his stance on plans to stream a public execution, Vance cast doubt on whether they would happen.

But he noted that Hasan, who was a US Army psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived".

World.title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
World.content:
Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in PenonomÃ© collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.

Another video showed a local hotel had almost completely collapsed.

Ricardo Brown, who lives in the southern Herrera province, told news agency Reuters that the earthquake had damaged several homes in his neighbourhood of Las Minas.

"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked and we're afraid it could fall on us," the 74-year-old said.

The full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, though several large aftershocks were also reported near the initial earthquake, potentially complicating the situation on the surface.

The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.

Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, and were seen taking to the streets or sitting in nearby parks until the shaking had ceased.

Damage in the capital appears to be limited to that caused by debris falling from roofs.

Panama's President JosÃ© RaÃºl Mulino said his entire government was mobilising in response to the earthquake, adding: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."

World.title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
World.content:
Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.

Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.

Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.

Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".

Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".

Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.

It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".

The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.

The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.

Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.

Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.

Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".

Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".

Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.

Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.

Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

World.title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
World.content:
A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.

The candidate for the centre-left Ahora NaciÃ³n party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.

Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing RenovaciÃ³n Popular PerÃº by just 25 votes.

Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.

Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.

He was born in the district in the central department of HuÃ¡nuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.

That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.

Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba SÃ¡nchez had been elected mayor of YÃºngar in 2018.

He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir RodrÃ­guez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".

A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

World.title: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".

Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃ­a Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom".

Pillay dedicated her award to "all the survivors of international crimes" and the practitioners of international justice "whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".

Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.

She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.

Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president. She was elected to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2003.

From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.

The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.

The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".

The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.

Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".

It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."

World.title: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend
World.content:
Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.

JesÃºs Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs are yet to be sentenced - but they are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a Mexican prison.

Debra Robinson, the brother's mother, told the courtroom in the northern Baja California state the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

During the trial the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico.

Debra Robinson and her husband Martin Robinson have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict.

"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said Martin.

Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link.

Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".

During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs "El Kekas" Gerardo, was sentenced in a separate trial to twenty years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.

At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

Amid the demands for action, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ãvila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state.

"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.

"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

World.title: NCDMB pushes for greater access to assets to boost indigenous participation in energy sector
World.content:
It identified access to assets, financing, technology, and markets as critical drivers of sustainable growth.

The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB) has called on indigenous oil and gas companies to strengthen their capacity and competitiveness in order to thrive in international markets. It identified access to assets, financing, technology, and markets as critical drivers of sustainable growth.

Speaking at the 2026 Energy Conference of the Association of Energy Correspondents of Nigeria (NAEC), held on 8 October at Eko Hotel and Suites, Lagos, the Board’s General Manager of Corporate Communications, Dr Obinna Ezeobi, made the appeal while representing the NCDMB.

He highlighted that the conference theme, “Access to Assets: Empowering Players and Driving Growth,” resonates with the objectives of the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development (NOGICD) Act, which is designed to create meaningful opportunities for Nigerians to participate and excel in the industry.

He emphasised that the Nigerian Content 10-Year Strategic Roadmap, launched in 2017, is built on five core pillars and four enabling factors, with the ambitious goal of raising local content participation to 70 percent by 2027. The roadmap also seeks to expand access to critical assets for skilled Nigerian professionals while strengthening the capacity and competitiveness of indigenous operating and service companies.

Ezeobi highlighted several of NCDMB’s flagship interventions that have enabled Nigerian companies to build capacity, secure financing, and gain greater access to opportunities across the oil and gas value chain. Chief among these is the Nigerian Content Intervention Fund (NCI Fund).

He noted that over 130 indigenous companies have accessed more than US$400 million through the Fund, which is domiciled with the Bank of Industry and NEXIM Bank. He also referenced Project 100, an initiative designed to support high-potential indigenous companies through capacity development, market access, financial linkages, and tailored business support.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Other key programmes include the Nigerian Content Equipment Certification (NCEC), the Nigerian Oil and Gas Parks Scheme (NOGaPS), and vendor development initiatives—all aimed at deepening local participation and strengthening the competitiveness of Nigerian firms.

Ezeobi further explained that the Board is facilitating partnerships between Nigerian and foreign companies, while promoting regional collaboration to help local businesses expand beyond national borders. He expressed satisfaction that Nigerian content in the oil and gas industry has grown from just 5 percent in 2010 to 61 percent after 16 years of implementing the Nigerian Content Act. He stressed, however, that the next phase must focus on equipping indigenous companies with the skills, technology, and business systems required to compete globally.

In his welcome address, NAEC Chairman Ugo Amadi called for expanded opportunities for indigenous companies to acquire and develop oil and gas assets, identifying high entry costs, funding constraints, and lengthy approval processes as major barriers.

PETAN Chairman, Wole Ogunsanya, underscored the need for consolidation and stronger collaboration among indigenous oilfield service companies, enabling them to pool technical capabilities and execute larger projects.

Conference Chairman and Group Managing Director of Sahara Power Enterprise Group, Mr. Kola Adesina—represented by Head of Corporate Communications, Bethel Obioma—emphasized that access must extend beyond ownership to include capital, partnerships, markets, technology, and opportunities. He remarked that “access is actually much greater and more important than assets,” noting that every transformational journey begins with access to ideas, mentors, capital, and partnerships before physical assets.

Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Rt. Hon. Obongemem Ekperikpe Ekpo—represented by Senior Technical Adviser, Engr. Abel Nsa—stressed that Nigeria must move beyond mere ownership of its vast gas resources to their development, financing, and conversion into sustainable economic value. He explained that the Federal Government’s Decade of Gas initiative seeks to transform Nigeria from a resource-rich nation into one that leverages gas for industrialisation, power generation, transportation, manufacturing, fertilizer production, LPG adoption, and other productive uses that drive economic growth.

World.title: The audacity of Enugu’s education transformation, By Peter Mbah
World.content:
I am fascinated by the word – “Audacity”. It suggests courage and a willingness to attempt something that seems unreasonable. So, I want to begin with the circumstances that made our choices in Enugu necessary.

Nigeria is one of the youngest countries in the world. Almost two-thirds of our population is under 30. In that fact lies an extraordinary possibility. This generation could become the greatest engine of growth, creativity and productivity Nigeria has ever known. But there is another possibility. That youth bulge, as I have said before, can become a demographic dividend. Or it can become a demographic catastrophe. And we should be clear about what will determine the difference.

Today, the Nigerian statistics in relation to the world’s out-of-school children is unflattering. Equally worrying is a recent UNICEF report arising from proficiency tests in basic subjects for children at Junior Secondary 2. The report shows that pupils are, more or less, merely going through the motions of learning – without actually imbibing any knowledge.

Think about that. We are not simply dealing with an access crisis. We are dealing with a learning crisis. And it is playing out against a world in which knowledge is becoming more valuable by the day; in which technology is transforming work before our eyes; in which the countries that prosper will increasingly be those capable of creating, applying and adapting knowledge. That is the world into which this enormous generation of young Nigerians is coming.

So, when we talk about transforming education, we are not having an abstract conversation about schools. We are talking about the future productive capacity of this country.

When we came into government in Enugu, we had to look at that reality very closely. We could have repaired the existing system. We could have renovated some classrooms, supplied some desks, put computers into a few schools and called it reform. But we had to ask ourselves a more difficult question: would it be enough? Would an education system essentially designed for the world of 40 years ago prepare an Enugu child for the world of 20 years from now? Our answer was “no.” And once we accepted that, the scale of our response had to change. This is where the idea of audacity begins to acquire some meaning. We did not decide simply to improve the old classroom.

We decided to rethink the nature of education in Enugu entirely. We committed ourselves to building 260 Smart Green Schools, one in every ward of Enugu State. So far, that’s more than 7,000 classrooms built.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

And we deliberately took them beyond the urban centres, into communities where children had too often inherited the quality of education that geography and circumstance happened to give them.

We moved from rote learning towards experiential learning; from memorising the answer towards understanding the problem; towards collaboration, critical thinking, digital capability and the practical application of knowledge.

We put our money behind that conviction. For three successive budget cycles, approximately one-third of our state budget has gone to education. This is an extraordinary commitment of public resources.

But it came from an equally strong conviction: if we are serious about ending poverty, we have to get to its roots. For us, one of those roots is lack of knowledge; lack of know-how; lack of the capabilities through which people create wealth, find employment, build enterprises, participate intelligently in society and determine the direction of their own lives. And the brutal calculation we made was that whatever education costs us today, ignorance will cost us far more tomorrow.

Of course, none of this exists in isolation. A child cannot flourish in a school surrounded by a failing society. So, while we were transforming education, we were also confronting insecurity, rebuilding roads, expanding healthcare, restoring water, modernising transport and creating the conditions in which investment could return.

Over 1,500 kilometres of roads have now been constructed or reconstructed. Across the same 260 wards in which we have placed our Smart Green Schools, we have been building 260 Type-2 Primary Healthcare Centres.

And critically, we have had to find the resources to sustain that scale of ambition. In 2022, before our administration came into office, Enugu State generated approximately N27 billion internally. In 2025, our internally-generated revenue exceeded N400 billion. While tax revenue accounted for N51.5bn or 12.6 per cent, N355.2bn or 87.4 per cent of the total sum came from non-tax revenue, mainly from our investments and the revival, optimisation, and monetisation of our hitherto moribund assets.

Again, this remarkable income growth has not occurred in isolation. We must recognize and compliment the Federal Government’s macroeconomic adjustments and reforms that have created fiscal strength, improved public financing and external buffers. The result is adequate fiscal capacity at the sub-national level.

The point here is straightforward: Transformation cannot survive on aspiration alone. Eventually somebody has to pay for it. What we have attempted in Enugu is therefore not a collection of education projects. It is a change in the entire development model – a quantum leap.

There are moments when incremental improvement is responsible. There are other moments when incremental improvement simply preserves the distance between where you are and where the world is going. We concluded that education in Enugu had reached such a moment.

But let me also say this: building schools is the visible part. Changing an education system is much harder. That’s because, ultimately, a school is only as transformative as what happens between a teacher and a child. And no education system can rise above the quality of its teachers. That may be the single greatest challenge in everything we are attempting.

We are asking teachers who themselves grew up within a particular educational tradition to help us create a different one. For decades, the dominant method was familiar: the teacher stood at the front; knowledge travelled in one direction; children copied, repeated, memorized and reproduced.

Now we are asking something very different of both teacher and learner.

This is a profound cultural change that requires us to build the human capacity to sustain it.

That is why teacher development, continuous professional learning and the work of the Centre for Experiential Learning and Innovation are so important to us. The buildings may be new. But unless the culture of learning changes with them, we will simply have recreated the old system inside more beautiful walls.

Occasionally, however, something happens that allows you to glimpse what all this might become. I had one of those moments recently. Let me share a riveting story:

There is a young boy at our Smart Green School in Owo. He has been there for about two years. Owo is not in metropolitan Enugu. It is the sort of community where, until very recently, a child could have gone through most of his basic education without meaningful contact with a computer.

This boy was recently invited to help train students from other schools. I watched the video. He was standing in front of boys from schools in the city, encouraging them as much as teaching them.

In barely two years, he had learned to use technology confidently, build websites, work with digital platforms and understand how Artificial Intelligence could make him more productive. Now he was passing that confidence on, sort of prodding his audience: “you can do this too. Believe in what you are capable of.”

I had goosebumps watching him. Here was a young boy from Owo, from a community where this kind of access would once have been unimaginable, now showing students from the city what was possible.

Education had not simply given him digital skills. It had changed his sense of his own possibility – and already he was enlarging the possibilities for others. That, for me, is the transformation in action. We must judge the system by what our children know, what they can do, and who they become.

And perhaps it also answers something about what we mean by inclusion. The talent was always there; The intelligence was always there. What was missing was access.

Yet, Distinguished guests, evident transformations do not necessarily erase doubts. I understand such doubts.

If you live in a community where the road is poor, where you need running water, where your immediate concern is feeding your family, a Smart Green School can sound like an elitist luxury.

If you are a teacher who has worked in one way for twenty years, transformation can sound suspiciously like somebody telling you that everything you know is obsolete.

And if you are responsible for public finances, committing one-third of a state budget to education raises a perfectly reasonable question: can we afford this?

I would turn that question around: can we afford not to? If we fix the road today but fail to educate the child who will maintain it tomorrow, how sustainable was our investment in the road? If we build factories but lack the skilled people capable of running increasingly sophisticated production systems, where is our own Industrial Revolution going to come from?

If Nigeria is to become a creation economy rather than a consumption economy — a knowledge economy able to compete, collaborate and contribute to the world — then we must equip our young people not simply to use what the world creates, but to research, design, engineer and create what the world needs.

And if millions of young people reach adulthood without the knowledge and capabilities to participate meaningfully in the economy, what exactly do we imagine the social cost of that will be?

I have never regarded our investment in education as discretionary spending. It is preventative investment in the future stability and prosperity of our society.

There is also something that’s unusual – politically – about education. Much of what governments build can be commissioned within a term of office. Education does not give you that satisfaction.

Some of the three-year-oldsh entering our schools today will not reach the height of their productive lives for another 20 years. I will not be Governor then. Most of us sitting in this hall will never know the full return on the investments we are making now.

I described this recently as a labour of love. We are investing enormous resources belonging to the people in outcomes that may fully reveal themselves only after you have left government.

But that is precisely what leadership sometimes requires. Our responsibility cannot end at the boundary of our tenure. A child’s education lasts far longer than the tenure of a governor or commissioner.

So, I return to the title of this address: “The Audacity of Enugu’s Education Transformation.” Yes. The turn should be that audacity and necessity are not opposites. The deeper you understand the necessity, the more audacious the response has to become.

I’d reshape it like this: yes, perhaps it took some audacity to commit a third of our budget to education. Perhaps it took audacity to attempt 260 Smart Green Schools simultaneously across every ward.

Perhaps it takes audacity to ask an entire education system—government, teachers, parents and children—to step beyond familiar methods and embrace something fundamentally different.

But audacity does not mean acting recklessly. Sometimes it means having the courage to recognise what is necessary — and then acting at the scale that necessity demands.

Because what was the alternative? Nigeria has one of the largest populations of young people on earth. We have enormous ambitions to become a creation economy rather than a consumption economy; a knowledge economy able to compete, collaborate and contribute to the world.

We want to eradicate poverty, create wealth, and enable our young people to build meaningful futures here. How do we achieve any of those things without the knowledge base to research, design, produce and create? That is the connection we must make. And once we make it, audacity becomes necessity.

I believe Nigeria has reached the point where we must treat education as a national emergency. Not rhetorically, but in our budgets, our teacher development, our infrastructure, the standards we demand, and the partnerships we build between the Federal Government, states, development agencies, communities and the private sector.

Our future prosperity depends upon the knowledge and capabilities of our people, after all. And that means every Nigerian child, wherever they are born, must have access to an education capable of preparing them for the world they are entering.

Once we understand that, the question changes. It is no longer: can we afford to make this quantum leap? It becomes: What will happen to us if we do not?

Our demographic dividend could be extraordinary. But that future will not simply arrive. We have to build it. And if Enugu’s experience offers one lesson, I hope it is this: when the scale of the challenge demands a quantum leap, audacity is not a luxury. It is a necessity.

Thank you.

*Being excerpt of the keynote address delivered by the Governor of Enugu, Peter Mbah at the 2026 Enugu State Education Summit themed “Transforming Education for the Future: Leadership, Innovation, Partnership, Financing and Sustainable Reform”

World.title: Abiodun family awards over N100m scholarships to 831 indigent students
World.content:
The family of Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, has awarded scholarships worth over ₦100 million to 831 indigent students across different levels of education under the Gbemiga Abiodun Memorial Education Support Programme, an initiative established to sustain the humanitarian legacy of the governor’s late son.

Governor Abiodun announced this at the third edition of the programme, held at Christ Apostolic Grammar School, Iperu, noting that the initiative had supported a total of 1,277 students since its establishment in 2023.

The governor explained that the foundation was established in honour of his late son, Gbemiga Abiodun, to sustain his passion for helping others, particularly the less privileged.

According to him, the initiative was inspired by Gbemiga’s desire, while alive, to make a positive difference in the lives of others. Following his death, the family resolved to preserve that spirit of generosity through a structured intervention to support indigent students and ensure that financial difficulties did not deprive them of educational opportunities.

Abiodun said the beneficiaries for the 2025/2026 award year were selected from approximately 3,000 applications received through the programme’s online portal.

The beneficiaries comprised primary school pupils, secondary school students, technical college students and students in tertiary institutions, with the scheme designed to promote access to education and ease the financial burden on disadvantaged families.

He disclosed that 150 new beneficiaries were selected for tertiary-level scholarships, while 124 continuing beneficiaries brought the total number of students supported at that level to 274.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The governor also announced additional support for 80 Senior Secondary School students preparing for their examinations and seeking admission into tertiary institutions. The students will receive assistance with registration for the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) and the Senior School Certificate Examination (SSCE), alongside revision and practice sessions through the LEARN MORE WhatsApp platform.

The programme will also sustain engagement with beneficiaries and their parents to provide guidance and support throughout their academic journey.

Abiodun assured that the initiative would be sustained and expanded to enable more disadvantaged students to access quality education, describing it as a practical demonstration of the family’s commitment to preserving Gbemiga’s legacy of kindness and generosity.

He explained that the scholarship scheme, which initially focused on the Remo axis, had expanded to cover all nine local government areas in Ogun East Senatorial District following its success and growing impact.

Highlighting the vocational education component introduced in 2025, the governor said beneficiaries in technical colleges received ₦120,000 each to acquire essential training equipment.

According to him, some beneficiaries had already begun practising their trades, undertaking paid assignments and improving their livelihoods, demonstrating the potential of vocational education to promote self-reliance and economic empowerment.

He further disclosed plans to provide 20 selected beneficiaries with business development training, mentorship and start-up support of up to ₦250,000 each to encourage entrepreneurship.

In another intervention aimed at preparing young people for emerging opportunities, Abiodun announced that 30 selected tertiary institution students would participate in a digital skills development programme covering digital marketing, software development, data and analytics, cybersecurity, and user interface and user experience (UI/UX) design.

The governor called on wealthy individuals and organisations to support efforts to improve access to education for vulnerable members of society, urging the beneficiaries to make the most of the opportunities provided and remain committed to their studies.

The Commissioner for Education, Science and Technology, Prof. Abayomi Arigbabu, commended the initiative for providing academically promising but financially disadvantaged students with opportunities to pursue their educational ambitions.

He urged the beneficiaries to remain focused and disciplined, noting that commitment to their studies would help them realise their aspirations.

Lamisa Abiodun, sister of the late Gbemiga Abiodun, congratulated the beneficiaries and encouraged those in technical colleges to take their training seriously and use the skills acquired to build meaningful and productive lives.

Representatives of educational institutions and some beneficiaries expressed appreciation to the governor and his family for the support, noting that the initiative would ease the financial burden on parents and guardians while helping students continue their education.

In his opening remarks, the programme coordinator, Reverend Bola Oyeledun, said the initiative had evolved from a family’s response to personal tragedy into a programme offering hope and relief to students whose families could not afford the cost of quality education.

He added that the programme, which initially focused on the Remo axis, had expanded to cover all nine local government areas in Ogun East Senatorial District.

World.title: Court gives Abba Kyari, others final chance to file defence witnesses’ list in cocaine trial
World.content:
Judge Emeka Nwite of the Federal High Court in Abuja on Friday gave suspended Abba Kyari and four other police officers facing cocaine charges the final opportunity to file their lists of defence witnesses.

The judge warned that failure to comply could lead to a forced closure of their defence.

He issued the warning after expressing displeasure over the defendants’ failure to obey his 5 October order directing them to submit the names of witnesses they intended to call for their defence.

Judge Nwite said the court’s records showed that none of the defendants had complied with the directive.

“The orders of court must be obeyed,” Judge Nwite said, warning that he would not take violations of the court’s orders lightly.

Mr Kyari, a deputy commissioner of police under suspension by police authorities, is standing trial alongside four members of his now-defunct Police Intelligence Response Team (IRT): Sunday J. Ubua, an assistant commissioner of police; Bawa James, an assistant superintendent of police; Simon Agirgba and John Nuhu, both inspectors.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) accused the five officers of dealing in 21.35kg of cocaine seized from two traffickers at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, on 19 January 2022.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The prosecution also charged them with tampering with the narcotic sustance by removing 17.55kg from it and replacing the portion with another substance.

The agency also accused Mr Kyari, in a separate count, of offering $61,400 to an NDLEA operative to prevent the cocaine from being tested. All five denied wrongdoing.

Final opportunity

Friday’s ruling followed a disagreement over whether the defence could question an officer who appeared in court with a list of NDLEA personnel who were on duty at the Enugu airport when the two cocaine smugglers arrived from Ethiopia.

The defence had sought the list through a subpoena to support its case to show the circumstances under which the two cocaine traffickers passed through airport security before their arrest by Mr Kyari-led IRT on the airport ground.

The subpoena stirred controversy on Wednesday after the prosecution challenged it on the grounds that it was addressed to the NDLEA’s director-general, a position the prosecutor said did not exist at the agency.

The prosecution, however, indicated that an officer would produce the requested document, and the case was adjourned until the following day.

On Thursday, Ojebir Victor, whom the prosecution identified as an assistant commander and principal staff officer in charge of personnel statistics, appeared with the list.

After Mr Victor presented the document and took the witness’ oath, the prosecution and defence disagreed over whether an officer subpoenaed to produce the NDLEA airport duty roster could be questioned.

NDLEA’s prosecution lawyer Joseph Sunday argued that the subpoena required the officer only to produce the document, not to give oral evidence, and that the defence should have obtained a separate subpoena requiring him to testify.

The defence lawyer maintained that the officer could be questioned to clarify the document’s contents.

Judge Nwite reserved his ruling until Friday, 9 October, when he rejected the defence’s position and discharged the officer without allowing cross-examination.

The defence then requested an adjournment to prepare for its case.

Mr Sunday opposed the request, arguing that the officer’s discharge did not prevent the defendants from calling another witness. He reminded the court of its earlier order directing the defence to file its witness lists.

He also urged the judge to restrict the defendants from calling additional witnesses and sought costs over the series of adjournments.

Ruling, Judge Nwite rejected the defence’s argument that the circumstances surrounding an officer who produced a subpoenaed document could excuse its failure to comply with the order.

The judge said the officer’s discharge could not have prevented the defendants from identifying their intended witnesses and filing their lists of defence witnesses.

He decided to all the defendants another opportunity to file their lists of defence witnesses, “in the interest of justice.”

He warned that he could “foreclose” their defence should they fail to comply with his directive by the next sitting on 12 October.

How the case has progressed

The case began in March 2022, when the NDLEA arraigned Mr Kyari alongside four other police officers and two cocaine smugglers on cocaine-related charges.

NDLEA accused them of offences linked to 21.35kg of cocaine seized from Chibunna Umeibe and Emeka Ezenwanne, the two suspected traffickers who smuggled the substance into the country through the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, in January 2022.

The police officers, including Mr Kyari, allegedly tampered with the cocaine after seizing it from the two smugglers who arrived Nigeria from Ethiopia by taking 17.55kg from it and replacing that portion with a look-alike substance.

One of the charges directed solely at Mr Kyari accused him of offering $61,400 to a senior anti-narcotics operative to prevent the testing the cocaine to detect the adulteration.

While Mr Kyari and the four officers pleaded not guilty, Mr Umeibe and Mr Ezenwanne admitted the charges. They were convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment each, terms they have since completed.

The prosecution opened its case against the five officers in July 2022, nearly two months after their arraignment. The NDLEA called 16 prosecution witnesses and tendered about 52 electronic and documentary exhibits.

One prosecution witness, Peter Joshua, an operative of the NDLEA, testified that Mr Kyari offered him $61,400 after he weighed and conducted preliminary tests on the cocaine.

Another prosecution witness, Mohammed Ajia, testified in October 2022 that forensic examinations found that 80 per cent of the substance tested positive for cocaine, while the remaining 20 per cent was another substance.

The prosecution closed its case in July 2024.

In April 2025, Judge Nwite rejected the defendants’ no-case submission, ruling that they had cases to answer and directing them to present their defence.

Mr Kyari opened his defence in July 2025, calling Adeshina Fasasi, a team lead with MTN’s incident management unit, as his first witness.

Subpoenaed at Mr Kyari’s request, Mr Fasasi testified about call data records linked to the suspended police officer.

He told the court that the records did not establish contact between Mr Kyari and a telephone number associated with a suspected cocaine trafficker known as Mike Coke. He also testified that the number saved under the name “Coke” was registered to Ruth Ayuba, not Mr Kyari.

Mr Fasasi explained that MTN’s call data records did not contain the content of telephone conversations, WhatsApp messages or names saved in users’ phone contacts. During cross-examination, he acknowledged that he was not directly employed by MTN Nigeria and had not read the full report tendered before the court.

Defence evidence hits a setback

The second defence witness, El-John Nwonke, a police inspector, started taking the witness stand in January 2026, testifying that he was part of the police team that interviewed convicted Mr Umeibe and Mr Ezenwanne following their arrest at the Enugu airport in January 2022.

Mr Nwonke told the court that the two men had confessed during the interview that NDLEA officers at Enugu airport helped them pass through security checks before they were arrested with the suspected cocaine.

The interview was recorded on a digital video disc. The court admitted the disc in evidence as Exhibit D-3 on 28 February and the defence played the video recording in open court on 16 March. In the recording, the two men alleged that NDLEA officers helped them evade airport security.

Mr Nwonke’s testimony, however, did not reach cross-examination after he repeatedly failed to attend court.

On 29 September, the defence lawyer sought an adjournment, explaining that the witness was outside Nigeria on an official assignment. When he failed to appear again, the defence submitted a letter seeking more time on the grounds that he was ill.

The prosecution opposed another adjournment and asked the court to close the witness’s evidence. Judge Nwite reluctantly granted more time but warned that the testimony would be foreclosed should the witness fail to appear.

Mr Nwonke was absent again on 7 October, prompting the prosecution to renew its request for the forced closure of the witness’ evidence. The judge granted the request, “foreclosing” the police inspector’s testimony and striking out his evidence. The judge said the witness had been given sufficient time to testify and submit to cross-examination.

Consequently, the prosecution did not cross-examine Mr Nwonke on his testimony.

World.title: Alleged Mad Man Comment: Wike asks INEC to sanction Amaechi over inciting, inflammatory remarks
World.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has called on the Independent Electoral Commission (INEC) to sanction Rotimi Amaechi over his recent political utterances, which he described as “irresponsible and inciting”.

The News Agency of Nigeria reports that Mr Amaechi, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice presidential candidate, had on Thursday in Benin City, during the party’s town hall, said that only mad people and thieves would vote for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election.

“I read ‌‌‍‌‍⁠⁠‍‌‍‌‌‌on social media that it is only in 2027 that we will know how many mad men we have in Nigeria. Only a mad man can vote for Tinubu.

“If you are not a mad man, then Tinubu should not win here,” Mr Amaechi was quoted as saying.

Reacting, Mr Wike told journalists after a meeting with FCT area council chairmen and head of security agencies in Abuja on Friday that such ‘irresponsible behaviour’ should not be allowed to go unchallenged.

He expressed disappointment over regulatory inaction on what he called inflammatory statements by the former Minister of Transportation.

“Up till now, I have not heard that INEC has been able to call the attention of Amaechi.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“All of us watched on television yesterday (Thursday) when he said it’s only thieves that can vote for President Tinubu, and that only mad people will go and vote for Tinubu, and that if Edo people vote for him, it means the people are mad,” he said.

Mr Wike condemned the comments, calling them unacceptable for a high-ranking political figure aspiring to national leadership.

“This is supposedly a vice presidential candidate of a political party seeking to take over power and preside over the affairs of this country. Not just an ordinary politician — a vice presidential candidate – telling voters and telling Nigerians that only thieves and mad people will vote for President Tinubu.

“If he continues along this line, it will be difficult for him to campaign in Rivers. We will make it difficult for him.

“You cannot sit down, call voters madmen and thieves, and expect to walk away free,” he said.

The minister expressed deep concern over the rising trend of personal insults and public incitement in campaign rhetoric.

He called on INEC to enforce electoral regulations strictly and hold political candidates accountable for non-issue-based campaigns.

“You see, one problem we have in this country is that agencies or commissions should be able to take their functions seriously.

“Many Nigerians have called on INEC to sanction political parties, candidates or some politicians who, in their campaigns, incite the public or raise matters that are not issue-based.

“We have been told to go on campaigns based on issues—what are you going to do for the people—not on attacking personalities or insulting individuals,” he said.

Mr Wike also scolded media organisations for failing to challenge political candidates when they resort to derogatory attacks rather than discussing policy issues.

Both Messrs Wike and Amaechi are former governors of Rivers State.

(NAN)

World.title: Atiku asks Tinubu to “step down” over economic hardship, says 30-day petrol discount exposes policy failure
World.content:
Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar has accused President Bola Tinubu of worsening Nigeria’s economic hardship, describing the federal government’s proposed 30-day petrol discount as an admission of failure and an inadequate response to the rising cost of living.

Atiku, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) for the 2027 election, said the temporary relief measure could not compensate Nigerians for the years of rising food prices, transport fares, energy costs and declining purchasing power under the Tinubu administration.

He spoke on Friday at the inauguration of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council at the Shehu Musa Yar’Adua Centre in Abuja, where he outlined his economic proposals and called on Nigerians to vote Mr Tinubu out of office in the January 2027 election.

“Bola Tinubu has had more than three years to improve our lives. What has he given us? A bag of food that costs more each time we go to the market. A journey to work that eats up our salaries. A business that cannot keep its lights on. A farm we may be too afraid to visit,” Atiku said.

He argued that the administration had imposed painful economic adjustments on Nigerians without delivering sufficient relief, accusing the president of seeking electoral credit for a temporary intervention after years of rising living costs.

“Bola, your government has made life unbearable and called it reform. You have demanded painful sacrifices from the people while you, your family, and friends are junketing all over the place,” he said.

The former vice president questioned the timing and sustainability of the proposed petrol discount, arguing that a 30-day interventions would do little to address the underlying pressures driving up the prices of goods and services.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He challenged the government to explain what would happen when the discount expires, particularly for commuters, farmers, traders and manufacturers whose operating costs are affected by petrol prices.

“More importantly, you owe Nigerians an answer: what happens on day 31?” he asked.

Atiku also accused the Tinubu administration of adopting his proposed production subsidy after previously criticising the idea, but implementing it in a manner he said stripped it of its intended economic benefits.

He said his proposal would provide targeted support for petroleum products refined in Nigeria and sold to Nigerians, with the intervention capped, provided for in the national budget and subjected to independent audits.

“My production subsidy proposal is a lasting, targeted plan. Yours is a temporary palliative dressed up as a solution,” he said.

The ADC candidate argued that supporting locally refined petroleum products could strengthen domestic refining, reduce dependence on imported finished products and ease the pressure of fuel costs on transport, food production and businesses.

He also called for public disclosure of the cost of the intervention and the savings it generates, insisting that imported finished petroleum products should be excluded from the proposed subsidy.

“Support petroleum products actually refined in Nigeria and sold to Nigerians. Cap the support. Put it in the budget. Audit it independently. Exclude imports. Show the public what it costs and what they save,” he said.

Atiku said his economic relief plan was not limited to petrol prices, adding that a government seeking to improve living standards must also make food affordable, restore reliable electricity, create jobs, secure roads and farmlands, and remove barriers confronting young entrepreneurs.

“A speech about growth means nothing to a family that cannot afford dinner,” he said.

He accused the president of failing to take responsibility for the economic consequences of his policies, arguing that the rising cost of petrol, declining purchasing power and closure of businesses were problems the administration must address rather than blame on previous governments.

The former vice president also urged his campaign council to take the party’s economic proposals to markets, motor parks, farms, campuses and communities across the country, insisting that members must explain both what the party intends to do and how it would finance its plans.

He described the 2027 election as a “rescue mission”, urging eligible voters to use their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) to demand a change in government.

“Another four years of Bola Tinubu means another four years of hunger, hardship and national decline,” he said.

Atiku demands electoral transparency

Beyond the economy, Atiku called for reforms to improve the transparency and credibility of the 2027 general election, arguing that economic recovery would mean little if Nigerians could not trust the electoral process.

He demanded the immediate publication of polling-unit results, protection for political parties and election observers to independently verify results, and the live broadcast of state and national collation proceedings.

He also called for independent audits of election technology before and after elections, as well as the establishment of an independent commission to investigate and prosecute electoral offences.

Atiku said accredited party agents, civil society organisations and election observers should be allowed to operate situation rooms and verify results without being treated as substitutes for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

“Transparency is not a crime,” he said, adding that electoral technology should serve the electorate rather than conceal the process.

The ADC candidate also warned against attempts to restrict opposition parties from campaigning in parts of the country, citing an alleged attempt to prevent an opposition candidate from campaigning in Benue State.

He said the ADC would campaign across the country and challenge restrictions on its candidates through lawful means, including the courts and the ballot box.

“We will campaign in every state, from the creeks to the savannahs, and resist any effort to stop our candidates from reaching Nigerians,” he said.

Atiku concluded by calling on Mr Tinubu to step down, arguing that the proposed 30-day petrol discount could not erase the economic hardship Nigerians had experienced during the President’s tenure.

“Bola, thirty days cannot erase three and a half years of hardship. Nigerians have heard your excuses and endured your failed promises.

“They are ready to judge your record. After this latest admission of failure, the honourable thing to do is step down. Nigerians deserve a government that will do the work and make life affordable again.”

Campaign chairman links economic hardship to rising prices

Earlier, the Chairman of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Kashim Ibrahim-Imam, described the inauguration as the beginning of a political campaign aimed at addressing economic hardship, insecurity, unemployment and the rising cost of living.

He urged council members to see their appointments as a responsibility to Nigerians rather than an opportunity to occupy political positions.

“Let no one mistake this gathering for a ceremony. We have not come here to collect titles. We have come here to begin a rescue,” he said.

Mr Ibrahim-Imam cited food inflation, growing public debt, insecurity and unemployment as evidence of what he described as the Tinubu administration’s failures.

He referred to figures he attributed to the National Bureau of Statistics, putting food inflation in Adamawa State at 38.85 per cent in August 2026, followed by Zamfara at 37.96 per cent and Bayelsa at 36.20 per cent.

The campaign chairman used the figures to illustrate the pressure on households, particularly in states where residents struggle to afford food despite the country’s agricultural and natural resources.

He also criticised the growth in Nigeria’s public debt, saying the country’s total debt had risen from ₦87.38 trillion when Mr Tinubu assumed office to ₦166.79 trillion as of 30 June 2026.

Mr Ibrahim-Imam argued that Nigerians had yet to see sufficient benefits from government borrowing and questioned whether the administration’s economic policies had improved living standards.

He also cited insecurity, including killings, kidnappings and attacks on schools, as reasons the administration should not be returned to office.

The chairman urged the campaign council to mobilise voters across the country and ensure that polling-unit results were protected and counted accurately.

He called on Nigerians to respond to Mr Tinubu’s 2022 campaign slogan, “Emilokan”, meaning “it is my turn”, with “Awalokan”, which he presented as a call for the turn of ordinary Nigerians.

“The Council is inaugurated today. The work begins tonight,” he said.

Akobundu promises issue-based campaign

In his acceptance speech as Director-General of the ADC/Atiku Abubakar Presidential Campaign Council, Austin Akobundu said the campaign would focus on the everyday economic concerns of Nigerians rather than abstract economic indicators.

Mr Akobundu, who represents Abia Central Senatorial District, said the campaign would address the difficulties facing families struggling with food prices, transport costs, rent, school fees and healthcare expenses.

“This is not a ceremonial role. It is a call to lead a campaign for Nigerians who are asking a simple question: How can I afford to live?” he said.

He accused the All Progressives Congress (APC) administration of asking Nigerians to endure economic hardship without delivering the relief promised by its policies.

Mr Akobundu said the campaign would present Atiku as an alternative, with affordability, domestic production, job creation and social welfare at the centre of its agenda.

“Our campaign will make that reality impossible to ignore. We will take people’s experiences seriously, explain how the government’s choices affect their daily lives, and offer a credible alternative,” he said.

The campaign director-general also warned against what he described as intimidation and harassment of ADC members by state agencies and political opponents. He said the party would respond through a disciplined campaign and resist attempts to restrict its political activities.

He further criticised the reported detention of the campaign council’s Deputy Chairman, former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai, describing it as an affront to the rule of law. The circumstances and legal basis of Mr El-Rufai’s reported detention were not detailed in the speech.

Mr Akobundu said the ADC campaign would be guided by respect for the rule of law and would pursue policies aimed at reducing the cost of living and improving access to essential services.

He said Atiku would introduce a targeted production subsidy for fuel refined in Nigeria from the first day of his administration, with the aim of supporting local refining and reducing the country’s dependence on imported finished petroleum products.

He also promised to review the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), pursue student debt forgiveness and make education more accessible and affordable.
