World.title: Nigeria: American Lobbying Firms Disagree Over $57m U.S. Lawsuit Against Tinubu
World.content:
DCI Group has rejected allegations in a $57 million US lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu and others, while Femi Fani-Kayode's office says he has not been formally served.

American lobbying firm DCI Group has rejected allegations made by Washington-based lobbyist Karl Von Batten in a $57 million lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, former aviation minister Femi Fani-Kayode and the firm.

DCI has been hired by the Nigerian government for lobbying activities in the United States, while Mr Von Batten is doing the same work for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office also told PREMIUM TIMES that he had not been formally served with the court papers and maintained his earlier denial of the allegations.



The case, filed at the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on 28 September, concerns allegations of defamation and a conspiracy to kidnap and physically harm Mr Von Batten. The claims are disputed and have not been established by a court.

DCI, Fani-Kayode respond

In an email to PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday, Craig Stevens of DCI Group dismissed the allegations.

"Mr. Von Batten's allegations are so far past unfounded that they reach the point of the absurd," Mr Stevens said.

He said DCI's work for the Nigerian government focused on strengthening relations between Nigeria and US policymakers and referred the newspaper to the firm's disclosures under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Mr Stevens did not address the specific allegations individually.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office, responding separately, answered "No" when asked whether the former minister had been formally served. It also confirmed that he stood by his earlier denial of the allegations.

Mr Fani-Kayode had previously indicated that he would pursue a $100 million counterclaim against Mr Von Batten.

Asked whether the counterclaim had been filed or lawyers instructed to commence proceedings, his office replied: "All in good time."

The response did not confirm any filing.

What the lawsuit alleges

The US federal court docket identifies the case as Von Batten v. Tinubu et al., No. 1:26-cv-03374, before Judge Randolph D. Moss.

The defendants include President Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, Mr Fani-Kayode, DCI Group AZ, LLC, and 10 unidentified persons.

In a public announcement, Von Batten-Montague-York said it was seeking $36 million jointly from President Tinubu and the Nigerian government, $3 million from Mr Fani-Kayode and $18 million from DCI.

The firm alleged that the defendants were involved in efforts to defame, kidnap or physically harm Mr Von Batten over his advocacy concerning US government records relating to President Tinubu.

Close 

The publicly accessible docket records the filing and issuance of summonses, although this does not establish that the defendants have been formally served.

PREMIUM TIMES has requested the complete file-stamped complaint and exhibits to examine the allegations and the damages sought.

Presidency, others yet to respond

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Presidency through Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Information and Strategy, seeking its response to the allegations, confirmation of any formal service and its position on the court's jurisdiction.

The enquiries were sent by email and WhatsApp, followed by telephone contact and reminders.

The newspaper also contacted Mr Atiku's ADC campaign to establish whether the former vice president or his representatives knew about the lawsuit before it was filed and whether they endorsed its allegations.

The campaign was further asked about the status of Mr Atiku's $1.2 million lobbying agreement with Mr Von Batten's firm, payments made and their source.

Mr Von Batten was separately contacted for the full complaint, supporting documents and his response to the denials by DCI and Mr Fani-Kayode. PREMIUM TIMES also sought clarification on the alleged threats, the damages claimed and whether the incidents had been reported to US law-enforcement authorities.

During a telephone call to his firm's office on Thursday, an answering-service representative took the reporter's contact details and said the enquiry would be forwarded.

By the time this report was filed, the Presidency, the ADC campaign and Mr Von Batten had not provided substantive responses.

World.title: Kenya: U.S. Report Flags Kenya's Failure to Act On Officials Linked to Human Trafficking
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya has failed to report meaningful enforcement action against public officials and recruitment agencies allegedly linked to human trafficking, with a new United States report warning that official complicity continues to undermine the country's efforts to prosecute the crime.

The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report said Kenyan authorities investigated three Ministry of Labour officials suspected of accepting bribes to facilitate potential trafficking involving migrant workers travelling to the Middle East, but highlighted broader concerns over alleged collusion between public officials and recruitment networks.

The report also found that the government had not reported action against recruitment agencies allegedly owned by government employees and suspected of facilitating trafficking, with authorities frequently pursuing lesser offences such as failure to register recruitment companies.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes remained significant concerns, inhibiting law enforcement action during the year," the report stated.

The findings raise questions about accountability within institutions responsible for regulating overseas recruitment and protecting Kenyans seeking employment abroad.

Media reports cited in the assessment indicated that more than 10 per cent of Kenyan government officials held ownership interests in private employment agencies, including firms recruiting migrant workers for jobs overseas, creating potential conflicts of interest.

Observers also alleged that criminal syndicates colluded with law enforcement and immigration departments at border checkpoints and airports to transport trafficking victims into and within Kenya.

The report further cited allegations that some Kenyan embassy officials in Saudi Arabia demanded sex or cash payments from women seeking government assistance to escape abusive employers and return home.

The allegations come against the backdrop of declining anti-trafficking prosecutions and convictions.

Kenya convicted six traffickers in 2025, down from 21 in 2024, while prosecutions fell from 44 cases to 14.

The government investigated 43 trafficking cases during the year, compared with 42 in 2024.

The report also detailed allegations involving the fraudulent recruitment of more than 1,000 Kenyan men to fight for the Russian military in the war against Ukraine, with officials reporting that Kenyan and Russian officials had colluded with illicit recruiters to facilitate the recruitment.

Despite the concerns, Kenya remained on Tier 2 in the US assessment, which recognises significant efforts to combat trafficking while finding that the government has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating the crime.

Close 

The report credited Kenya with identifying more victims, repatriating citizens exploited in overseas online scam operations, and securing its first civil judgment against a fraudulent recruiter.

However, it said persistent concerns over official complicity continued to hamper law enforcement and victim identification, while protection services for adult survivors remained limited.

World.title: South Africa: Navi Pillay's Nobel Win Draws Attention To Her Work Defending Media Freedom And Beyond
World.content:
Navi Pillay speaking at the South African National EditorsÂ Forum (SANEF) Nat Nakasa Award for Courageous Journalism in 2022.

Recognised by the Norwegian Nobel Committee for her efforts to promote peace and international law, Navi Pillay is being celebrated by African media, legal and civil society voices for a career advancing justice, accountability and human rights — including the right to report freely and safely.

Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize, announced on Friday, 9 October, is drawing attention to her support for media freedom and a career spanning some of the most consequential developments in international human rights law.

The South African jurist has backed initiatives to strengthen legal protections for free expression and promote a free and pluralistic information space.



Pillay is the fifth South African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, following Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk.

Announcing the Nobel, Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes linked Pillay’s early legal work under apartheid to her later role in international justice, from defending Nelson Mandela and others who opposed apartheid to serving as a judge in major international cases.

The committee said she had helped strengthen the international legal order and institutions responsible for holding perpetrators of serious crimes accountable. It also highlighted the uneven application of international law and the ability of powerful states and leaders to evade responsibility.

“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence," the committee said.

Pillay’s win is particularly being celebrated by the media fraternity in Africa, most of whom are citing her efforts in defending media freedom.

Reacting to the announcement, Moky Makura, executive director of Africa No Filter said Pillay “embodies African agency”.

“For decades, she has worked tirelessly to create the change she wants to see in the world. This Nobel Prize shines a well-deserved spotlight on her extraordinary contribution. It is a reminder that African progress is not always about what is happening, but also about what the world is failing to see,” Makura said.

Churchill Otieno, president of The African Editors Forum (TAEF), also said Pillay’s record held particular significance for journalists because of its emphasis on accountability and the right to report freely.

“From her struggle against apartheid to her work in international human rights and law, she has shown that peace cannot endure without accountability,” Otieno said.

“For us journalists and media workers, her record also speaks directly to the right to report freely and safely. As UN High Commissioner, she called for journalists to be protected from political interference and physical threats. Her recognition affirms that defending human dignity, press freedom and the rule of law takes courage, especially when powerful interests resist scrutiny.”

In February 2025, Pillay delivered the keynote address at the launch of South Africa’s Free Expression Legal Network in Johannesburg. Developed by the South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF), the Press Council, the Campaign for Free Expression and other organisations and legal experts, the network connects journalists and others facing legal threats over their expression with support, including legal representation.

Information and digital rights activist Izak Minnaar notes that Pillay had actively supported the network and advanced media freedom initiatives internationally.

“As the only South African on the global Information and Democracy Commission, she has been spearheading initiatives to support media freedom in South Africa and beyond,” Minnaar explained.

Anton Harber, director of the Henry Nxumalo Foundation, said Pillay had been particularly consistent in defending independent journalism.

“Navi Pillay has stood firm on many human rights issues, but has had particularly clear, strong and consistent views in defence of media freedom and the importance of independent journalism.”

“Whenever called upon to defend the media, she has been quick to stand up and be counted, even when it was not an easy thing to do. Her prize will be celebrated by journalists,” Harber added.

At the network’s launch, Pillay stressed the value of collective action. “If you clap with a single hand, nobody yells for you. But if a lot of people form a network clap, they will be heard,” she said, according to SANEF.

In its statement congratulating her, SANEF recalled Pillay’s call for governments to promote a free press that can “combat disinformation, build public trust and advance the promotion and protection of human rights.”

She also emphasised the need to protect those who help journalists expose wrongdoing. “I would say that such action must also protect media sources and whistle-blowers,” she said, according to SANEF.

Pillay served on the International Commission on Information and Democracy, convened by Reporters Without Borders in 2018. The 25-member commission developed principles for protecting freedom of expression and democratic debate in the global information space. Its declaration described information and communication as a common good and called for freedom, pluralism and reliable information.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award recognised Pillay’s contributions to peace and human dignity in South Africa and internationally.

“She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place,” Ramaphosa said.

Mameltwe Sebei, president of the General Industries Workers Union of South Africa (Giwusa) and an attorney at Lawyers for Human Rights, described the Nobel as recognition of Pillay’s legal career serving oppressed and marginalised people.

Her work defending anti-apartheid activists and involvement in international cases concerning atrocities, including the Rwanda genocide and the occupied Palestinian territory, made the award a source of pride for South Africans, he said.

“Most importantly, this should affirm our commitment to the principles of justice that underpin the work of any lawyer who stands on the side of the oppressed,” Sebei said. “She represents that type of jurist, that type of lawyer, and this Nobel Peace Prize is a well-deserved recognition of that.”

South Africa’s parliamentary Portfolio Committee on International Relations and Cooperation also described the award as a source of national pride, citing Pillay’s contribution to international justice and accountability for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

Na’eem Jeenah, Senior Researcher at Mapungubwe Institute for Strategic Reflection (MISTRA) and political analyst said the award carries significance beyond South Africa.

“This then is an honour not only for South Africa but for the whole of Africa, a continent that is battling with its own conflicts and violations of international law,” Jeenah said.

While he believes the Nobel Prize would not change conditions for Palestinians nor stop the violence in Gaza, it “adds to the body of moral and legal evidence against Israel, including several UN reports (including on genocide), and the ICJ genocide case”.

Born on 23 September 1941 in Clairwood, Durban, to a family of Indian Tamil descent, Pillay grew up under apartheid. She graduated from the University of Natal with a bachelor’s degree in 1963 and an LLB in 1965.

In 1967, she became the first Black woman to open her own law practice in Natal, now KwaZulu-Natal. She represented political detainees and exposed abuses including torture and solitary confinement. In 1973, she successfully challenged restrictions preventing political prisoners from accessing legal counsel, according to South African History Online.

After earning postgraduate law degrees at Harvard University, she became the first Black woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court in Natal in 1995. She also participated in the Women’s National Coalition during the country’s constitutional transition and co-founded Equality Now, an organisation campaigning for the rights of women and girls.

In 1995, Pillay joined the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, established to prosecute those responsible for the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. She became its president in 1999, serving until 2003.

A landmark case during her time on the tribunal was the trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former local official convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity. The tribunal’s 1998 judgment established that rape and other forms of sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part.

Pillay later served in the International Criminal Court’s Appeals Division from 2003 to 2008. She became United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008, serving until 2014, a period that included the Arab Spring uprisings and the Syrian civil war.

Close 

Her later work included international proceedings and investigations into alleged serious crimes. In December 2019, she was appointed an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over alleged genocide against the Rohingya minority. The court confirmed its jurisdiction and ruled the application admissible.

From 2021 to 2025, Pillay chaired the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.

In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel rejected the conclusion. The finding was made by a UN commission of inquiry, not a final judgment by an international court.

The commission’s work highlighted a central challenge for international law: translating findings of serious violations into consequences for those responsible, particularly when powerful states are involved.

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said the award underscored the importance of international law at a time when its institutions face growing pressure.

“Throughout her long career, Navi Pillay has set a high moral example, speaking out and standing up for justice, accountability and the rule of law,” said SIPRI director Karim Haggag.

Haggag said the award also recognised the institutions Pillay had served, warning that powerful states were increasingly resorting to power politics and transactionalism while international law and its institutions faced attack.

South African investigative organisation Open Secrets also welcomed the award, saying it affirmed the importance of international law and its promise of holding human rights abusers to account.

Pillay was a panellist at the first People’s Tribunal on Economic Crime in the arms trade, convened by Open Secrets and civil society partners in 2018. The tribunal sought accountability for arms companies and politicians in the aftermath of apartheid and State Capture.

The announcement also prompted a lighter moment. Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay joked with supporters, “If you clap a little bit louder, I may share this prize with Trump,” according to an amateur social media clip.

World.title: Liberia: 'Stop Following America' - Sirleaf Urges Liberians
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has urged Liberia to reduce its dependence on the United States for policy direction and embrace homegrown solutions that reflect the country's development priorities and national interests.

Sirleaf said Liberia must break away from longstanding patterns of dependency and take greater responsibility for shaping its future through policies, institutions and development strategies suited to its own circumstances.

"We have to stop following the United States of America. Let's join the new era of sovereignty, respectability," the former president declared.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Her remarks signal a call for greater national ownership of Liberia's development agenda, particularly in a changing global environment where countries are increasingly reassessing their political and economic relationships.

Sirleaf made the statement during a brief interview with journalists on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, following her participation in a one-day symposium organized by the Governance Commission on 3rd Street in Monrovia.

The symposium, held as part of activities marking Good Governance Month, was organized under the theme, "Promoting Good Governance Through Accountability and Transparency in Liberia."

The observance was established by presidential proclamation in keeping with the Governance Commission's founding Act of October 9, 2007.

Speaking to journalists, Sirleaf emphasized the need for Liberia to rethink traditional approaches to governance and development, arguing that the country must adapt to changing global realities rather than continue relying on policies and systems developed elsewhere.

Her comments come against the backdrop of Liberia's longstanding diplomatic, historical and development relationship with the United States, a partnership that remained particularly strong during her 12-year presidency.

Sirleaf, who served from January 2006 to January 2018, became Africa's first elected female head of state after defeating George Manneh Weah in Liberia's 2005 presidential runoff election.

Her administration inherited a country devastated by years of civil conflict and prioritized post-war reconstruction, international debt relief, infrastructure development, institutional reforms and the restoration of Liberia's international standing.

During her presidency, the United States remained one of Liberia's major development and diplomatic partners, providing substantial assistance in governance, economic recovery, health, education and security-sector reform.

Sirleaf also maintained close relationships with successive American administrations.

In March 2006, shortly after assuming office, she addressed a joint session of the United States Congress, highlighting Liberia's recovery efforts and appealing for continued international support.

Then-U.S. President George W. Bush visited Liberia in February 2008, while his successor, Barack Obama, hosted Sirleaf at the White House in 2010 and 2015.

The relationship became particularly significant during the 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic, when the United States provided major emergency assistance to Liberia, including medical personnel, logistical support and resources to help contain the outbreak.

Her administration also secured substantial international debt relief and development assistance as part of efforts to rebuild Liberia's economy and strengthen public institutions.

Against this historical background, Sirleaf's latest remarks represent a notable emphasis on national self-reliance by a former president whose administration benefited significantly from close American cooperation.

However, her statement did not explicitly call for Liberia to abandon its diplomatic relationship with Washington or reject international partnerships.

Close 

Rather, her comments focused on the need for Liberia to exercise greater independence in determining its national priorities and developing solutions to its governance and economic challenges.

The former president did not outline specific policy changes or identify particular American-supported programs that Liberia should reconsider.

Nevertheless, her remarks raise broader questions about how Liberia can balance its longstanding relationship with the United States against the need to strengthen domestic institutions, promote economic self-reliance and exercise greater control over its development agenda.

For a country whose reconstruction and development efforts have depended heavily on international assistance, Sirleaf's message places renewed attention on the distinction between maintaining strategic partnerships and relying on external powers to shape national policy.

Her central argument is that Liberia must increasingly take ownership of its future while engaging international partners on terms that reflect its own priorities and interests.

World.title: Daniel Lurie argues progressivism led San Francisco astray on public safety, drug crisis
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said Thursday that the city had lost its way and was focused on the wrong things, arguing that the California city was "entrapped in our progressive values."

"We lost our way as a city," he told CNN's Dana Bash in an interview. "We were focused on the wrong things, and today we're focused on common sense. We're focused on good governance. We're focused on delivering results for the people of San Francisco. I said from day one, public safety was going to be my number one priority. The crisis on our streets, the mental health and drug crisis is another top priority of mine. And I want to get the basics of governance right."

Lurie, a moderate Democrat and heir to the Levi Strauss fortune, was elected in 2024 after defeating incumbent London Breed.

"I mean, we got so entrapped in our progressive values and talking about progressivism, that we weren't taking stock of what was happening on our streets," he told Bash. "We had 810 people die of overdose in San Francisco three years ago. There's nothing progressive about that. There's nothing progressive about 30,000 car break-ins. Everyone had to deal with whether or not their car was going to be broken into," the mayor said, adding that the number of car break-ins had dropped 90%.

SAN FRANCISCO STILL HASN'T RECOVERED SINCE PANDEMIC EXODUS: REPORT

Bash asked Lurie about progressivism again, specifically how he defined the word. The mayor said he supported progressive values, such as taking care of the city's immigrants, and the LGBTQ+ community.

"But, we got to a point where we said, 'Well, it's that person's right to be on the street using drugs,' or is that person — it's okay for someone to just go in and take what they want from a small business," he said.

"In my mind, that's not progressive," Lurie continued. "There's nothing progressive about small businesses having to shutter up because they're a victim of crime over and over again. There's nothing progressive, as I said before, about 810 people dying of overdose. I'm not going to walk by somebody on the street and not do anything anymore."

NEWSOM BLASTS DEMOCRATS FOR THEIR 'VICTIM MINDSET' THAT ENABLED HOMELESS CRISIS

President Donald Trump praised Lurie during a cabinet meeting in March for "really trying" to improve San Francisco since taking office.

"I know they have a mayor who’s trying very hard. He’s a Democrat, but he’s trying very hard," Trump said at the time.

Socialism has been on the rise in the U.S., as several states have seen socialist candidates win their primary elections. In some places, progressive candidates were rejected for more moderate voices as well.

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that even more liberal voices were calling out progressivism.

"Lurie is right, and it’s not just more moderate voices like his calling this stuff out — we’ve seen AOC try to distance herself from ‘Woke 1’ as well," he said. "Some on the left have absolutely allowed themselves to get bullied into silence and, as funny and extreme a case as it was — that is how you get stories like that Massachusetts lesbian bar with the masking debacle."

"Progressive policies are increasingly popular across the country, particularly on economic issues in these hard economic times," Shroff continued. "But there is also a sense that the DSA left can’t get out of its own way and can never be satisfied."

"It’s not popular to say, but there is a real contingent on the left that uses these movements to center themselves and try to control others — beyond actual progressive aims," he added. "That is what Lurie is hitting on here and that is in some sense what happened in SF before his tenure. Yes, we want policies that are pro-family, pro-worker, pro-immigrant — that doesn’t mean letting the loudest voices dictate everything at the cost of a functioning city."

World.title: Tyreek Hill changes divorce battery trial testimony, claiming he didn't push wife but was verbally abusive
World.content:
NFL free agent wide receiver Tyreek Hill spent his second day on the stand of his divorce battery trial admitting to verbally abusing his wife Lakeeta Vaccaro but insisting he had not harmed her physically.

And through the former player's testimony on Friday, the attorneys for Vaccaro have not yet produced incontrovertible evidence of physical violence by Hill against their client.

Instead, what we saw on Friday was Hill on the stand trying to erase a significant problem he created for himself the day before, while Vaccaro's attorneys pressed the issue.

TYREEK HILL DENIES MOST ABUSE CLAIMS BUT ADMITS TO SHOVING WIFE INTO WALL

Hill on Friday morning changed his testimony from Thursday in which he admitted to pushing Vaccaro, which caused a hole in the wall of their Sunny Isle condominium.

"I told her don't you ever touch me again in your life. I pushed her against the wall. And I tried to force her to get off me," Hill testified on Thursday. "I created a hole in the wall, trying to force her to get off me that night."

His testimony on Friday changed to a door caused the hole.

"The door, the main door," Hill told his attorney. "I was trying to evade [Vaccaro], but I'm not trying to harm her or push her against the wall or, like, do anything crazy. As I was trying to evade, I put a hole in the wall with the door."

Hill's attorneys also made sure Hill explicitly denied ever hurting his wife's breasts, which Vaccaro alleged on the stand earlier in the trial.

But Vaccaro's attorneys, on cross-examination, then tried to muddy up Hill further.

The plaintiff attorneys got Hill to admit he spoke in an explicitly insulting manner about his wife to her and some of his friends.

"The language, I'm gonna take that all on this end, I'm not proud of that," Hill testified. "I am ashamed. I don't even go back home because my marriage failed ... The language was terrible. Was terrible. I wish I could have been better in every single moment, but I'm not perfect.

"The only thing I can do is learn from it and move forward and never talk to my co-parent like that again."

Vaccaro's attorneys pointed to multiple instances in which Hill's testimony Thursday contradicted statements he made during his deposition.

They impeached Hill on his testimony that Vaccaro may have had something to do with a house fire at the couple's Southwest Ranches home in Broward County when, in fact, the cause was determined to be a child playing with a lighter.

They attempted to impeach Hill's contention on the stand Thursday that Vaccaro was "stealing" money from the family account.

They impeached Hill on his suggestion on the stand Thursday that Vaccaro had something to do with him performing worse after the marriage than before, making the point it was Tua Tagovailoa throwing the passes and coach Mike McDaniel calling the plays.

"She wasn't calling the plays on the field, but at home she was calling the plays" Hill said, sticking by his guns. "If you got a real good support system at home, that's what's important."

NFL PUTS 'INSPIRE CHANGE' AND 'CHOOSE LOVE' ON FIELDS BUT NOT SO AGGRESSIVE ABOUT ITS DOMESTIC ABUSE ISSUES

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Hill did, however, admit that saying Vaccaro played a role in his diminished performance was his opinion.

"I'm not sitting here blaming wifey for that, bro," Hill said. "I'm not."

Attorneys then impeached Hill's testimony blaming Vaccaro for Hill's mom becoming homeless. In fact, Hill moved his grandmother, which he refers to as his mom, into a hotel.

Vaccaro's attorneys used video from a nanny camera inside the house to try to prove Hill emotionally hurt his wife — and Hill acknowledged that he did.

"In that moment, yes," Hill agreed. "In that moment."

Did Hill want to break Vaccaro mentally, Vaccaro's attorney asked?

"That's not what I wanted to do, bro," Hill replied.

But Hill admitted he verbally abused his wife.

"When you say verbally, you mean with words, right? Hill asked. "Oh, yes sir."

The trial in Miami-Dade County court is ongoing and reconvenes on Monday.

World.title: Texas think tank accuses Houston parent coalition of using 'socialist' tactics to push radical agenda
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A conservative Texas think tank is warning against a Houston education advocacy coalition, accusing the group of using socialist-aligned tactics to push radical policies in public schools.

In a report released by the Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF), researchers argue that Community Voices for Public Education (CVPE) — which presents itself as a grassroots group of parents, teachers and community members — acts as a front for teachers' unions and far-left organizations working to preserve the status quo.

"There are several policies that they're advocating for which are questionable at best, but very harmful," Kate Bierly, campaign director for TPPF's Next Generation Texas Campaign, told Fox News Digital.

WATCHDOG REPORT EXPOSES TEACHERS UNION 'POLITICAL MACHINE' FUNNELING MORE THAN $1 BILLION TO LIBERAL CAUSES

CVPE has been an outspoken opponent of the state's 2023 takeover of the Houston Independent School District (HISD), Texas's largest school district. The Texas Education Agency (TEA) intervened following years of academic underperformance at select campuses — a move that drew sharp accusations of political overreach from critics.

State metrics, however, show noticeable academic gains since the intervention. Reading and math scores on the State of Texas Assessments of Academic Readiness (STAAR) improved among grades 3 through 8 over the past three school years, while the number of A- and B-rated campuses in HISD jumped from 93 to 197.

SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'

"F-rated campuses went from 56 to five, and the whole district moved from a C rating to a B rating," Bierly said. "The results were amazing. But from this, several critics emerged ... suggesting destructive replacement policies. One of the main groups behind these proposals is CVPE."

The local group, Bierly said, uses tactics similar to those employed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which has gained traction in recent years as a political force with the election of several DSA-endorsed candidates across various levels of government.

DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY'

Beyond opposing the state takeover, CVPE advocates against mandatory STAAR testing and urges parents to boycott the exams. The group also calls for divesting from campus policing — ending student arrests except in severe cases such as murder — and encourages participation in walkouts and political protests.

TPPF contends that CVPE actively instructs parents on how to organize student demonstrations outside schools, while CVPE maintains that peaceful advocacy is essential to improving school environments and curricula.

"Some of the things they are advocating for is that parents should boycott the STAAR exam because the test allegedly supports racism and inequality," Bierly added. "Scrapping this testing removes a key pathway for low-income kids to access advanced academic tracks."

FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS

CVPE defends its platform, maintaining that restorative justice and expanded mental health resources foster safer learning environments than punitive measures, insisting "HISD students should be heard and not herded."

Ruth Kravetz, co-founder of CVPE, pushed back on both TPPF’s report and the state's academic claims. Speaking to Fox News Digital, Kravetz dismissed assertions that her group relies on DSA tactics, emphasizing that CVPE supporters span the political spectrum.

"Some of those parents are Republicans. Some are Democrats, some are socialists, and some are unaffiliated," Kravetz said.

POWERFUL TEACHERS' UNIONS SHARE STRIKING LINK WITH STATES STRUGGLING TO TEACH KIDS TO READ

Kravetz also criticized high-stakes standardized testing, arguing that it fails to improve student outcomes.

"It undermines educational quality," Kravetz said. "It narrows instruction and reduces deeper, more meaningful learning ... I don't think any parent ever said, ‘I hope my kid grows up to be able to fill in a multiple-choice test well.’"

Kravetz previously challenged the "Texas Miracle" touted by HISD Superintendent Mike Miles and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, alleging that recent test improvements were artificially-engineered.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The truth is that HISD’s Mike Miles didn’t allow qualified students to even take Algebra I," Kravetz said. "This skewed the STAAR results and played a shell game with scores. Most importantly, they denied opportunities to countless kids just to make the numbers look better."

HISD did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

World.title: Trump eases Russia sanctions, says Putin will release diesel as prices spike
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin would “immediately” release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel onto the global market.

Trump made the announcement on Truth Social and said the action would will help bring diesel prices down.

Since its illegal invasion of Ukraine, wide-ranging sanctions have been applied to Russia. In order to get the diesel fuel moved, the Treasury Department simultaneously announced Friday that it would be easing sanctions on Russia through April 7.

“Today, at President Trump’s direction, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market,” the Treasury Department said on X.

A document posted to the Treasury’s website said that “the sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation into the United States, of diesel fuel of Russian Federation origin are authorized through 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time, April 7, 2027.

In a separate statement, Putin said that he had informed Trump of Russia’s “readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.” Putin did not offer any specifics, however, such as when a potential release would begin or how much fuel it would entail.

Since the start of the Iran war in February, the price of diesel fuel has soared almost 70%, and economists have warned that the price hikes will have wide-ranging inflationary effects on the global economy.

In recent weeks, sharp escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war have caused diesel to spike even further, and for multiple weeks the price of diesel set repeated all-time records.

World.title: Food pantries overwhelmed by Trump cuts
World.content:
“There’s a decent chance we could run out,” said Likens, who runs the food pantry in Dunlow as director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, a small brick church he attended growing up.

“I don’t want them to sit in that line and not get anything,” he said. “But I don’t have a lot of extra food these days.”

Increasingly, the job of feeding the nation’s hungry is falling on the shoulders of everyday Americans like Likens, who have become the last bulwark against hunger in a land of plenty.

Likens and others on the front lines of feeding their neighbors say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. Food distribution programs are getting less food from federal programs to feed the hungry after cuts by the Trump administration. At the same time, restrictions on food stamps from the Republicans’ “big, beautiful bill” have driven up demand, while rising gas prices because of the Iran war have cut into the budgets of households and food banks alike.

Bill Likens, director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, grew up hungry in Dunlow. Now he works to make sure that doesn't happen to other kids. Mike Belleme for NBC News

The challenges extend far beyond Appalachia. An NBC News survey of 48 of the largest food banks across 35 states and Washington, D.C., found that nearly three-quarters said more people are showing up at their doors over the past year, from workers on their lunch breaks to older adults overwhelmed with medical expenses. At the same time, more than 80% said the food and funding they received through the U.S. Department of Agriculture had dropped and they were struggling with higher fuel costs for transporting food.

In Maine, Good Shepherd Food Bank said the USDA cut the amount of food it received from 13 million pounds to 9 million pounds in one year. A Michigan food bank, Forgotten Harvest, said it’s handing out less food to make sure there is enough to go around: one bag of potatoes instead of two, two tubs of yogurt as opposed to six.

“People are facing multiple hits to their budgets,” said Poonam Gupta, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a think tank that researches social and economic issues. “It is really difficult to find a way to continue affording a healthy and nutritious and balanced diet when you just have these constant hits.”

Food banks’ struggles started in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term when officials cut a $400 million Covid-era program to supply food banks with food from local farmers and paused an estimated $500 million in other planned food purchases by the USDA. Funding from Congress for a separate decades-old program to supply food banks with emergency food assistance has increased over the past several years, but many food bank leaders said they’re still getting less overall than during the Biden administration.

We want to hear from you Have you been affected by changes to the SNAP/food stamp program? Share your story here.

Trump also signed into law the new restrictions on who can receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, or food stamps, requiring nearly all able-bodied adults not caring for young children to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month. Since the law was enacted, more than 5 million people, including at least 1 million children, have lost their food benefits.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the administration’s policies, saying Trump is “uplifting every American’s financial situation” through tax cuts and efforts to increase jobs and business investments.

“President Trump is strengthening SNAP for the Americans who need it by ensuring these programs are sustainable for future generations,” Kelly said, including measures to “crack down on waste, fraud and abuse.”

World.title: Early vote analysis: Mail ballot concerns are changing how Democrats vote
World.content:
Democrats are changing how they vote, requesting fewer mail ballots than in past elections but returning the ones they do request more quickly, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the early vote conducted in coordination with the University of Pennsylvania.

The findings, which come less than four weeks before Election Day, reflect a midterm landscape shaped by concerns about mail-in voting and doubts about the reliability of the U.S. Postal Service. The shift among Democrats suggests they may be abandoning mail ballots in favor of in-person voting, or taking precautions to ensure their ballot arrives on time.

The implications could be significant. Since 2020, Democrats have been far more likely than Republicans to vote by mail, creating predictable patterns in how early election tallies shift as additional votes are counted. But if those habits are changing, it will be more difficult to gauge which party has more enthusiasm from early voting figures, while the now-familiar red and blue “mirages” seen on recent election nights could unfold differently.

For the analysis, we compared current and historical data on mail ballot requests and returns at the same point in time across four states: North Carolina, Georgia, Virginia and Pennsylvania. We gathered publicly available data from three states and sourced Virginia data from L2, a leading voter data firm.

Trump order supercharges concerns about the Postal Service

President Donald Trump has long attacked mail voting as rife with unfounded claims of fraud. Heading into the midterms, his administration exerted increased control over the Postal Service, whose slowed delivery times had already prompted voting rights groups and Democrats to push their voters to consider using other methods of voting.

Just months before the first mail ballots of the midterm elections were scheduled to go out, the Postal Service followed a Trump directive to impose new rules about how election officials could send those ballots to voters. The new requirements will ultimately not apply to this year’s midterm election, but the high-profile legal battle magnified worries about the reliability of the Postal Service.

Confidence that the Postal Service would deliver mail ballots on time plummeted among Democrats from 86% before the 2024 election to 60% now, according to polling conducted by Marist in September, just after the Supreme Court blocked the new Postal Service rules from going into effect. Confidence among Republicans remains unchanged. Meanwhile, more Democrats said they planned to vote in person this year than said the same at this time in 2024, according to NBC News polling.

The early vote data we examined suggests that what these Democratic voters may actually do is dependent on when voters may request mail ballots in each state.

In some states, voters may join a permanent list of mail voters or an annual list at the start of each year. If voters could request their ballot long before concerns about the Postal Service became national news, Democrats are still voting by mail, but taking steps to get those ballots back to election officials more quickly, the analysis shows.

But if Democrats face the choice about whether to request a mail ballot only after the Postal Service challenges, it’s more likely that ballot requests are down from previous election years.

Changing early voting patterns

In North Carolina, where the Senate race is poised to help decide control of the chamber, registrants typically apply for a mail ballot in the months before each particular election. As a result, few individuals had requested mail ballots for the upcoming midterm before the Postal Service attempted to impose its new rules.

So far, Democrats in the state are both less likely to request and more likely to return mail ballots compared to 2022, the most recent midterm election year. The decrease is larger among Democratic registered voters at 40% than among Republican registered voters or independent or third-party registrants at 18% and 23%, respectively. Further, the Democratic registrants who have requested mail ballots are more likely to have already returned them in 2026 (22%) than in 2022 (17%).

In Georgia, a state with competitive Senate and gubernatorial contests and a similar mail ballot request policy, we see the same pattern. While it’s not possible to directly replicate the North Carolina analysis because registrants in the state do not declare a party of registration and domestic mail ballots only went out this week, we can use how each precinct voted in 2024 as an approximation of the partisanship of voters.

As in North Carolina, the analysis shows that mail ballot requests are down more in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Kamala Harris (52%) than in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Donald Trump (39%).

The story is different in Virginia. Unlike North Carolina or Georgia, Virginia allows registrants to 

But as in Georgia and North Carolina, Democrats are returning their mail ballots faster. In the most Democratic precincts, 69% more ballots were returned at this point in the 2026 election compared to 2025, compared to 5% fewer returned ballots in the most Republican precincts.

One advantage of analyzing Virginia is that it is one of the few states with a significant amount of early in-person voting at this point in the electoral calendar.

Relative to 2025, there are more early in-person ballots already cast in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Harris (+10%) in 2024 than in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Trump (-14%). But only a small portion of this increase is caused by people shifting from voting by mail to voting early in person, so it does not explain most of the increase in early in-person voting.

Still, the relatively higher rate of people voting early in person in Democratic precincts compared to Republican precincts suggests that most Democrats who are shifting away from mail balloting, including in North Carolina and Georgia, may move to voting in person rather than not voting at all.

Finally, consider Pennsylvania, which maintains an annual list for mail ballot applications. Of the four states analyzed, it had the highest share of ballots cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election — 27%, versus Virginia at 11%, North Carolina at 5% and Georgia at 5%.

When registrants request a mail ballot in Pennsylvania, they are permitted to request a mail ballot for every subsequent election in that calendar year. Many registrants who request a mail ballot for the May primary election also request a mail ballot for the upcoming general election.

As in North Carolina and Georgia, there are fewer mail ballot requests from Democrats at this point in 2026 than in 2022. However, there is no difference among Democrats requesting mail ballots by May. Instead, the decline is concentrated among mail ballot requests after May, likely reflecting the increased uncertainty about the Postal Service since the summer.

Further, consistent with the other findings, Democrats are returning their mail ballots faster than in the past. A higher percentage of mail ballots requested by registered Democrats have already been returned (20%) than at this same point in 2022 (15%).

Why changing voting habits could complicate election night analysis

These changes in Democratic voting behavior present two challenges for election analysts: determining what the early vote data reveal about voter enthusiasm, and understanding what’s happening on election night as results are processed.

At this point, it is difficult to use the initial mail ballot data to gauge each party’s likelihood of success.

The relative decline in mail ballot requests could be interpreted as a sign that Democrats have less momentum heading into the midterm election than current polling indicates. But Democrats may also be shifting from voting by mail to voting in person, as the findings in Virginia suggest.

Conversely, the relative increase in mail ballot returns among Democrats might mean the party’s voters are particularly enthusiastic about the upcoming election. But this pattern is also consistent with these Democrats returning their mail ballots faster to address concerns about Postal Service slowdowns.

Observing who casts early in-person votes over the next several weeks will help test these competing narratives. Still, we won’t have a clear picture of voter enthusiasm until we see who turns out on Election Day.

Beyond that, our findings underscore the need for caution when interpreting early voting data and election-night results.

Analysts often rely on voting patterns from past elections as key benchmarks to assess how each party is performing on election night. But if more Democrats vote in person, or get those mail ballots in faster, the timing of when Democratic votes are reported and counted could change in important ways. Thus, what may seem to be either a Democratic over- or under- performance on election night could instead be the reflection of the election landscape shifting once more.

World.title: James Talarico back on the trail after absence with flu drew scrutiny
World.content:
After drawing scrutiny for his absence from the campaign trail, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who had been sick with the flu, returned to the stump in Texas on Friday.

“James Talarico is back on the campaign trail talking to voters at Austin City Limits,” Talarico campaign spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement.

Social media posts showed Talarico walking on the grounds of the festival on Friday.

Talarico revealed on Sept. 30 that he was sick, when he had to appear virtually instead of in person at a forum. His prolonged absence drew daily scrutiny from his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Paxton’s campaign asked for “proof of life” and called on Talarico to produce a photo of himself and a newspaper with a current date. Republican Sen. Ted Cruz poked fun on social media, featuring a milk carton with Talarico’s face with the word “MISSING.”

Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser and, according to his virtual remarks to the Hispanic Business Council the following day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.

Then, Talarico appeared visibly ill, blowing his nose and coughing through the event.

“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”

His absence from the trail in the crunch time of the election prompted some consternation among Democrats.

“Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

World.title: Vance suggests Fort Hood shooter’s execution won’t be livestreamed, contradicting Hegseth
World.content:
Vice President JD Vance suggested Friday that the federal government would not livestream its planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad, contradicting the plan announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“First of all, I’ve seen these announcements. I don’t know that that’s going to happen,” Vance told reporters while traveling to a campaign event in Ohio.

He said that if the execution, which is scheduled for December, is livestreamed that he wouldn’t watch it.

00:42 Vance says he would not watch livestreamed execution 00:00 00:00

“But what I try to remind people is: look, this is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” the vice president said.

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a shooting at Texas’ Fort Hood Army base in 2009.

While visiting the USS Abraham Lincoln as it docked in San Diego on Thursday, Hegseth told conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice that Hasan is “going to get a firing squad of soldiers, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.”

It wasn’t immediately clear Friday why Vance contradicted Hegseth. The White House and Pentagon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Nidal Hasan in court in 2015. Bell County Sheriff's Department

The decision to publicly show Hasan’s execution has been met with intense backlash from both some Republicans and many Democrats.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who has said he is considering a run for president in 2028, opposes broadcasting the execution.

“If it were me, I wouldn’t televise it or publicize it or whatever they’re doing,” Kennedy said Friday while campaigning with GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Sterling Heights, Michigan. “I just think it makes — it makes our society coarser, and I wouldn’t do it. But there are arguments, you know, on both sides.”

Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, wrote in a post on X Friday, “Seneca warned that Rome’s bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them. A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” he said. “Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”

Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., a frequent Trump critic, said in a post on X Thursday, “Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote, “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”

Rep. Ann Wager, R-Mo., wrote, “Justice will be served, but the United States of America does not and should not livestream executions.”

Reps. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., and Tom Barrett, R-Mich., who are among the most vulnerable GOP members seeking re-election in November, posted similar sentiments on X.

“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision. Nidal Hasan is an evil person. He betrayed our country, killed 13 American soldiers, and wounded dozens more at Fort Hood — a place I trained the year before his brutal attack,” Barrett wrote. “That does not change the fact that our American values should strive to elevate human dignity. Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.”

Bresnahan said the live stream should not happen. “The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he wrote.

The military’s last execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old girl in Austria. The military last executed someone by firing in 1945, when it put Pvt. Eddie Slovik to death after he was court-martialed for desertion during World War II.

World.title: State Department IG probing Kimberly Guilfoyle amid alleged $100,000 demand
World.content:
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and the embassy she leads are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News.

The government watchdog’s probe comes as legal consultant and longtime Donald Trump supporter and donor Eric Deters has accused Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 confirmation hearing in exchange for access to senior administration officials.

“She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview Thursday.

“She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he said of Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, Trump campaign surrogate and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr.

Deters provided NBC News with a PDF document of texts and Signal messages with Guilfoyle, which were first reported Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal. The Daily Mail first reported the watchdog investigation.

One of the messages provided by Deters appears to show Guilfoyle instructing him to wire the money directly to American Express because “it won’t show up anywhere” that way. He said he did not pay her the money.

An attorney for Guilfoyle did not respond to a request for comment, but told the Journal she disputed the authenticity of the messages while not providing specifics.

Vice President JD Vance said Friday that “these are accusations” and “we don’t try people in the court of public opinion.”

Deters’ claims, he said, are “one person’s story.”

“Let’s actually see what the facts are. Let’s see what the truth is, and obviously if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said.

The White House had no comment.

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio last week asking for more information about additional allegations that appeared in The Wall Street Journal.

On Thursday, Rubio chided a reporter for asking him about the accusations against Guilfoyle while he was with her in Athens.

“We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you,” he said, adding: “I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.”

A senior diplomatic official, meanwhile, said the news of probe set off alarm bells throughout the State Department. The official described the investigation as rare and said that watchdog is known primarily for performing routine embassy inspections rather than investigations.

A spokesperson for the State Department inspector general’s office said the watchdog does not confirm, deny or comment on investigations.

The State Department declined to comment on the accusations against Guilfoyle or any investigation.

Watchdog investigations into potential ethics violations by U.S. ambassadors are rare, but not unprecedented.

During the first Trump administration, Woody Johnson, then the U.S. ambassador to the U.K. and a longtime Republican donor, was investigated by the State Department’s inspector general, who found he made “inappropriate” comments on race, gender and religion to embassy staff.

The State Department rejected recommendations for Johnson, saying he had watched a government video on workplace harassment and instructed senior officials to do the same, and also encouraged staff to take a training course on “mitigating unconscious bias.”

Under President Joe Biden in 2024, the watchdog investigated U.S. Ambassador to Singapore Jonathan Kaplan, finding the political appointee threatened his staff and failed to submit about $48,000 in travel expenses on time or with proper documentation.

In Kaplan’s case, State said it was taking the recommendations seriously and made organizational changes.

“The president always wants his representatives ... to manage people with dignity and respect,” former White House National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said at the time. “He’s comfortable that the State Department is taking this seriously.”

World.title: Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Conservative commentator Katie Zacharia will be named the next White House press secretary, replacing Karoline Leavitt, President Donald Trump confirmed Friday.

Katie Zacharia on Dec. 14, in Franklin, Tenn. Terry Wyatt / Getty for 2521 Ent. and Angel Studios

“It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration.”

Zacharia wrote in her own post on Friday that the appointment is “the honor of a lifetime.”

“Thank you to President Trump for the distinguished privilege of serving as White House Press Secretary,” Zacharia wrote on Truth Social. “The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day.”

Zacharia added that she looks “forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out.”

Two White House officials and a source familiar with the decision first told NBC News about the selection earlier on Friday.

Zacharia currently serves as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group, which runs President Donald Trump’s Truth Social website. She also briefly worked for the Department of Homeland Security in a communications role earlier this year, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Trump wrote on Friday that Zacharia was also involved in his campaigns, “assisting in key Swing States.”

“She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump wrote.

The New York Times was first to report the selection.

She will replace Leavitt, who left the White House in late August. Fox News announced this week that it had hired Leavitt as an on-air contributor.

Zacharia wrote Friday that “following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting.”

Trump also praised Leavitt in his post on Friday, writing, “Katie is replacing the fabulous Karoline Leavitt, who did a fantastic job as Press Secretary.”

Trump, of late, has complained that his accomplishments are being overshadowed ahead of the midterm elections because of poor public relations efforts.

“Our country has never done better. We cannot get the word across because of the fake news and because ... we’re doing a great job in running the country, but we’re not doing a good job of public relations,” he said at a rally in Durant, Oklahoma, last week.

The day before that, at a Hispanic Heritage Month event in the East Room, Trump acknowledged that he has done a bad job of discussing how “well” the country is doing.

“I’ve done a very bad job of explaining how, how good the country is doing,” he said, later adding: “We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion, and an extremely great job of running the country.”

Zacharia’s start date and other details have yet to be announced.

She is a regular presence on conservative media, including appearances on Fox News, Fox Business and Newsmax, and she often defends the Trump administration on her X account.

Zacharia lives in California and has four children. She earned a law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law and serves as a member of its dean’s council.

World.title: Judge strikes down DOJ's policy of reviewing state voter rolls
World.content:
A federal judge has struck down the Trump administration's plan to check state voter rolls against federal immigration databases, a blow to the administration's election-related efforts in the run-up to the midterms.

In a 78-page ruling, D.C.-based U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan wrote Friday that the Justice Department "cannot run roughshod over longstanding laws that were carefully crafted to protect the rights of the American people."

The Trump administration has mounted a nationwide push to obtain complete voter rolls from every state, including sensitive information about registered voters. The Justice Department has argued the information is needed to ensure states are complying with two federal voting laws — the Help America Vote Act and the National Voter Registration Act — which aim to ensure states have programs in place for maintaining accurate voter rolls.

Eighteen states fully cooperated with the Justice Department's request for voter files, Sooknanan said. The department has brought lawsuits against most other states, and has lost almost all of the suits, according to a CBS News analysis. One state settled with the federal government.

The ruling applies to the voter files that the Justice Department has already received, as well as the files it is still litigating over.

Sooknanan rejected the Justice Department's argument that it has legal authority to demand voter lists, compare those lists against citizenship databases and urge states to remove voters who it claims are ineligible to vote. The judge also said the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Privacy Act, and said the federal databases could contain "inaccuracies."

"Today's decision does not prevent the federal government from taking lawful steps to support states' efforts to maintain accurate voter rolls. Neither does it prevent states from maintaining their own voter rolls. And to state the obvious, the Court's decision does not pave the way for ineligible voters to vote in our elections," Sooknanan wrote. "Rather, the Court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more — a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans."

She continued: "The challenged policy represents the federal government's attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always placed it: with the states."

The legal challenge against the voter roll policy was brought by advocacy group Common Cause and individual voters.

Common Cause CEO Virginia Kase Solomón called the ruling "a victory for voters and yet another loss for the Department of Justice" in a statement Friday.

A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency is reviewing the decision.

Under the Trump administration, the federal government has sought a larger-than-usual role in elections, which are typically administered by states with some regulation by Congress. President Trump argues more federal scrutiny is necessary in order to prevent noncitizens from voting and curb fraud — though most election experts say fraud and noncitizen voting are extremely rare.

The government's push to run state voter rolls through the Department of Homeland Security's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database has faced court setbacks, as more than two dozen judges have denied the Justice Department's requests to compel individual states to share their voter lists.

Sooknanan also ruled in June that the Trump administration's overhauled SAVE database — which includes data from the Social Security Administration — was created unlawfully. The Supreme Court temporarily paused that ruling last month.

In practice, the impact of recent court rulings on the November midterms could be limited as federal law bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters from their voter registration lists within 90 days of an election.

Another Trump administration policy that set new rules for the U.S. Postal Service's handling of mail-in ballots was also blocked in the courts, with the Supreme Court declining the government's request to allow the rules to take effect.

World.title: Trump creates committee to investigate Fed's Lisa Cook
World.content:
Washington — President Trump established a committee to look into allegations that Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, made false statements on mortgage documents, the latest step in his renewed effort to fire Cook from her post with the central bank.

The president signed a memorandum, dated Wednesday, creating what he said is a "committee of inquiry" that will be made up of three members: the assistant to the president for economic policy, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and head of the Office of Government Ethics.

After conducting its investigation into Cook, the committee will report to Mr. Trump whether there is "cause" to remove her from the Fed Board. The three-member panel will hold an in-person hearing at the White House on Nov. 5 to "consider the evidence and allegations" against Cook, according to the memorandum. The hearing will not be public, but will be transcribed, the White House said.

Cook has the opportunity to submit a "written position statement" to the committee in response to the accusations against her and can appear at the proceeding, the president's memorandum stated.

"Governor Cook may present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations," it continued. "The Committee may also question Governor Cook about any representations she or her counsel make during the hearing, or it may authorize its representatives, including Department of Justice personnel, to conduct that questioning."

Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, Cook's lawyers, said she "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her."

"In light of the President's repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook — regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law. But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," they said in a statement. "We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise."

The president's creation of the committee to investigate the claims against Cook appears to be the latest attempt by Mr. Trump to ensure any effort to fire her can stand up to legal scrutiny. The president first attempted to oust Cook from the Fed last year after a senior member of his administration, Bill Pulte, claimed she made false statements on mortgage documents related to two properties before she joined the central bank.

Cook challenged her removal, arguing that it violated federal law, which allows a president to remove a member of the Fed's board "for cause."

The Supreme Court ruled in June that Cook could continue serving in her post while her legal challenge to her purported removal continued. In a 5-4 decision, the high court found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law — specifically notice and the opportunity to respond to the allegations before she was fired.

"That is not to say that a Federal Reserve Governor is entitled to an audience with the President or a fullblown judicial trial," Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority. "Instead, all that is required is notice 'to the officer of the charges made against him' and 'an opportunity to be heard in his defense.'"

Roberts continued: "We see no reason why that opportunity 'may not be had on written materials only,' with no oral presentation. All that is required is 'the right to support his allegations by argument however brief, and, if need be, by proof, however informal,' before a final decision is made."

Mr. Trump mounted another attempt to fire Cook after the Supreme Court ruled in her favor. In a letter to the Fed governor in August, the White House informed Cook that Mr. Trump was considering removing her because of the mortgage-fraud allegations and laid out the claims against her. The White House also set a deadline for Cook to respond.

Cook denied the accusations and argued in a response to the White House that she has "never committed mortgage fraud." Lowell, Cook's lawyer, said that attempting to remove her on the basis of the mortgage-fraud allegations would "ignore the facts and the law."

World.title: "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" guests for Oct. 11, 2026
World.content:
Here are the guests for Sunday, Oct. 11, on CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan":
