World.title: A Newfoundlander got a random call from a bunch of Hollywood stars — and just went with it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | The importance of chatting with strangers: The Current 9:54 Jax Irwin’s “best wrong number” she’s ever called

Paul Matthews was at home washing blueberries in Brigus, N.L., last month, when he got a call from a woman he didn’t know. He told her she’d called a wrong number, but then they started chatting — and Matthews stayed on the line.

“Why not?” Matthews told The Current on Friday. “I'm just picking through blueberries and life is good and I'm just relaxed.”

The woman said her “chubby fingers” must have dialled the wrong number — but that was a fib. On the other end of the line, it was really Jax Irwin, a broadcaster who makes viral videos cold calling phone numbers on the East Coast, just to chat.

On that particular day, she was calling random numbers to film a promotional video with the cast of a new Netflix show, Below , filmed and set in Newfoundland and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton and Mackenzie Davis.

“We wanted to stay true to calling completely random numbers,” Irwin told The Current.

“Mackenzie and Charlie and Josh, they've spent, obviously, a lot of time in Newfoundland. So they were equally pleased, excited, and also familiar with how lovely folks from Newfoundland can be.”

I couldn't have asked for a better person to pick up the phone Jax Irwin

Matthews delivered. They chatted about Brigus, its beautiful rock walls and winding paths. He told her he used to be the town’s deputy mayor but was getting older now. When Irwin called him a mover and a shaker, he said these days he’s “moving slower and shaking more.”

But Matthews had his own surprise in store. He’d heard an interview with Irwin on The Current , just the week before.

“I was listening to CBC Radio and they had this lady on and she does this as a sort of a hobby, she cold calls people,” he told her that day, prompting a stunned Irwin to respond: “Can I tell you a secret? That's that lonely woman who calls people, calling you right now.”

“I wouldn’t be surprised," Matthews replied.

Irwin told The Current she “couldn't have asked for a better person to pick up the phone.”

Netflix released the video of their call on social media this week, where it’s already racked up almost 900,000 views across TikTok, Facebook and Instagram.

Matthews said he’s had a lot of calls and texts from family and friends who’ve seen the video. He joked he might need to hire a publicist.

“I think I am on second nine of the 10 seconds of fame,” he laughed.

Newfoundland has its 'own type of magic'

Below, which premiered this week on Netflix, stars Hartnett as a fisherman in a small Newfoundland town that is terrorized by an unknown sea creature.

Harnett spoke to CBC Radio’s Q this week and said the people of St. John’s really helped him prepare for the role, from a fisherman who showed him how to tie nets, to locals who taught him how to properly use “skeet” in a sentence.

“You get this sort of feeling of being in a place that has its own type of magic,” he told Q. “What that is, I can't really put a finger on, but it feels unlike anything else.”

Matthews, second from right, ended up attending a screening of Below with his wife Tina Matthews, right, and daughter Zara Tai Matthews. They met the star of the show, actor Josh Hartnett. (Netflix)

Hartnett also listened to hours of CBC’s Newfoundland show, The Broadcast , to nail the accent — with Matthews saying the overall cast did “reasonably well” on that score.

The streaming giant also invited Matthews and his family to attend a screening of the show in St. John’s, where he said they got to chat with Hartnett and were very well looked after. In another coincidence, his daughter, Zara Tai Matthews, appears in the show’s sixth episode.

WATCH | Jax Irwin calls a stranger to ask what they're having for dinner:

Irwin started making the calls in part because she felt lonely and homesick after moving to Toronto from Dartmouth, N.S. She’s not too worried about people knowing it’s her calling, if the extra publicity blows her cover.

“I also don't want to be too much of a sneaky snake, right? So if people know what I'm doing, I'm just always happy to connect with anybody who will pick up the phone,” she said.

Matthews thinks Irwin is doing good by making these connections, and he can see why she calls smaller communities on the East Coast to have these chats.

“People in those big cities are just so rushed, and I well appreciate that,” he said.

“What may be one of the very attractive features of our lifestyle is that we take time to live and enjoy the vagaries of life, wherever they come.”

World.title: How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?

Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.

The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.

"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.

"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."

But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.

Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.

Here's what we know.

Is everyone getting sick right now?

According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.

Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.

It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.

But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.

"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.

WATCH | B.C. launches fall immunization campaign: B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign | Duration closed caption 7:05 Flu season has started early this year and the province has launched its fall immunization campaign to prevent the spread. Dr. Jennifer Vines with the B.C. Centre for Disease Control shares what the vaccine rollout will look like and what precautions people can take to stay healthy.

He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.

"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."

Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.

In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.

WATCH | Ontario deals with earlier-than-usual flu season: You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year | Duration closed caption 2:10 Some Ontario doctors say they're noticing an early start to this year's flu season in their waiting rooms, as influenza cases tick up across the province ahead of schedule.

"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.

"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."

Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.

How effective is the flu shot this year?

The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.

This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.

He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.

It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.

About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)

Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.

When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?

Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.

New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.

Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.

In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .

In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.

In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.

Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.

Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

World.title: Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You can accomplish a lot in five hours.

Fly direct from Toronto to Vancouver, for instance. Or play an entire 18-hole round of golf. Run a full marathon at an average pace. Smoke a rack of ribs.

It's an objectively long stretch of time. Now, imagine holding a plank, one of the most notoriously challenging core exercises, for the amount of time it takes to cook a Thanksgiving turkey?

"I just love it," laughed DonnaJean Wilde, who at age 61 just broke her own world record for the longest time holding an abdominal plank position (female) during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.

Wilde is a grandmother of 12 and retired teacher from Welling, Alta. And on Tuesday, in front of a cheering crowd and several judges, she held an abdominal plank for five straight hours, shattering her previous 2024 world record of four hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds.

WATCH | Alberta woman holds plank for 5 hours: Canadian woman holds plank for 5 hours, breaking world record | Duration closed caption 7:30 DonnaJean Wilde, 61, a two-time plank world record holder and a grandmother of 12, broke her own Guinness World Record for holding the longest female abdominal plank. Wilde held her plank for five hours during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.

On Friday, she told CBC News Network she was "feeling good" and waiting for Guinness to make the record official.

"It just becomes easier to do the more repeated times you do it," Wilde said.

An abdominal plank is an isometric core exercise where you hold your body straight like a plank of wood. Most adults can hold a plank for 20 to 60 seconds, according to Health magazine.

Guinness World Records notes that to successfully achieve the record, the challenger's forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times. "The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout."

Not her only world record

Wilde says she started planking about 15 years ago when she broke her arm and was looking for a way to stay fit.

"I love to work out. I love fitness, and I discovered I could plank with a cast on," she said.

"And when the cast came off, it became a habit that I actually embraced and fell in love with."

When she first started, she says she could hold a plank for about a minute or minute and a half, but she kept practicing. With her family's encouragement, she kept going and minutes became hours. By 2024, she broke the Guinness World Record.

Wilde, seen in the midst of achieving her latest world record, says that while she holds her hours-long planks she likes to multitask: reading, writing and earning her master's. (Submitted by DonnaJean Wilde)

And, for good measure, she broke a second one that year by completing 1,575 pushups in one hour — the most push ups in one hour (female) . She told the Guinness World Records she fell in love with doing pushups while doing 500 every day as training for her planks.

Now, she planks every day for at least a few hours. But it doesn't eat into her time, she says. She multitasks.

"Just read, do texts, whatever, do schoolwork. I did a master's degree while I was planking. Wrote a book," she said.

The book, From Minutes To Hours: I Wrote This Book While Planking, came out last year.

CBC News did not attempt to write this story while planking.

World.title: After days of giving French-only answers in legislature, Kinew wants schools to cover '80s language battle
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitoba's premier wants the schools in the province to teach students about the bitter fight against the expansion of francophone rights in the 1980s.

Premier Wab Kinew is calling for the addition to the education curriculum, after his decision to speak almost exclusively in French during four days of question period at the legislature was celebrated by some and questioned by others.

He also said he'd like to see a live French-to-English translation of question period offered for people watching online — which the legislative assembly is working on.

"I hope that after this week, we can use this experience as motivation to renew our education system to share our own history as Manitoba, including those struggles and challenges for the Francophonie to protect your language and your culture," Kinew told host Jérémy Laniel in a Friday French-language interview with Le 6 à 9, Radio-Canada's morning radio show in Manitoba.

Kinew was referring to the French-language crisis of the 1980s, when a government bill calling for provincial services to be offered in French sparked an outcry and protests from some English-speakers.

Th e offices of the Société de la francophonie manitobaine were targeted by an arson , and the opposition Progressive Conservatives spent nearly two weeks blocking a vote on the government bill.

The NDP government succumbed to the public pressure, withdrawing the bill in 1984.

By the next year, however, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled Manitoba's unilingual laws were unconstitutional. The laws needed to be translated into French to be re-enacted, the court ruled.

Kinew said many Manitobans aren't aware of this history.

"The reality in Manitoba is that the French language is the language of your mothers, your fathers, your grandparents. And then they had to hide their books, they had to hide their signs with French text," he said in French.

Kinew said the government would consult with the Franco-Manitoban School Division, Société de la francophonie manitobaine and other experts who understand that history before incorporating it into the curriculum.

Bernard Lesage, board chair of the French-language school division, said he's pleased that if the changes are approved, all students will get to learn more about Franco-Manitoban history.

Criticized for French answers

Since La Vérendrye MLA Konrad Narth was appointed interim leader of the Opposition Progressive Conservatives two weeks ago, Kinew has answered every English-language question put to him in the legislature in French.

In late May, Narth — who doesn't speak French — got into hot water when he was overheard saying Kinew showed a "basic lack of respect" for responding to his question in French.

Narth later said he asked the question in English, not French, prompting heckling from NDP MLAs who accused him of disrespecting the language, according to an audio recording of the exchange.

He later apologized for how his comments came across. Narth also said he appreciates that he can ask questions in the language he's most comfortable in, and Kinew can respond in French with translation available to all MLAs.

The premier has denied that he's speaking French in the chamber because of Narth's actions from May. He told reporters this week Narth was "disrespecting the bilingual tradition."

Interim Progressive Conservative Leader Konrad Narth said this week he has no issues with the premier speaking in French in the chamber. Narth doesn't speak French, but can listen to a live translation in the chamber. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

By Friday, Kinew suggested he feels "a bit like Forrest Gump" — the movie character famed for going on an epic cross-country run "for no particular reason."

Kinew said he started speaking French, "and then I thought it was important to keep going. But I don't really know the exact reason."

Kinew has previously spoken French in the legislature but usually only regarding francophone matters.

Boosting national profile: political scientist

He disagreed Friday that he is politicizing the use of French, as Raymond Hébert, a professor emeritus of political studies who wrote a book on Manitoba's French-language crisis, has suggested.

Hébert also said the premier's conduct might undermine his government's efforts to advance bilingualism by antagonizing anglophones.

Kinew said he respects Hébert, but "Manitoba has changed a lot," pointing to growth in French-immersion scho ols and the many people who speak and respect the language and its history.

His NDP gove rnment has vowed to make the province a "truly bilingual" province. The province consulted with people last year, and a provincial strategy is scheduled for release in March 2027.

While Manitoba's courts and legislature operate in English and French, other government services are offered in both languages only in designated areas where there is a "concentrated" francophone population. The province is not officially bilingual by law.

A political scientist in Quebec suggested Kinew's use of French in the legislature may be about more than scoring political points or appealing to Franco-Manitobans.

"I think that is someone who might have national ambitions, and certainly someone who has a national profile" as a popular premier, said Daniel Béland, director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.

"Showing to the rest of the country, and including to people in Quebec, that he speaks French … increases his profile across the country."

Kinew also told Radio-Canada he doesn't think it "would be a huge deal" to offer live translation of question period. MLAs already receive a translation through an earpiece on their desks.

He said those decisions are up to the legislature's Speaker, who, earlier this year, made picture-in-picture American Sign Language interpretation available during all question period broadcasts.

Rick Yarish, clerk of the legislative assembly, said the legislature doesn't currently have the technological capacities to provide the translation but is working to implement the service. No timeline is available.

He said the goal is to have a second video feed of question period airing exclusively on the assembly's broadcast page, which would include a live French-to-English translation. The primary video feed, featuring whichever language is being spoken, would remain as is and broadcast simultaneously on YouTube.

World.title: 'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn’t exist
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An investor and friend of Aiden Pleterski showed up at the lakefront mansion of the self-described "Crypto King" in June 2022 to "get proof in person" of how much money was in Pleterski’s investment account — after receiving a screenshot and video showing a balance of $311 million.

Mitchell Learning, who said he invested $400,000, took the stand Friday, on the fourth day of Pleterski’s fraud and money laundering trial in Toronto. Both the screenshot and video showing the trading account were shown to the jury in Superior Court.

Pleterski has pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering.

The jury in Aiden Pleterski's trial was shown this photo on Friday of Mitchell Learning holding his own phone with a screenshot he testified Pleterski sent him of Pleterski's trading account with a balance of more than $311 million. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)

Pleterski wasn’t home when Learning arrived at his Burlington, Ont., home.

In his absence, Learning testified he was able to gain access to Pleterski’s email account on his computer and found an email from the trading platform FXChoice confirming Pleterski had "successfully deleted" the account where the $311 million was supposed to be.

He then told mutual friends to come to Pleterski’s mansion, and one of them recorded a video, also presented in court, of Pleterski’s emails. Those included account statements from another trading platform Forex.com.

Aiden Pleterski's Burlington, Ont., mansion. Friend and investor Mitchell Learning, who said he invested $400,000 with Pleterski, says he went to his home seeking proof of an investment fund. (Pelin Sidki/CBC)

"Looks like it’s never been higher than $1,000, oh my god," the friend says on the video as he and Learning look through the statements.

Referring to the "available margin" on another statement, the friend says, "400 f–king dollars, I’ve been f–ked."

Confronting the 'Crypto King'

Later, Learning said Pleterski returned home and told him and Pleterski’s girlfriend "a story" where Pleterski was trading and everything was going well until the summer of 2021 "where apparently things took a turn."

"At the end of the summer, around September 2021, he had $40 million in a trading account," Learning said about what Pleterski told him.

"It only kept going down from there. He tried to make riskier trades to make money back, essentially losing the remainder of the money and then from that point on starting running a Ponzi scheme."

Mitchell Learning testified at the Superior Court in Toronto on Friday on the fourth day of 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski’s fraud and money laundering trial. (Pam Davies/CBC News)

Afterward, Learning said he left the house and didn’t really know what to do.

"There were a lot of emotions and I was definitely very upset about everything," he said in court.

Two days later, Learning said he recorded a phone call with Pleterski.

Pleterski promises to 'make it right'

The 30-minute call was played in court Friday afternoon. In it, Pleterski expresses regret for not being "f--king straight up with everybody" when "the investment went to s--t, trading went bad, everything was lost."

Learning also gets angry at Pleterski for the position he says Pleterski put him in.

"You did me so f--king dirty," said Learning on the June 2022 phone call recording.

"You lied to me. You got me to show fake f--king s--t to people, put my neck out for you, meet people, be the f--king, like, face? And just, like, all of it was just a f--king lie."

Pleterski then tells Learning, on the recording, that he's going to fix it and will "make it right" to get everyone their money back.

In court, Pleterski chose not to cross-examine Learning.

"I'm unable to come up with questions for the witness," he said.

The Crown is alleging Pleterski guaranteed investors' money given to him for trading, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, the Crown argues Pleterski spent the money on himself, including on exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.

Range Rover, McLaren on Instagram

Earlier Friday, Learning explained how he first met Pleterski when they played a season of baseball together in 2014. They followed each other on Instagram, and in 2020 when Learning saw Pleterski post a photo of Range Rover and McLaren, Learning said he reached out to find out what Pleterski was up to. Pleterski said he was trading.

In Sept. 2020, Learning first gave Pleterski $2,500 to trade on his behalf. His investment later grew to $400,000.

"I got quite a lot of money out originally," said Learning. "I think it was just over a million dollars."

Aiden Pleterski posted these photos from the Burlington, Ont., mansion where he was living on his Instagram account. (aiden.ptrs/Instagram)

Learning testified that he eventually gave some of that money to family and friends who also invested and were trying to get their principal funds back.

Earlier on, Learning also said he tried to get more involved in Pleterski’s operation and would pick up and deliver bank drafts from investors for Pleterski, at one point getting paid $2,000 a week for six weeks to do these and similar errands.

Learning went on three trips with Pleterski, where they flew on private jets — one to Ohio for a boxing match, a second to Florida for a week and a third to Turks and Caicos for Pleterski’s girlfriend’s birthday in March 2022.

Pleterski was arrested in May 2024 after a lengthy investigation by Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission. Police allege he operated a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme.

So far at trial, nine investors have testified to giving Pleterski more than $2 million collectively to trade on their behalf. Most of them said they didn’t get any of that money back.

The trial is expected to continue Tuesday.
