Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.title: ‘Violation of privacy?’ Senate court takes down Sara Duterte trial livestream
World.content:
TAXES. Bureau of Internal Revenue Office of the Commissioner chief of staff Anne Lorraine Garcia-Marquez takes the witness stand on Day 36 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on October 8, 2026.

The BIR witness says the copy of the Letter of Authority displayed during the trial showed the names of some revenue officers

MANILA, Philippines – In the impeachment trial of Sara Duterte, it’s been the defense that has repeatedly objected to the presentation of the bank and tax records of the Vice President and her husband, Manases “Mans” Carpio, citing confidentiality issues.

But on Day 37 of the trial on Friday, October 9, there was a twist.

Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero ordered the Senate Clerk of Court to take down the livestream of the highly public proceedings over concerns on displaying the private information of some personnel of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR).

Escudero issued the directive after lawyer Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez, chief-of-staff of the Office of the BIR Commissioner, expressed worry following the defense’s flashing of the copies of the confidential letter of authority (LOA) the BIR issued to Duterte’s husband.

Carpio himself had consented to the presentation of the LOA but Garcia-Marquez said the documents showed the names of the revenue officers.

“I just want to raise that when the copy of the LOAs were flashed on the screen earlier… the names of some revenue officers were displayed. It should have been redacted,” Garcia-Marquez said.

Escudero said the court will redact the names on the documents to be submitted in court but the witness said her worry was due to the showing of the sensitive data of the BIR officers.

“We manifest, Your Honor, that there has been a violation of the privacy of the people involved. Their names were flashed for everyone to see,” private prosecutor Erwin Matib said.

The court vowed to address the issue.

After an hour-long break, Escudero asked the Clerk of Court to remove the original livestream and re-upload it with the redaction of the names of the BIR officers.

The livestream was taken down past 1 pm.

“We would like to remind not only [defense] Attorney Kristine [Ferrer] and the counsels for the respondent but also the counsel for the prosecution to be careful next time insofar as revealing names or addresses,” said Escudero.

“Given the public nature of these proceedings, as it might violate some provisions of the Data Privacy Act, as well as the security of certain officials of government engaged in various activities as part of their official functions and duties,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

Play Video

LATEST UPDATES

World.title: Bida ang saya: Is your fave Jollibee spot owned by Sara Duterte?
World.content:
At the trial, the prosecution presents Jollibee receipts issued by Gencorp, a company in which VP Sara Duterte is a stockholder

We know by now that Vice President Sara Duterte has some links to Jollibee because the company she declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) has franchises of the fast-food giant.

But just how many branches does Gencorp Industries Inc. (Gencorp) operate?

During the impeachment trial on Friday, October 9, the prosecution presented receipts from Jollibee branches in Davao City showing Gencorp as the owner.

RISIBO. A composite of five receipts of Jollibee branches in Davao City owned by Gencorp Industries where Vice President Sara Duterte is a stockholder. These receipts were presented by the prosecution in the impeachment trial on October 9, 2026.

There are at least five branches:

Jollibee Bolton is a known hangout spot of the Dutertes.

FAST FOOD. Former president Rodrigo Duterte (right) and Senator Bong Go (left) eat in Jollibee Bolton Street in Davao City on June 28, 2022, after Duterte’s son Baste took his oath as Davao City mayor. Photo by Bong Go/Facebook

Rappler first reported that Gencorp cornered millions of pesos in contracts with the Davao City government in 2022, coinciding with the time that Sara became the Vice President, and her brother Sebastian assumed the mayorship of their hometown. The arrangement raises questions on conflict of interest, and potential violation of the Constitution.

While Duterte herself declared that she is a stockholder of Gencorp in her SALN, the absence of her name in the company’s Securities and Exchange Commission documents has been a head-scratcher.

Play Video

“The reason why I think VP Sara included Gencorp in her SALN is because its value is huge,” prosecution witness, financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, theorized on Friday.

He explained that an investor would need between P35 million to P50 million for a Jollibee franchise with P35 million being a “very conservative [figure]…because you need working capital pambayad sa crew, pambayad sa manager, pambayad sa rent, initial inventory (to pay for the crew, the manager, rent, initial inventory).”

Cabrera, who reviewed voluminous financial records of Duterte, said upon comparison of Gencorp’s bank inflows and financial statements, it was concluded that the firm has P1.1 billion in undeclared wealth.

Cabrera said that overall, Duterte has P817 million in undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025, including P212.6 million from undeclared income from Gencorp.

How did the analyst compute that figure when Duterte’s stake at Gencorp hasn’t been disclosed in corporate filings?

“We applied a conservative 20% percentage,” Cabrera said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Financial analyst tells impeach court: Sara Duterte has P817M in undisclosed wealth
World.content:
The amount includes undeclared cash, properties, and income of the Vice President, her spouse Mans Carpio, and their companies

MANILA, Philippines – A financial forensic analyst called as a witness by the prosecution told the impeachment court on Friday, October 9, that Vice President Sara Duterte’s undeclared wealth tops P800 million.

Alexander Cabrera, a certified public accountant and a lawyer who is chairman emeritus of PwC Philippines, said that based on his review of voluminous financial records of the Vice President and her husband, Mans Carpio, the couple has around P817 million in undisclosed assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

The amount covers their undisclosed personal cash based on discrepancies between their audited financial statements and declarations in the Vice President’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), undeclared other personal and real properties, and undeclared income of their companies Cale88, Metro Chow, and Gencorp based on the mismatch between income tax returns and bank inflows.

Cabrera explained that Carpio’s financial records were included in the analysis because they have “absolute community of property” as a married couple.

“We used a conservative method. There’s no duplication in count,” Cabrera added.

The forensic report he produced also flags other behaviors in Duterte’s financial records, which he found suspicious, such as:

single, large credit card purchases, such as P205,007.29 for Ginza Inakaya and P111,109.24 for Don Quijote in Japan;

17 insurance policies not declared by the Vice President in her SALN;

and a variation of check kiting (Cabrera calls it “nagtitinikling ang pera“), where funds move in and out of an account through manager’s checks so the amounts won’t be included in year-end reports

Cabrera will be cross-examined by the defense on Monday, October 12.

He is already the last witness of the prosecution panel, which has decided to drop the bribery case against the Vice President. – Rappler.com

World.title: Cale88’s workforce, financial records draw scrutiny in impeachment trial
World.content:
Manases Carpio-owned Cale88 listed only two employees in its general info sheet despite reporting P150 million in sales in 2024

MANILA, Philippines – Senator-judges on Friday, October 9, scrutinized the financial records and workforce of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte‘s husband, Manases Carpio.

On Day 37 of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva raised concerns over Cale88’s 2024 general information sheet, which listed only two employees despite the company reporting P150.6 million in sales and P6.13 million in losses.

“This is alarming, Your Honor. You’re looking at a company with P150 million sales and P6.13 million in losses but only [has] two employees,” Villanueva said.

Citing the company’s financial records, Bureau of Internal Revenue chief of staff Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez said Cale88 reported P150,595,605 in sales classified as exempt from income tax and P169,564 in sales subject to regular income tax in 2024.

The company also reported a loss of around P6.13 million in the same year, Garcia-Marquez said.

Villanueva questioned how the company managed its operations with very few employees and who funded its continued operations.

Marquez said she had no personal knowledge of Cale88’s operations, adding that it would seem “impossible” for a banana chip manufacturer to operate with only two employees unless machinery handled much of the work.

Hontiveros flags Ukrainian remitter

Meanwhile, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros flagged Ukrainian company Arkmen LLC, one of the foreign-based entities that sent inward remittances to Cale88, citing alleged involvement in a fraud and money laundering investigation in Ukraine.

Hontiveros said her office checked the background of the foreign-based companies that remitted to Cale88 and found that Kyiv authorities investigated Arkmen LLC over alleged fraud and money laundering involving 1.225 million euros in May 2025.

Authorities reportedly ordered a search of its premises in March, while its assets were frozen in April.

“The last remittance of Arkmen LLC to Cale88 was in May 2025 after the start of the criminal proceedings,” Hontiveros said.

Hontiveros asked Marquez whether legitimate transactions involving international remittances from Arkmen LLC to Cale88 should have been reported as sales and subjected to tax.

“If these were sales, they should have been reported in the annual income tax return,” Marquez said.

Hontiveros had previously claimed that some Chinese companies that sent funds to Cale88 were Chinese state-owned enterprises that could be “advancing the interests of the Chinese Communist Party.” – Rappler.com

World.title: CHR chair faces graft complaint over alleged corruption in allowance
World.content:
CHAIR. Commission on Human Rights Chair Richard Palpal-latoc attends the House quad committee investigating extrajudicial killings during the Duterte administration, at the House of Representatives, on September 12, 2024.

The NBI claims CHR Chairperson Richard Palpal-latoc allegedly still received allowances for a trip already funded by a foreign sponsor

MANILA, Philippines – Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Chairperson Richard Palpal-latoc and three other individuals are facing a graft complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman over alleged corruption involving a month-long training.

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed the complaint on Friday, October 9, for alleged violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. Other respondents are as follows:

Onesimo Cuyco

Maria Teresa Dolor

Russel Mani

“Respectfully transmitting for Preliminary Investigation are the results of the investigation conducted by this Bureau’s Public Corruption Division as represented by xxxx,” said the NBI’s transmission document to the Ombudsman.

Rappler has already reached out to CHR for a statement. We will update this story once they respond.

According to the NBI, Palpal-latoc attended the 54th International Institute for Human Rights Summer School in 2025. It was a month-long training with the airfare, accommodation, meals, and subsistence fully funded by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom (FNF).

The CHR chairperson, however, allegedly still claimed daily subsistence allowance and representation for the period of the training.

The NBI argued that Executive Order No. 77, series of 2019 prohibits claims for public officials if the travel is covered by the sponsor. It added that Section 16(b) “specifically disallows representation expenses for officials attending trainings or travelling on donor-funded trips.”

In addition, the disbursement voucher also allegedly concealed the funding arrangement and did not contain a disclosure of the foreign donor.

“Despite missing mandatory documents, the mismatched program documentation, the prohibited claims, and the undisclosed sponsorship, the voucher passed through every control point. Mani certified the supporting documents as complete. Dolor certified that funds were available. Cuyco approved the voucher for payment,” said the NBI.

“Taken together, these acts establish liability of Palpal-latoc, Cuyco, Dolor, and Mani for violation of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 and for Gross Misconduct: Public officers acting in their official functions: the Chairperson as claimant, and the certifying and approving officers in processing the voucher. Manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence: a claim for expenses already paid by a sponsor, a concealed donor, and certifications issued over facially defective documents,” the NBI added.

In 2022, Marcos appointed Palpal-latoc, a former Malacañang deputy executive secretary for legal affairs, as CHR chairperson.

Palpal-latoc has experience in anti-corruption prosecution. He served assistant prosecutor at the Quezon City prosecutor’s office. He had also served in various positions in the Office of the Ombudsman and in the Department of Social Welfare field office in Calabarzon, including as graft investigation and prosecution officer under the Ombudsman. – Rappler.com

World.title: A local’s playbook to Makati-maxxing
World.content:
So many cities in the world, but no one quite like her (Makati)

Makati has been gaining popularity (not that it has ever been out of its game), but social media, especially TikTok, has given the city a brand-new personality. Trends like “Salcedo girlie” and “United States of Makati” show just how many interesting things the city has to offer. All of a sudden, the routines locals have had for years have been given names and tied to certain aesthetics.

But when you have lived here for most of your life, what feels like a spectacle to others can simply be the norm. The places people intentionally visit might just be where you usually buy late dinner or somewhere your family has been taking you since childhood.

So what is it actually like to live here, move through here, and call this city home? If you think this is a list of the newest or coolest places in the city, well… it’s not. Instead, it’s a field guide to the spots that have stood the test of time and captured the hearts of many Makati residents.

When Makati feels like a neighborhood

Ayala Car-Free Sundays

On Sundays, one of Makati’s busiest streets becomes one of its most inclusive and democratic public spaces.

CAR-FREE SUNDAYS. Makati opens Ayala Avenue to runners, cyclists, families, and visitors.

You will see all kinds of people here — runners, families, athletes, and sometimes even a celebrity. For a few hours, Ayala Avenue kind of becomes an equilibrium. You’ll see people from all walks of life sharing the same road, stripped of whatever separates us during the week.

You come to realize that, after all, we are just people longing for an open space in the heart of the city.

Power Plant Mall

Power Plant or “Rockwell” to locals, is actually less of a mall and more like one big living room.

THE ICONIC ROCKWELL CENTER SKYLINE. A prime example of life in a curated community, where everything you need is within walking distance.

There’s a running joke that if you go here on a Sunday, you’ll bump into everyone you’ve ever known: old classmates, former coworkers, and even ex-situationships (lol).

Rockwell’s tight-knit community is exactly its appeal, which is why it has earned its place as a third space for many locals.

POWERPLANT MALL. For many locals, this place can be familiar ground where errands easily become mini reunions.

For when you want to gather family and friends

Romulo Café on Jupiter Street and Milky Way along Arnaiz Avenue

The OGs! For lunch with family — or any group large enough to make choosing a restaurant complicated — there are these two.

Both are reliable classics that serve homestyle Filipino food for multigenerational tastes. It also helps that they have warm, stand-alone settings that feel more like grandma’s house than usual commercial spaces.

A FAMILY FAVORITE. Romulo Café pairs homestyle Filipino food with a setting made for large family gatherings.

A MAKATI INSTITUTION. Milky Way has served classic Filipino dishes and generations of Makati families for decades.

They have also been around long enough to witness many milestones in the lives of Makati residents. A baptism, an engagement party, a birthday celebration — eventually, another generation grows up and returns with a family of their own.

Pablo Bistro

A MICHELIN Guide-selected Spanish restaurant in the heart of Salcedo Village, Pablo Bistro is one of those places that is easy to keep in mind if you live or work in Makati.

WHERE REGULARS RETURN. Pablo is a true neighborhood favorite for its Spanish comfort food and warm atmosphere.

It is open from 7 am to 12 mn, so it works for almost any kind of plan. That flexibility makes it an easy meeting place for all kinds of groups. Whenever everyone becomes available, there is a good chance it is still open.

Papillon

Also selected by the MICHELIN Guide, Papillon is for girls’ night or date night when you want something a little more elevated. Its dramatic Asian interiors give you a reason to turn up the ante a bit.

It can get busy as it often hosts private events, so it’s worth reserving ahead.

FOR SPECIAL NIGHTS. Papillon offers a refined take on Southeast Asian cuisine.

Where Makati feels a little fancy

The Peninsula Manila lobby

Sometimes, you want to feel a little fancy, and for that, there is the Pen lobby. This place carries an older image of Makati in all its grandeur, reflecting the dreams and ambition Makati has always represented.

There is always the piano, and from Thursday to Sunday, an orchestra. It’s where you can have your usual coffee or tea when you want something a little more upscale than a café.

THE ICONIC PEN LOBBY. Have lunch, sip coffee, and savor live music beneath Napoleon Abueva’s Sunburst.

For when you want to go solo

Commune

Commune lives up to its name. Apart from serving Philippine coffee, it has become a meeting place for the different communities that pass through Poblacion.

A MAKATI HOME FOR CREATIVES. Commune is a place for laid-back moments within Poblacion.

Its second floor also serves as a haven for creatives. You can catch a workshop, an improv show, or a small performance. It’s a place that has actually built a community for various creative groups.

The Curator

This well-loved place understands the city like no other. It’s a café by day, then come evening, its not-so-secret bar opens. After more than a decade in the Legazpi Village neighborhood, it remains the kind of place both locals and visitors make a point of visiting.

A MODERN CLASSIC. After more than a decade, The Curator still sets the standard for handcrafted drinks.

Makati before the aesthetic

Chino Roces area (Little Tokyo, Makati Cinema Square)

Long before Japanese food went ubiquitous, locals flocked to Chino Roces for reliable favorites at Little Tokyo, while nearby Makati Cinema Square (officially Makati Central Square) retains its unpretentious charm — a retro hub where you can find old-school eateries, bowling alleys, art galleries, and eccentric bars. The ukay-ukay stalls here also draw a younger generation of thrift shoppers.

THE ORIGINAL JAPAN TOWN. Little Tokyo has remained a favorite for Japanese food and a taste of old Makati.

STILL STANDING STRONG. Makati Cinema Square has outlasted trends by remaining stubbornly itself — eccentric and unapologetically old-school.

To see Makati as a local is to know the city in all its contradictions. It is glass towers and narrow side streets, MICHELIN-recognized restaurants and Jolly Jeep meals, and so much more.

People may come for the version of Makati they have seen online, but when you’ve lived here most of your life, you come to recognize it in all its versions. Still, Makati has never belonged only to those who live here.

Every day, it welcomes people who come to work, eat, explore, or simply find their place in the city. And maybe this is why “Makati-maxxing” has captured the attention of many. The city leaves enough room for everyone to make some part of it their own. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pope Leo approves Tagle as first Asian dean of Catholic cardinals
World.content:
IN ATTENDANCE. Cardinal Luis Tagle attends Pope Leo XIV's inaugural Mass in Saint Peter’s Square, at the Vatican, on May 18, 2025.

The dean of the college of cardinals is considered the 'first among equals' among the Church's highest-ranking clerics and is responsible for taking charge of the secretive conclave process

VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV approved Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle‘s election as the dean of the Catholic Church’s college of cardinals, the Vatican said on Friday, October 9, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to lead the elite group that one day will choose Leo’s successor.

A former archbishop of Manila, Tagle has served as a senior Vatican official since 2020. He was widely seen as a likely papal candidate in the May 2025 conclave that elected Leo to lead the Church after the death of the late pope Francis.

Tagle, 69, replaces Italian Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, who is 92 and retiring from the role.

Leo, 71, is relatively young for a pope, plays sports, and is in good health.

The dean of the college of cardinals is considered the “first among equals” among the Church’s highest-ranking clerics and is responsible for taking charge of the secretive conclave process, held in the Sistine Chapel, once a pope dies or resigns.

The dean, elected by his peers and approved by the pope, serves a five-year term that can be renewed once, according to Church law. The role has mostly been filled by Europeans, but was held by the late Beninese Cardinal Bernardin Gantin from 1993-2002.

Tagle was seen as a close ally of Pope Francis and is known for an infectious smile and is sometimes called by his diminutive nickname “Chito.” He leads the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization, effectively the Church’s missionary arm. – Rappler.com

World.title: Over Two-Thirds of Myanmar’s Population Poor or at Risk of Poverty: UN
World.content:
More than 37 million people—over two-thirds of Myanmar’s population of more than 54 million—are experiencing or at risk of “multidimensional poverty,” according to the latest report from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released on Thursday.

Drawing data from a nationwide household survey of nearly 7,500 people in 2025, the UNDP’s latest analysis examines what it calls multidimensional poverty, which looks beyond income and also covers non-financial deprivation, including access to education and healthcare, and other basic needs, amid economic and political crisis and natural hazards.

It said nearly 18 million people (32.6 percent) in Myanmar are multidimensionally poor, while more than 19 million (35.5 percent) others are vulnerable. That brings the total figure to more than 37 million people (68 percent) who either face poverty or are at risk of falling into it.

“Myanmar may no longer dominate international headlines, but the hardships facing millions of people continue to deepen,” said Kanni Wignaraja, UN assistant secretary-general and UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific. “We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded.”

The survey found that people in rural areas are poorer than those in urban areas.

In terms of both severity and scale, the UNDP report highlights Rakhine State as the worst-affected area, with approximately 1.66 million residents enduring the most intense multidimensional poverty. Sagaing Region followed with a larger total of approximately 2.38 million people experiencing less severe poverty. Ayeyarwady Region ranked third.

The UNDP’s analysis indicated that poverty is driven by a combination of long-standing household vulnerabilities, including low education levels, insecure jobs and limited income, and wider pressures such as rising prices, natural hazards and armed conflict.

In war-torn Rakhine and Karenni (Kayah) states, poverty has been compounded by conflict, displacement and restrictions on movement.

To address poverty effectively, the report concluded that aid must provide intensive support to hard-hit conflict zones while reaching larger numbers of poor residents elsewhere, with assistance tailored to local needs.

World.title: Regime Shuts Down Myanmar’s Surging Online Gold Market
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has moved to ban online sales of gold and jewelry, citing the risk of flawed products and market destabilization.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Ministry announced it has suspended issuance of licenses for selling gold, raw gold, jewelry, art objects, and household items via online platforms. It threatened unlicensed traders with prosecution under the 2013 Essential Commodities and Services Law, which carries six months to three years in prison and fines up to 500,000 kyats (roughly US$ 240).

Under existing rules, online sellers must obtain a Commerce Ministry license, while those dealing in gold and gemstones must also secure a permit from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Conservation.

Industry insiders told The Irrawaddy that more than 700 businesses have applied for licenses to sell gold and jewelry online in recent years. However, the ministry has now refused to extend expired permits, with inspections and enforcement expected to begin at the end of this month.

Online gold and jewelry shopping has become popular in Myanmar over the past few years, with internet outlets hiring actors and celebrities to promote their livestream sales.

Traders say the clampdown follows growing complaints from buyers that jewelry purchased via livestream “flash sales” was later rejected by pawnshops or gold shops.

“Online customers have no way of verifying the weight, quality, or reference price of their purchases. That leads to disputes and losses,” one Yangon jeweler explained.

Last month, Mandalay police announced the arrest of 11 foreign nationals and 17 Myanmar citizens accused of running online gemstone scams. Authorities said the suspects were using fake jade to defraud buyers in livestream sales.

Online gemstone sales remain permitted provided merchants hold a license from the Myanma Gems Enterprise and refrain from selling gold.

While the Yangon Region Gold Entrepreneurs Association has set the domestic reference price for 24K gold at 7.1 million kyats per tical, the market price exceeds 10 million kyats — a gap of 3 million kyats. Before the 2021 coup, a tical sold for under 1.4 million kyats.

Business owners warn that banning online sales will hurt digital commerce and marketing, which had surged during the pandemic. “Shops that relied on livestream promotions will struggle. Now we can only depend on walk-in customers,” one trader said.

World.title: China Takes Top Investor Crown in Myanmar, and More
World.content:
China now Myanmar’s top investor, trade partner

China is now officially the top foreign investor and trading partner in Myanmar, consolidating its economic grip as others retreat, according to a report by Japan External Trade Organization.

In fiscal year 2025 ending this March, Myanmar approved US$472.6 million in foreign direct investment, down another one-third or 31.5 percent from a year earlier. But inflow from China rose 2.1‑fold to $201.1 million, meaning it now accounts for 42.6 percent of the total.

The previous leader due to long-standing commitments, Singapore, dropped to second place with $155 million, while Hong Kong contributed $54.9 million, the report said citing data from Directorate of Investment and Company Administration.

Much of the Chinese and Hong Kong capital is in light industry, particularly garment and shoe factories.

Myanmar’s exports to China also climbed 24.7 percent to $4.312 billion over the period, while imports surged 42.6 percent to $5.952 billion. That means China now accounts for over one-third of of Myanmar’s total trade or 35 percent, up from 27.8 percent the previous year.

With the border disruptions, trade has shifted to alternative routes, says the report. The figures did not count China’s trade with territories controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State bordering Yunnan.

Chinese documentary maps scam empires in lesser-known Shan hubs

A docuseries aired this week by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV has shed light on scam syndicates that thrived in four areas along Myanmar’s northern border. While Kokang’s scam empires have long made international headlines, the documentary focuses on three lesser‑known hubs—Wa, Mongla and Muse—as it boasts of Beijing’s “achievements” in cracking down on them.

The show identifies quasi-autonomous Wa territory as the incubator of regional scam economy. At the height of the boom, Mong Pawk alone hosted 265 scam centers involving nearly 60,000 people. But unlike the Kokang clans, who resisted Beijing’s demand to halt operations, the long- ruling United Wa State Army (UWSA) cooperated after one leader was arrested in Kunming and warrants were issued for others.

In October 2023, Wa authorities launched large‑scale sweeps of scam compounds, the documentary reveals. Since then, the UWSA has reported regular transfers of Chinese suspects and illegal immigrants, introducing procedures for voluntary return. More than 1,400 Chinese nationals have been reportedly handed back this year.

But it was in Mongla, controlled by the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), where Beijing started its crackdown in September 2023, and the group cooperated with Chinese authorities. A second strike in July 2024 led to a border law enforcement cooperation agreement between Yunnan police and Mongla authorities, establishing monitoring and repatriation mechanisms.

The crackdown proved most difficult in Muse, where Beijing identified 33 distinct local armed groups and militias, each with over 100 members, alongside Myanmar military‑aligned forces. Unlike the fortified scam parks in Kokang, Muse syndicates operated out of ordinary hotels, apartments, and villas. Despite joint raids in April 2024, scam sites keep popping up like a game of Whac-a-Mole, with arrests continuing this year.

Scam arrests in junta-aligned territory

This week Naypyitaw reported the arrest of 87 scammers—75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar—in the remote valley of Hopong in the Pa-O Self-Administered Zone in southern Shan. They were reportedly operating in makeshift huts, with dozens of computers, more than 500 phones and Star Link satellite dishes.

The self-administered zone, which also includes Hsihseng and Pinlaung townships, is controlled by the Pa-O National Army that is allied to the Myanmar military. Its leaders including Aung Kham Hti have close ties to regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

The Chinese docuseries admitted that scam centers once entrenched in northern Shan State near the China–Myanmar border have relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy on Thai border since the crackdown in late 2023 but did not say where else they have scattered. The Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar has been identified scam operations in at least 17 townships in Shan including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse.

Taiwan warns against travel to Myanmar

Taiwan issued a fresh warning against travel to Myanmar this week, citing risks related to online scam centers, escalating conflict, and limited options for citizens’ rescue. The Taiwanese Foreign Ministry singled out the regime’s aerial massacre in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State in late September which killed at least 50 and injured 58, as evidence of insecurity.

At a press conference in Taipei, Michael Lin of the ministry’s Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs said fighting between ethnic groups and the military regime make emergency rescues “extremely difficult.” He also warned of risks from scam centers, which are known to abduct unwary travelers, noting that its overseas missions have “almost no options” to assist citizens who get into trouble.

“If you know relatives or friends who insist on visiting these areas, make every effort to dissuade them, to avoid unnecessary trouble for themselves and their families,” Lin added.

The warning comes as the military regime intensifies its efforts to woo Chinese tourists from mainland China. Myanmar drew barely over 250,000 Chinese visitors in 2025, a sharp decline from the pre-coup boom.

Chinese explosives depot in KIA territory blows up

A blast at a Chinese road-building firm’s explosives warehouse in the village of Lagwi in Kachin State’s Chipwi Township killed seven and injured 11 on Oct. 2. The area is under the control of the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), which seized it in 2024 to secure its major export to China—rare earths.

The blast was so powerful it destroyed nearby homes and school buildings and was the third deadly incident at explosives depots in ethnic armed group territories this year. On May 31, a warehouse controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army in Namhkam Township blew up, killing more than 50 and injuring over 70. And on Sept. 8, a site under the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) in Hseni exploded, leaving at least 15 dead. Chinese companies are involved in mining in both areas.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader Says Will Take Back Migrants From Malaysia ‘as Soon as Possible’
World.content:
PUTRAJAYA, Malaysia—Myanmar will accept more returning migrants currently held in Malaysia “as soon as possible,” the war-torn nation’s leader said Thursday despite human rights concerns over the opaque repatriation scheme.

Min Aung Hlaing made the pledge on a visit to his counterpart in Malaysia, as he works to bring his country back into the international fold after staging a 2021 coup.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited Min Aung Hlaing, now installed as civilian president, for a two-day visit to discuss the return of thousands of migrants to his country.

Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar, hosting 190,000 refugees or asylum seekers from the nation—mostly Rohingya—according to the UN.

But Anwar is making a repatriation push amidst an uptick of anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia, defying concerns from the UN that his scheme cannot guarantee their safe return.

The country has been wracked by war since Min Aung Hlaing’s putsch, and there are fears the persecuted Rohingya may return to a country where they suffer violent persecution many deem genocide.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” Min Aung Hlaing said at a joint news conference with Anwar, in Putrajaya, the administrative capital.

‘Enhance collaboration’

Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since his putsch unleashed a civil war, but Anwar invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants.

Nearly 1,500 migrants arrived in back in Myanmar on Sunday after a five-day navy vessel voyage from Malaysia, where they were being held in detention centers before being shipped out.

Anwar in July announced that Myanmar agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya members, but the Malaysian government later said those sent back would be of “various ethnicities,” not only Rohingya.

Myanmar last month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.

Min Aung Hlaing’s two-day trip also comes as he makes a push for diplomatic recognition after being installed in April as civilian president, following elections branded a charade by democracy watchdogs.

Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) said in July they were seeking “gradual” engagement with Myanmar.

The 11-nation organization has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, presenting a united front to pressure its leaders into engaging in its conflict resolution plan.

But analysts say the consensus is now fraying.

Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he transitioned to ruling the country as nominally civilian president.

A five-point peace plan adopted by ASEAN’s leaders in April 2021, which among other things call for an immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar, has shown very little signs of progress.

This was highlighted by a Myanmar military airstrike late last month on a market in western Myanmar killing some 50 people—one of the deadliest recent bombings of the civil war.

Said Anwar on Thursday: “Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration.”

The aim ultimately was to “take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN.”

World.title: From Refuge to Repatriations: Malaysia’s Myanmar U-Turn
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia—Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim once urged his Muslim-majority nation to show solidarity with the persecuted Rohingya who fled Myanmar en masse, but this week rolled out the red carpet for the man accused of orchestrating their genocide.

Min Aung Hlaing touched down on Wednesday, invited for a two-day visit to discuss thousands of Myanmar migrants being sent back under a repatriation scheme touted by Anwar.

Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar by persecution or conflict.

The nation hosts 190,000 Myanmar refugees or asylum seekers, according to the UN, two-thirds of them from the Muslim Rohingya ethnic group.

But experts say fears that they burden Malaysia have been amplified by a cocktail of misinformation and an embattled Anwar, who hopes to capitalize on anti-Rohingya sentiment ahead of upcoming elections.

To carry out the repatriation plan, he has welcomed Min Aung Hlaing—previously shunned and credited with ordering the 2017 crackdown that sent legions of Rohingya fleeing to Malaysia in the first place.

Domestic hostility

Myanmar says it has repatriated around 8,000 citizens by air and 1,500 by sea so far this year, while Malaysia announced it is preparing 3,500 more to go back.

Kuala Lumpur has declined to say what proportion of returnees are Rohingya.

But experts say Malaysian attitudes towards migrants, particularly the Rohingya, soured during the COVID-19 pandemic when they became targets of misinformation about the disease.

“That hostility did not simply disappear afterwards,” Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor at Universiti Malaya, told AFP.

“This year there was another very visible surge in anti-Rohingya rhetoric online, alongside harassment.”

Newer resentments include claims that Malaysians are losing jobs to migrants, as well as the narrative that they are straining public resources or involved in crime.

“The early sympathy was very strong because Malaysians largely encountered the Rohingya through the language of persecution,” said Khoo.

“They were Muslims fleeing horrific violence in Myanmar, so religious solidarity and humanitarian sympathy came together quite naturally.”

But James Chin, a Malaysia expert at the University of Tasmania in Australia, said the nation was now dealing with a popular backlash against “allowing too many Rohingya to come”.

“This is ironic, because the only reason they were allowed to come in the first place is due to Islamic solidarity,” he told AFP.

“It has now changed completely the other way around.”

‘Election ploy’

In the past, Anwar appealed to Malaysians for solidarity towards migrants who fled upheaval in Myanmar credited to Min Aung Hlaing.

Min Aung Hlaing was the leader of the military when it began a 2017 crackdown evicting Rohingya in droves from their homes in western Myanmar.

The campaign is currently being weighed as a potential genocide by the International Court of Justice, but many rights monitors and some nations already deem it one.

Anwar’s about-face, which has seen him welcome Min Aung Hlaing and send back migrants, is partially due to a shift in domestic politics, experts say.

His Pakatan Harapan coalition has suffered setbacks in recent state elections in the runup to regional and national polls, which must be held by February 2028.

Among their defeats were losses to a coalition fronted by the United Malays National Organization, a formerly dominant party that draws much support from the Malay majority.

Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with NGO Fortify Rights, said Anwar’s repatriation push was an “election ploy” to court the vote of ethnic Malays.

“Anwar is being outflanked from the right in Malaysia. The conservatives and the nationalists have fashioned themselves as champions of the Malay majority interests.”

Targeting immigrants allows him “to be seen as a defender of the collective interest against outsiders,” said Yap, a powerful message for political campaigning.

‘Greater scrutiny’

Malaysia says all returned migrants have been sent from detention centers where they made voluntary decisions to go home.

But the UN has panned the scheme for being opaque and failing to provide guarantees of safety on return, as required by international law.

Min Aung Hlaing staged a 2021 coup that plunged the country into a grinding civil war, causing a fresh wave of upheaval sending yet more citizens fleeing abroad.

He is now making a push to normalize diplomatic ties after being installed as civilian president in April, following elections staged by his military junta and derided by democracy watchdogs.

Deals to return migrants may improve Anwar’s electoral prospects at home, but experts say it could tank Malaysia’s credibility abroad.

The repatriation came days after Malaysia’s foreign minister spoke at the UN General Assembly, advocating for international law to come to the aid of Palestinians.

“Malaysia speaks so strongly about the protection of civilians, humanitarian principles and the consistent application of international law in Palestine,” said Khoo of Universiti Malaya.

“There will inevitably be greater scrutiny of how those same principles are applied closer to home.”

World.title: Malaysian Firms Linked to Myanmar Military Aviation Supply Chain: JFM
World.content:
Several Malaysian companies, including some with direct financial ties to the state, are actively supplying or seeking to supply aircraft parts and maintenance services to the Myanmar military, which has been widely condemned for bombing its own civilian population, an investigation by Justice For Myanmar (JFM) revealed Wednesday.

JFM’s findings, based on leaked documents and commercial trade records, were announced during Myanmar coup president Min Aung Hlaing’s controversial official visit to Malaysia on October 7-8 at the invitation of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

The rights group said three Malaysia-based aerospace procurement and services companies—FJ Global Aeroparts (M) Sdn Bhd, Asia AeroTechnic Sdn Bhd (AAT), and Skyways Technics Asia Sdn Bhd—supplied or sought to supply parts to the regime military and its brokers, or in one case was approached to perform repairs, between 2023 and this year.

FJ Global sought to supply the regime with spare parts and critical components including weapons system parts for Russian- and Chinese-made aircraft used by the regime in its aerial campaigns, JFM said, adding that the company has sent multiple requests for quotations to international suppliers for spare parts for the regime’s warplanes and drones.

In February, FJ Global secured financing from state-backed Perbadanan Usahawan Nasional Berhad (PUNB), a company under the Prime Minister’s Department that is wholly owned by Yayasan Pelaburan Bumiputra, which is chaired by Anwar.

AAT is wholly owned by MARA Corporation, which is owned by MARA, an agency of Malaysia’s Ministry of Rural and Regional Development. According to JFM’s sources, regime military engineers visited the company in February 2026 regarding repairs to an Airbus A-319 owned by the Myanmar military.

JFM also claimed that Skyways Technics Asia, the Malaysian subsidiary of Denmark-based Skyways Technics A/S, has made numerous shipments of aircraft parts to arms brokers Light Head Group of Companies, KLS Aviation, United Five and Lucky High, which are registered suppliers to the Myanmar army’s Directorate of Procurement. JFM assessed that the Air Force was the likely end user.

Regime-controlled Myanmar National Airlines and Mingalar Aviation Airline (formerly Air KBZ), owned by the 24Hour Group founded by tycoon Aung Zaw Zaw, a crony with close ties to the junta boss, have also sought export approval to send aircraft parts to Skyways Technics in Malaysia for repair or exchange, the rights group said.

It noted that by knowingly providing support to the Myanmar military, which is widely accused of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity, Malaysian businesses could be aiding and abetting the regime’s crimes.

JFM also highlighted Malaysia’s ongoing facilitation of the regime’s participation in regional defense and security programs. Kuala Lumpur has invited a police official of the regime’s notorious Special Branch to attend the 29th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Intelligence Community Conference (AICC) in Kuala Lumpur in November.

Regime military officials were also allowed to participate in the 14th ASEAN Defense Minister’s Meeting (ADMM)-plus Experts Working Group on Counter-terrorism, which was jointly chaired by Malaysia and India in 2025.

The rights group said Malaysia’s support for the regime exposes the hypocrisy of its stated commitment to ending violence in Myanmar.

“It is deplorable that Malaysia is awarding false legitimacy to the war criminal Min Aung Hlaing and handing people back to his criminal junta while doing nothing to stop its companies from supplying a military that is committing mass atrocities,” said JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung.

The rights group added that “Instead of taking steps to cut off the resources needed for the junta to continue its violence, Malaysia has turned a blind eye to business complicity, while providing false legitimacy to the junta and handing Myanmar people to a murderous military that threatens their lives.”

“Malaysia’s stance on the Five-Point Consensus [ASEAN’s peace plan for Myanmar] and its calls for peace in Myanmar ring hollow while it fails to stop its companies from providing the military equipment and services that support its campaign of terror against the people,” Yadanar Maung said.

On September 28, regime airstrikes on a busy market and surrounding areas in Arakan Army-administered Kyauktaw town, Rakhine State, killed 50 civilians and injured nearly 60. The deadliest-ever aerial attack on civilians in the state drew global condemnation. However, the regime has continued its deadly aerial campaign of bombing civilian targets in resistance-controlled areas across the country.

Malaysia has faced widespread criticism from international rights groups and politicians for rolling out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, who faces an arrest warrant issued by an Argentine court over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya. The International Criminal Court’s prosecutor has also sought a warrant for his arrest over alleged crimes against humanity.

Malaysia recently defended its invitation as a necessary gesture to the coup leader for agreeing to receive deported Myanmar nationals.

World.title: Chinese Docuseries Hails Scam Victory as Myanmar Fraud Empire Rebuilds
World.content:
A Beijing-sanctioned docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry has hailed the extradition of fugitive tycoon She Zhijiang as the crowning achievement of China’s crackdown. Yet the telecom fraud empire he built in the border town of Myawaddy continues to thrive despite international pressure.

Once a bustling trade hub, Myawaddy is now among the most complicated combat landscapes in Myanmar, fought over by resistance forces, splinter factions, and regime‑aligned militias each tied to cross‑border commerce and illicit economies.

The fraud industry’s origins trace back to 2016–2017, when She Zhijiang’s Yatai International Holdings struck a deal with warlord Saw Chit Thu, commander of the military-aligned Karen Border Guard Force (BGF). Marketed as a U$ 15‑billion “New City” project, Shwe Kokko was pitched as a blockchain hub but quickly morphed into casinos, call centers, and cyber‑fraud parks.

Belt and Road Beginnings

Yatai stated the project was part of the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s flagship international infrastructure development scheme. Thousands of Chinese nationals poured in. But by 2020, civil society groups were sounding alarms about criminal activities under militia protection, prompting the Chinese Embassy in Yangon to declare that the project had nothing to do with the BRI.

Aung San Suu Kyi’s NLD government ordered a suspension, but admitted it was difficult to enforce given the involvement of armed groups. After the 2021 coup, civil war engulfed the country and the scam industry boomed.

Today, Myawaddy’s scam compounds are hosted by the BGF (now rebranded as the Karen National Army—KNA) and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), both allied with the regime. The documentary aired this week by China’s state-run CCTV made no mention of either militia.

At its peak, more than 40 heavily guarded scam compounds operated in Myawaddy, according to a Chinese police source quoted in the docuseries.

She Zhijiang was arrested in Bangkok in August 2022 and later extradited to China, but his legacy lives on in Myanmar’s borderlands.

Crackdown ‘Backfired’

The arrest of She Zhijiang had limited impact on the Myawaddy scam economy because he was just one of many investors, said one local China analyst.

“There are other criminal syndicates with longer tentacles than She Zhijiang. Since his arrest, nearly five dozen scam sites have sprung up across Karen and Shan states,” he said, adding that Beijing’s crackdown may have worsened the problem by forcing the syndicates to relocate deeper into Myanmar.

Beijing itself admits that syndicates uprooted from northern Shan State in late 2023 regrouped in Myawaddy, swelling the scam economy there.

China finally intervened in early 2025, forced into action by public anger over the trafficking of Shanghai soap actor Wang Xing into a scam compound. Wang was lured by a fake casting offer in Bangkok, whisked across the Moei River, and resold three times in four days by Myawaddy scam compounds before being rescued.

In March 2025, Beijing established a trilateral ministerial mechanism with Bangkok and Naypyitaw to combat scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border, pinpointing Myawaddy as a key target.

Later that year, under mounting international pressure, Myanmar’s military demolished scam compounds in Shwe Kokko and KK Park during high-profile raids. However, locals reported that syndicates simply relocated to less conspicuous sites in Myawaddy and neighboring townships, under DKBA and KNA protection.

Regime-Aligned Scam Militias Untouched

“We have a zero‑tolerance policy for crimes like online fraud and gambling,” regime boss Min Aung Hlaing declared on Police Force Day earlier this month. Yet his BGF/KNA allies—Saw Chit Thu, Saw Mote Thone, Tin Win and others—remain untouched along with scam compounds they protect that have defrauded billions of dollars from American citizens, according to US authorities.

The CCTV documentary also celebrates the extradition of Chen Zhi, accused of running a multibillion‑dollar cyberscam network from Cambodia.

Meanwhile, China’s Public Security Ministry claims telecom fraud cases have declined since October 2025, following the crackdown in northern Myanmar. Not so, states the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which reports a sharp rise in trafficking to scam centers across Asia, with victims from more than 80 countries coerced into the trade. The UN estimates compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos still employ around 300,000 people.

Last month, Beijing unveiled the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud with much fanfare, listing 46 founding countries including Myanmar. Officials hailed it as a landmark in global cooperation. Yet on the ground in Myawaddy, the scam industry remains a lucrative lifeline for militias and regime allies—a shadow economy still flourishing despite raids, indictments, and international pressure.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s New Labor Minister Outlines Mission: Milking Migrants
World.content:
Less than 48 hours after taking charge of the Labor Ministry, Maung Myint’s first public statement ignored protections for Myanmar workers and instead focused on squeezing them for revenue.

On Monday, the newly appointed minister declared that income tax for migrant workers was too low, while vowing to tighten the regime’s remittance rules. Posting on TikTok, he said overseas workers “represent the nation” and should therefore contribute more to the country.

Economic collapse driven by regime mismanagement, withdrawal of foreign investment, sanctions, and civil war following the 2021 coup has triggered a mass exodus of workers. As a result, remittances soared to US$ 5.6 billion in 2025 according to Bloomberg—nearly 7 percent of GDP and double the 2019 figure. While remittances have become a crucial lifeline for millions of struggling families, the cash-strapped regime has targeted them as lucrative source of foreign revenue.

Maung Myint served as labor minister under Thein Sein in 2012-13, returning this April as hotels and tourism minister for the rebranded regime before being shunted the Labor Ministry on October 3.

Two days later, he warned that overseas workers are required to remit 25 percent of their wages through regime-controlled banks. “But some fail to do so, meaning the state sees no returns from workers it has sent abroad. We need to correct this and ensure the regime benefits,” he said.

Emphasizing management of overseas workers as a “key duty” of his ministry, he added that remittances from Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, China, Cambodia, Laos, the Middle East, the US and Europe were “too small” and must be increased.

Thailand hosts the largest number of Myanmar migrants, estimated at 4-5 million, followed by Malaysia (300,000–350,000). Myanmar is now the second‑largest labor exporter in Asia after the Philippines.

Labor rights activists point to the regime’s remittance policy as textbook exploitation.

“It imposes rigid rules to grab as much tax as possible from migrant workers. Cash-strapped and incapable of running an economy, it can only think of targeting citizens abroad who face deepening hardship as a result,” said Aung Kyaw, a labor activist in Thailand.

Myanmar migrant workers traditionally rely on the informal hundi system to transfer money back home. However, under the regime’s remittance rule introduced in September 2023, workers must remit at least a quarter of their foreign currency earnings through official channels. Workers have denounced the rule as brazen exploitation due to the exchange rate gap.

“If they want us to remit 25 percent through legal channels, they should use the market exchange rate. Currently, the market rate is 130 kyats per baht, but the regime offers just 63 kyats. If I remit 5,000 baht via a regime bank, I lose over 300,000 kyat instantly,” one worker in Thailand told The Irrawaddy.

The Central Bank’s official rate is 2,100 kyat per US dollar though since December authorized banks have offered 3,600 kyats. However, the market rate is around 4,300 kyats.

In August, the regime instructed Yangon employment agencies to enforce a Family Remittance Management System to ensure workers comply with the rule. Over 100 licensed labor agencies were recently fined and suspended for failing to provide remittance records.

The ministry is now collecting lists of workers who ignore the remittance rule, threatening them with non-renewal of passports and Overseas Worker Identification Cards.

Adding to the burden, the junta imposed a 2 percent income tax on overseas workers starting October 1, 2023. Only those who can show tax receipts are allowed to renew passports or obtain new ID certificates.

Thein Sein’s government abolished the traditional taxation of overseas workers under military rule. Desperate for hard currency, the current regime has not only revived the practice but doubled down on milking the very diaspora it forced into exile.

World.title: Caspian Sea’s Shrinking Shoreline Puts Regional Economies at Risk, Tokayev Says
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for coordinated regional action to address the Caspian Sea’s shrinking water levels, proposing a shared digital monitoring platform and an international biodiversity fund. The environmental crisis also poses growing risks to regional economies and communities, he said, speaking at the Caspian Ecological Summit on Oct. 9 in Avaza.

According to him, the sea’s surface area had decreased by more than 16,000 square kilometers between 2000 and 2025, while the Caspian seal population had fallen from around one million to 270,000 over the past century.

“The Caspian is a unique natural treasure, a source of well-being for millions of people, and a key transport and energy hub for the entire Eurasian continent. Therefore, preserving the Caspian Sea’s ecosystem requires special attention, primarily from our states,” Tokayev said.
