Little National Hotel Adelaide has opened on North Terrace, bringing 237 rooms to a $100 million, 21-storey tower in the heart of the South Australian capital. But while the fourth Little National retains the compact rooms that have become the Australian brand’s calling card, this time there’s more room to move. The Little National Room is 18 square metres with a super king bed. For the first time, guests can book apartments, family-friendly configurations and even two penthouses, as owner Doma Group evolves the “luxury-lite” formula it introduced in Canberra. It’s a simple formula: rather than make guests pay for square metres they may not need, put the money elsewhere – towards, say, an excellent king-sized bed, good bathroom and sophisticated design – then compensate for compact bedrooms with generous communal spaces. It was evident when Little National Canberra opened in 2015, and then in Sydney and Newcastle.



The Adelaide site heralds an evolution. While 140 rooms are classic Little National Rooms, at the top of the building are two penthouses with generous living spaces and private bars stocked with premium South Australian wines. There are also 38 square metre Luxe Apartments for longer stays. 



But that began to change when the smart, keenly priced Ibis Adelaide opened behind Rundle Mall in 2014, then the Mayfair followed at the luxury end in 2015, before a steady succession of arrivals including Eos by SkyCity, Hotel Indigo, Sofitel, Vibe and Adelaide Marriott. Now there’s a new surge on. Rooftop bar and lounge area at Little National Hotel Adelaide. The 170-room Mayfair is undergoing an extensive refurbishment before reopening next year as Kimpton Mayfair Adelaide, bringing IHG’s luxury lifestyle brand to South Australia. And Little National won’t have the 2026 newcomer spotlight to itself for long.



The $130 million Crystalbrook Sam is scheduled to open on Halifax Street in December, with 196 rooms and suites, a day spa, heated outdoor pool and rooftop bar and grill. It will be Crystalbrook Collection’s first South Australian hotel. Related Article ★★★★

Hotel reviews A stylish central Sydney hotel for under $150 a night? It exists More are coming. A 248-room Treehouse Hotel above the redeveloped Adelaide Central Market is expected to open in early 2027, the brand’s Australian debut. Veriu is also due to make its Adelaide entrance in 2027. Further out, plans include the Westin Adelaide on North Terrace and a new 251-room Hilton in the East End. In all, the South Australian government says 15 hotel projects are at various stages of development across metropolitan Adelaide, 11 of them in the CBD. See littlenationalhotel.com.au

A man has been charged over alleged “offensive behaviour” on the footbridge at the centre of last year’s Bondi Beach massacre.

A 53-year-old man was arrested at 3pm on Friday at the beach’s northern pedestrian bridge, on which father-and-son gunmen Naveed and Sajid Akram stood as they killed 15 people.

Witnesses said the man had hung a flag from the bridge, NSW Police said in a statement. Unverified photos from social media show a Palestinian flag hanging over the side of the bridge.

Police said he had “performed offensive hand gestures”, but a spokesperson declined to detail what they were.

The man was taken to Surry Hills Police Station, where he was charged with behaving in an offensive manner in a public place. He was denied police bail and will face bail court later today.

World.title: Strong earthquake in Central America sparks Pacific tsunami fears
World.content:
A large quake has struck the Central American country of Panama, briefly prompting fears of a Pacific tsunami.

It hit at 6.56am NZ time in the south of the country, measuring magnitude 7.7 at a depth of 33km. It was initially reported as magnitude 8, downgraded to 7.6 then adjusted to 7.7.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) and GNS Science initially said it was assessing whether the quake had created a tsunami that could affect New Zealand.

"Based on current information, the initial assessment is that the earthquake is unlikely to have caused a tsunami that will affect New Zealand," it said about half an hour later.

There were no immediate reports of damage in Panama, Reuters reported, with television footage showing people evacuating buildings.

There were 51 New Zealanders registered with safetravel.govt.nz as being in Panama. Officials said they had not received any requests for assistance.

The US Tsunami Warning Center's latest issue said based on all available data, there was no tsunami threat to Guam, Rota, Tininan or Saipan, nor American Samoa or Hawai'i.

There were earlier warnings of potential tsunami across Central America and in Columbia and Ecuador.

The quake was felt in the capital, Reuters reported, and in Costa Rica.

Aftershocks measuring up to magnitude 5.8 followed soon after.

The Ford Football Ferns were in Panama during the earthquake and set to play the Panama team on Sunday.

New Zealand Football confirmed in a statement that all members of the squad were safe and accounted for.

World.title: National proposes new marine reserves, complete ban on ring-net fishing in Hauraki Gulf
World.content:
An earlier version of this story said the party proposed a ban on commercial fishing. This has been corrected to ring-net fishing.

The National Party would follow the Greens in banning ring-net fishing in the Hauraki Gulf's high protection areas, as part of its election fisheries policy.

The party says if re-elected, it will also establish a new marine reserve off Waiheke Island, expand the size of the Goat Island reserve, and ban the commercial sale of marlin.

It has stopped short of a ban on bottom trawling, with a policy document saying National would review bottom trawling on seamounts, with an aim to increase protections from 32 percent to 50 percent of New Zealand's exclusive economic zone by 2040.

A $20 million 'fish tech innovation fund' would, in partnership with the seafood sector, help reduce the impact of bottom trawling, aiming to improve fishing gear.

National is also ruling out a recreational fishing licence, saying "fishing for a feed is a Kiwi right."

Oceans and fisheries spokesperson Todd McClay said all fishers, commercial and recreational, depended on the health of New Zealand's waters.

"While some people catch their own fish, most New Zealanders enjoy seafood from their local supermarket or fish and chip shop. Ensuring the long-term sustainability of our fisheries is critical for both coastal communities and consumers."

Earlier this month, the Greens released their own fisheries policy, which included a total ban on bottom trawling, starting with seamounts and ecologically significant areas like the Hauraki Gulf.

It would also immediately ban ring-net fishing in the Hauraki Gulf's high protection areas, while National has not put a time-frame on its policy.

World.title: Election 2026 live: Animal rights group disappointed fireworks ban lacks support from major parties
World.content:
Campaining in the 2026 general election continues, with the major parties both vying for Aucklanders' votes this weekend.

Meanwhile, the Animal Law Association is disappointed Labour and National have not backed a ban on fireworks.

New Zealand First has pledged to introduce legislation within the first 100 days of a new government, to ban the public sale and private use of fireworks. Its coalition partners National and ACT rejected a recommendation to do so in July, arguing a ban would remove access to a longstanding legal activity.

World.title: Two dead, two seriously injured as homicide investigation launched in Christchurch
World.content:
A 58-year-old man has been charged after two people died and another two were seriously injured in Christchurch.

Police were called to an address on Olliviers Road, in the suburb of Phillipstown, overnight.

Police are wanting to reassure the public that there is no risk to their safety. Louis Dunham/RNZ

Detective Inspector Greg Murton said two people died at the scene, while two others were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

"The man will face two charges of murder, one charge of attempted murder and one for wounding with intent.

"He will appear in the Christchurch District Court on Monday 12 October."

Murton said police believed this was an isolated incident and are not seeking anyone else.

"Police want to reassure the public there is no risk to their safety but also appreciate this incident will be deeply upsetting and unsettling for those who reside in the area."

Police said people should expect an increased police presence in the coming days and appreciate their co-operation as scene examinations continue.

A neighbour said it sounded like an argument broke out at the east Christchurch house.

Louis Dunham/RNZ

He said the street was rowdier than usual.

"It sounded like it was a bit of a party going on, someone was pissed off or whatever. I heard a little bit yelling and doors constantly being slammed, banging on cars."

"I feel a bit shocked, but times are tough. Drugs are always an issue."

Detective Inspector Nicola Reeves is asking anyone who may have seen anything, or may have CCTV of the area, to contact 105.

World.title: 'Threatened to smash my face in': Mum of autistic teen struggles with awful noisy neighbours
World.content:
An Auckland mother says her autistic teenage daughter is being terrorised by noisy neighbours at their Kāinga Ora apartment complex.

"About six months ago new tenants moved in and have completely flipped our lives upside down," Jamie, who asked to keep her surname private to protect her daughter, said.

"They play extremely, extremely loud music that vibrates through my entire house. It's 24/7 constant banging, thumping, stomping, late night visitors, dogs barking. They are the most disruptive neighbours we've ever had."

Jamie said her daughter had severe noise sensitivity and was now wearing headphones all day to manage the noise.

"She can't eat properly, she's not sleeping, she stays up all night and sleeps during the day. She's isolated herself to her bedroom."

Jamie complained to Kāinga Ora, who visited and spoke to the neighbours, but said this didn't help.

"Basically I've just been stonewalled. Nothing seems to be changing."

"They either need to be issued some sort of warning that's going to stop this, or we need to be moved. They need to realise we can't live in an environment that's hostile to my daughter."

In a statement, Kāinga Ora regional director Taina Jones said staff had followed up on Jamie's complaints.

"We understand Jamie's daughter has autism and can be particularly sensitive to noise.

"We have taken Jamie's concerns seriously, however, as part of our enquiries we received differing accounts from those involved about when the music has been played, how loud it has been, and the broader circumstances surrounding the complaints."

Jones said the neighbours had been reminded of their obligations to be respectful to those around them, and that staff were still investigating Jamie's most recent complaint.

Jamie said she had attempted to resolve the issue herself by confronting the neighbours, but this went poorly.

"I had enough and I went to speak to them, just being very nice and calmly asked them, 'What is this banging? Is there something we can do to stop it?' and they were so hostile, threatened to smash my face in, and the police had to be called," she recounted.

"It's caused me to not want to leave my home, I'm isolated in my house. I go to step out my door and I've got to look left and right and then sometimes I decide I can't do it and go back inside and shut my door."

Jones said Kāinga Ora was aware of that altercation.

"Everyone has the right to feel safe and comfortable in their home. Our role as a landlord is to establish the facts and deal fairly with all parties involved.

World.title: Christchurch man charged over disappearance and death of Braydon Hepworth
World.content:
A 60-year-old Christchurch man has been charged in relation to the disappearance and death of Braydon Hepworth.

The charges relate to the concealment of the 21-year-old's body and making a false statement.

He will appear in the Christchurch District Court on Saturday morning.

Police found a body during a search of a Hereford Street property on Thursday.

The last confirmed sighting of Hepworth was on 3 September at Linwood Z Energy service station.

Supplied / Police

On Thursday, Detective Inspector Scott Anderson said a significant police operation was involved in finding Hepworth.

"This is a devastating outcome for his family, and our hearts go out to them. We are providing them with support at this extremely difficult time," he said.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, there is a small comfort in being able to bring him home."

Hepworth's mother Char Huntley earlier begged anyone who knew anything about her son's disappearance to "speak up".

World.title: Large fire extinguished at Lower Hutt home
World.content:
A large fire in the Lower Hutt suburb of Melling has been extinguished.

Fire and Emergency were called to a house around 6.30am on Saturday, which was found to be well-involved upon arrival.

Crews from Seaview, Avalon, Johnsonville, Thorndon, Wellington City, Wainuiomata, and Remutaka had responded.

While the fire had been extinguished by 7am, firefighters remain at the scene.

All people have been accounted for, but it is not yet known if any have been injured.

A spokesperson for Wellington Free Ambulance confirmed it attended the fire.

"As this involves a private residence, we are unable to provide further information to protect patient privacy and confidentiality."

World.title: Turning wasted wood into biochemicals, biofuels seen as 'the future for New Zealand'
World.content:
A bioenergy expert is promoting the production of wood-based fuels and biochemicals as the "future for New Zealand", as entrepreneurs map out manufacturing hubs in Bay of Plenty.

Investors have their hats in hand to build a new $50 million bio-manufacturing facility in Rotorua with aspirations of turning woody biomass into high-value products like biochemicals, ingredients or biofuel near the Kaingaroa Forest Estate, the country's largest forestry plantation.

The proposed biofactory would utilise raw biomass from forestry, agriculture, horticulture and aquaculture industries into value-add products, and would be a commercial testing ground for companies of all sizes.

Rendered image of the biofactory facility being tipped for Rotorua. SUPPLIED/The BioFactory

This week, Rotorua MP and Forestry Minister Todd McClay committed to matching industry's $15m in capital investment with funding from the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI). The project would require a private property developer with $20m in backing to fund the build.

Meanwhile, in the week prior, the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority announced $3.7m in funding for five forestry waste collection projects near commercial operations.

In a separate project, work to establish a biorefinery at Kaingaroa Forest Estate was also underway. Local firm with Singaporean backing NZ Bio Forestry and Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Manawa were still in the technical exploratory stage for the biorefinery, with iwi consulting the Kaingaroa village community on it.

Recycling forestry waste into value

The Bioenergy Association's executive officer Brian Cox said New Zealand had an abundance of forestry biomass that was under-utilised, especially in energy generation.

"We work with farmers, forestry business communities who've got access to wood and biomass and organic waste to extract value, for energy in our case.

"But those materials are also great for extracting biochemicals and other bioplastics etcetera, which are going to be the future for New Zealand."

Kaingaroa forest

Cox said about 20 percent of a commercial tree was discarded at present, such as being left in the forest or sawdust from the mills.

"We're getting better and better at packing that up and recycling it into valuable products."

"We can make it into a fuel for energy... We can also make from those residues other chemicals and those are the things that we're starting to do."

Cox said the move to biomass energy was still emerging in parts of the North Island that had relied heavily on gas, which was in short supply, and expensive electricity. He said bio-processing projects around Kaingaroa would have scale and sensible locations being near the forest.

Kaingaroa forest manager harnessing new opportunities

Foundational investor, Kaingaroa Tipu (formerly Timberlands) managed around 230,000 hectares of the Kaingaroa Forest Estate, that was returned to tangata whenua in 2009, where it produced four million logs each year.

Chief executive Ryan Cavanagh said a biofactory would unlock the value from wood, and reduce the concentration risk for forestry, which relied on logs for construction, residue markets like pulp and bark, and utility logs to China.

Ryan Cavanagh, chief executive of Kaingaroa Tipu, that manages the logging operation at New Zealand's largest forestry estate. SUPPLIED/Kaingaroa Tipu

"Ourselves and many other forestry companies within New Zealand sell broadly into three markets. For the last five years we've been thinking as a business hard about the future and what that entails. We still need to look for new markets for the future, hence why the biofactory and the bioeconomy is so attractive."

Cavanagh said there was huge opportunity in emerging sectors, away from typical forestry commodities like logs. He said it was important to think about the customers of tomorrow and trying to leverage the forest's scale.

"If a new opportunity comes in New Zealand and, for instance, we want to build a biofactory to make a chemical or to make a fragrance or to produce an energy pellet, we'd rather that's done either in our forest or very close to our forest. So we're looking at all of those opportunities there to create value for the future."

The biofactory was planned to host companies of all sizes, allowing them to test and scale their products and ideas while using abundant feedstock volumes available there. The BioFactory concept was led by the NZ Product Accelerator with support from the Bioeconomy Science Institute, Sequal and MPI. Similar government-backed biofactory models could be found in Canada, Belgium, Germany and the United Kingdom.

World.title: Bulldogs dominant in win over Bombers to start Pride Round
World.content:
The Western Bulldogs have brought a ruthless mentality to Pride Round in thrashing Essendon by 43 points.

Friday night's 10.5 (65) to 2.10 (22) result was the Bulldogs' seventh win for the season and sent a warning to the top eight sides on the cusp of finals.

It came despite their shaky start in front of a home crowd at Whitten Oval.

Essendon came out firing and Emily Gough kicked the first goal inside the first two minutes, spurring the Dons, who played with high pressure and repeatedly locked the ball in their forward half.

The Bulldogs responded with five unanswered goals with the help of an unstoppable Isabelle Pritchard, who had 30 disposals and 10 clearances.

"We weren't playing the style of game that we came to play," Dogs midfielder Jess Fitzgerald said after quarter time.

"We wanted to come into the game with a bit of a ruthless mentality, and we felt like we didn't bring that in the first.

"So, yeah, we turned that on."

Essendon were down by 25 points at half-time but hopes of repeating last week's win over the Giants, a comeback from 24 points down at half-time, were cut short by their inability to find the goals.

After Gough's early major, the Bombers kicked nine points until Sophie Alexander found their second just before three-quarter time.

The Bombers managed one more point in the final term, while the Dogs slotted another three goals.

Star forward Sarah Hartwig had a career-high four goals and helped the Western Bulldogs surpass the 60-point mark for the fifth time since 2025.

"Honestly, it's just that work rate and the pressure that we bring, especially in the forward line. That's what we pride ourselves on," she said.

Despite the win, the Bulldogs still have work to do in the season's run home, Hartwig said.

"We're not looking to finals yet. We've got three tough games coming up, so we're going to focus on that first," she said.

The Dogs will face Carlton, Melbourne and Geelong — all premiership contenders — in the final three games of the season.

Essendon will play North Melbourne, before facing Hawthorn and Collingwood.

AAP

World.title: Australia's Test start no disaster, but order issues hint at troubles ahead
World.content:
It was Steve Waugh — Mr Mental Disintegration himself — who once said the most emotionally taxing aspect of his time as the most important man in Australian cricket was not the burden of captaincy, nor the concurrent need to keep making big runs, but his role as a national selector.

How long to wait for a treasured teammate's form to come right, when the axe might end his career? Should he be replaced with fresh blood or someone on a second or third chance, as Waugh himself had once been? What was the right balance of talent and personalities?

Overnight in Durban, Waugh's man-management issues seemed trifling compared to the self-inflicted problems of Australia's current selectors. But you'd need a very specific combination of tarot cards and crystals to work out which question of George Bailey's led to the answer "Nic Maddinson".

The final analysis on day one was not entirely disastrous. Australia stumbled to 6-187 before bad light stopped play and there were at least positive signs in a few problematic areas.

One was a solid start from Marnus Labuschagne, whose momentary lapse on the brink of lunch ended a sparkling partnership with Steve Smith. The other was a steady hand from Matt Renshaw, who was undefeated on 46 at the day's premature end.

Renshaw renaissance rescues Aussies Matt Renshaw is stranded four runs short of his first Test half-century in nine years as bad light halts play on the first day of the opening Test against South Africa.

There were deeper currents, though. Troubling ones. What stood out was not just the sense of a well-drilled bowling attack reminding the world why South Africa was the reigning world champion, but of Australia, with its makeshift batting order and selection on the fly, presenting as an increasingly confused rabble.

Maddinson's mere selection was contentious enough; he had not played a first-class match in 19 months. The corollary was throwing him to the wolves as opener on a pitch offering lateral movement. That second part was so surprising to most onlookers that the host broadcaster initially had him down as batting at five.

But then, how else could it have played out? Had Cooper Connolly got the nod instead, he probably would have slotted in at five and Renshaw would have moved up to open with Travis Head, himself a world-class number five whose impact in Tests is now being blunted by his ongoing hostage ordeal at the top of the order. Further problems flow from there.

You had to feel for Maddinson. Mark Waugh, who was among the selectors who picked the left-hander for his first three Tests in 2016, has since admitted he had been discarded too quickly. Now he's been brought back almost at random and given this thankless task.

Maddinson's 33-ball duck was awful to watch, but one would hope he's backed to make a slightly better fist of whatever follows.

Another thing Steve Waugh used to do was make it clear to each player in his team what was expected of them in their specific role. It's hard to imagine things being phrased so plainly now. Aside from Labuschagne and Smith, could any current Australian batsman say he's in the right spot for the right reason?

Another cheap dismissal for Travis Head raises questions about his experimental role as opener. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

At 32, Head's identity crisis should, on current evidence, be considered a serious matter for the future of this team.

Right now, we are being asked to accept that Renshaw — an undoubtedly tough and capable player whose Test record is nevertheless modest — needs to bat where he is most comfortable, and that as a result, Head, now in his prime years, needs to play an essentially experimental role that is clearly not suited to him.

It is true that Bailey's job has been made harder by injuries to Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, and a dearth of irresistible opening candidates in the Sheffield Shield. But the strangest aspect of all the pre-tour kvetching over selection was how much of it centered on Labuschagne, who was and remains the logical choice at three.

Far more baffling, in hindsight, was the lack of focus on Bailey's claim that the number-three slot could be just as easily filled by Connolly, who has never made a first-class century, or the since-injured Inglis, neither of whom have batted higher than five for their state.

Even in this era of "false threes" and result pitches, the linchpin positions in the top order should surely not be devalued so casually. Australia is now approaching double digits for opening combinations of the post-Warner era.

Anyway, that is what Australia could have controlled. What it still can't, it seems, is the sideways movement of medium pacers. When this tour was merely on the horizon, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi loomed as the destroyers.

Both are missing in Durban, yet Marco Jansen and Wiaan Mulder caused Australia just as many problems without Jansen ever really hitting their stride.

It made for an absorbing battle, but for Australia things could actually have been far worse. We must now accept a world order in which the combination of the words "Ollie Robinson" and "Ashes hero" are not just plausible but a distinct possibility.

The consolation is that a Test series is never decided on its opening day and can therefore often be taken with a grain of salt, per Merv Hughes's tinder-dry diary entry following the first day of another Test series, three decades ago:

"Back to hotel. Few beers downstairs, then up to room … Have room service. Watch Cape Fear. Quiet night." Thus ended the day Shane Warne bowled the ball of the century.

Nothing so dramatic transpired this time around but, for Australia, you sense the road ahead will be trying.

World.title: Quick hits: Maddinson makes historic 33-ball duck as Aussie batters flounder
World.content:
Nic Maddinson's unlikely Test return has ended with a historic duck as Australia's battered floundered despite a South African DRS debacle.

Here are the quick hits from the opening day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Maddinson makes historic duck on return

Maddinson was unable to make the most of an early reprieve on day one. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

With almost a decade having passed since the last of his three Test appearances, veteran opener Nic Maddinson could have been forgiven for thinking his days in Australian whites were over.

But after being parachuted into the squad earlier this week, the 34-year-old's sensational return to the Test arena was cemented at the toss in Durban, with Pat Cummins confirming Maddinson would be the replacement for the injured Cameron Green.

In an even bigger surprise, he was in line to open his side's innings, with the also recently recalled Matt Renshaw dropping down the order.

Maddinson did not play at all in the last Sheffield Shield season, with his last First Class appearance having come back in March 2025.

And with Australia winning the toss and batting, he was put to the test immediately.

Maddinson looked both nervy and underdone in his drought-breaking Test knock, unable to get off the mark during his first 32 balls before being dismissed by his 33rd, the New South Welshman chopping onto his stumps off the bowling of Marco Jansen.

Unfortunately for Maddinson, it was a historic return as well as a miserable one, his 33-ball effort setting a new record for the longest duck by an Aussie opener in Test cricket.

Overall, it was the second-longest no score by an Australian in the history of the format, only behind Mike Whitney's 42-ball 0 in 1981.

2. South Africa in DRS debacle

Nic Maddinson was unable to make the most of an early reprieve. (Fox Cricket)

Only minutes earlier, Maddinson had been gifted a huge slice of luck.

With the opener swinging across the line wildly, a Wiaan Mulder delivery thudded into his front pad. There was a big appeal, but umpire Richard Kettlebrough was unmoved.

South African captain Temba Bavuma indicated Maddinson had gotten some bat on ball and opted against the first review of the series.

And there certainly were two noises but replays showed Maddinson's willow had gotten nowhere near the ball, instead clipping his pad.

The South Africans watched the big screen ruefully as it showed the three reds that would have sent Maddinson back to the pavilion.

It was an unconvincing start for the South Africans as far DRS was concerned, with Bavuma also burning two reviews on appeals that didn't have a whole lot going for them.

First, Marnus Labuschagne survived a referral on a ball that swung too sharply and was projected to be missing leg stump.

Then, the hosts wasted a second review when a steepling Marco Jansen delivery caught Renshaw on the arm. The ball had looped up to wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, who took a simple catch, and the South Africans were convinced it had brushed the Australian's glove.

It hadn't.

The replays showed Jansen had found nothing but arm guard and the hosts had just one review remaining.

3. Labuschagne departs on stroke of lunch

Labuschagne's innings came to an end on the stroke of lunch. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It was a gut-wrenching end to an innings of serious promise for Labuschagne.

The Queenslander, so desperately in need of a score to get his Test career back on track, reached the final over of the morning session on 37 and with one eye on kicking on after the first break.

He was able to see off the first five balls of the set, but fell on its last.

Angling into the right-hander, Mulder was able to sneak one past Labuschagne's outside edge and into the front pad.

It looked touch and go whether the ball made impact in-line with the stumps, but the umpire's finger was up.

Labuschagne didn't look overly hopeful sending the decision upstairs, but DRS showed how close he was to getting outside the line of off stump, with the Australian only having to leave the field because of the umpire's original call.

It is not the kind of luck you need when you've gone more than three years without a Test century.

4. Smith makes anticlimactic entrance

Smith couldn't make the most of his start. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

With all that had been made of Steve Smith's return to the country his Test career had so shockingly unravelled eight years earlier, the understated reception he received when entering the game felt at least a little anticlimactic.

There was no chorus of boos from the few spectators in place for the morning session as Smith joined Labuschagne at the crease, tasked with steadying the Australian innings with both Maddinson and Head back in the sheds.

And Smith began his innings like he had so often in the past: fidgety, idiosyncratic and paranoid, but set on getting himself into the game.

After seeing off the opening pace barrage, Smith stamped his authority on the morning with two big sixes back over the head of spinner Keshav Maharaj in the space of four balls.

Smith made it to lunch, but only lasted three balls after the first break.

He was struck on the finger by a rearing Marco Jansen length ball, before edging the very next delivery through to the slips.

Smith was out for 25 and Australia had lost two wickets in four balls either side of the lunch break.

5. Bad light robs Renshaw of drought-breaking milestone

Matt Renshaw was Australia's best on day one. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Coming in at number five, Renshaw was a bright spot in an otherwise dark day for the Australian batters.

The southpaw watched on as South African spearhead Anrich Nortje removed Alex Carey and Beau Webster in the space of three balls, and looked supremely confident in his new home in the middle order.

He made his way to 46 before bad light ended the day with over an hour left of scheduled play and just 65.2 overs bowled.

Renshaw will begin day two four runs away from his first Test 50 in more than 3,500 days, tasked with continuing to rebuild Australia's innings alongside Cummins.

World.title: Wallabies join former boss Rennie in mutual admiration society
World.content:
It had the potential to be one of the compelling plot lines in the build-up to tonight's first Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.

How does Dave Rennie feel about leading the All Blacks against the Wallabies, the team he coached until he was sacked in 2023?

But for Rennie and his former gold-clad pupils, there is no animosity.

Wallabies skipper Harry Wilson was handed a Test debut under Dave Rennie in 2020. (Getty Images/Nations Championship: Asanka Ratnayake)

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson could not have spoken more highly of Rennie when he addressed the media yesterday.

Wilson made his Test debut under the New Zealander in 2020, when he was thrown into the cauldron-like atmosphere of a Bledisloe Cup Test in Wellington a few months shy of his 21st birthday.

"I really enjoyed playing under Dave," Wilson said at the Wallabies' captain's run at Eden Park.

Wallabies must 'walk the walk' Confidence may be high, but the Wallabies know talk is cheap if they are to win their first Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park since 1986.

"He gave me my Test debut and I played a few Tests under him. I've always been really appreciative of that."

Wilson added: "I definitely learnt a lot from him … I know he has got a lot of respect from this group.

"He was, I guess, a very loved member of the Wallabies when he was [coach] and it's going to be different going up against him, that's for sure."

Rennie, whose contract as Wallabies coach was terminated in January 2023, was equally glowing in his praise of the players he coached during his time in Australia.

"I know a lot about the [Wallabies] players, obviously," Rennie said on Thursday.

"There's a big number of them who started in 2020 and they've now played 50, or 60 or 70 Tests.

"So what we know is they're a good side. They're experienced and they've played a lot of football together."

Rennie has 'no regrets'

Rennie was shown the door by Rugby Australia after returning a 38 per cent win record from 34 Tests in charge between 2020-22.

He was replaced immediately by Eddie Jones, who lasted 10 months in the role before resigning.

Jones coached the Wallabies to their worst showing at a Rugby World Cup in 2023, when they failed to reach the quarterfinals for the first time.

Dave Rennie took charge of the All Blacks earlier this year. (Getty Images/Nations Championship: Morgan Hancock)

Rennie's poor winning percentage was cited among the reasons for his axing.

What must be acknowledged, however, was the fact he inherited a struggling Wallabies program in the wake of their quarterfinal exit at the 2019 Rugby World Cup.

Rennie also had to contend with coaching a squad during the height of the COVID pandemic, although this did affect every international team.

Among the highlights of his tenure was a 24-22 triumph over the All Blacks in Brisbane in 2020, which was the last time the Wallabies tasted victory over their trans-Tasman rivals.

Rennie to coach All Blacks Three years after he was sacked as Wallabies coach, Dave Rennie is put in charge of the All Blacks for the next two seasons.

But inconsistent results proved his downfall, while Jones's availability following his sacking as England coach in late 2022 was also a contributing factor.

The opportunity to coach at the Test level for a second time seemed to have passed Rennie by until Scott Robertson's sudden departure from the All Blacks last January.

Rennie was handed the reins two months later, issued with the assignment of leading the All Blacks through to next year's Rugby World Cup.

Immediately, rugby fans on both sides of the Tasman were looking ahead to the opening Bledisloe Cup Test with added interest.

But at least publicly, Rennie says there are no hard feelings.

"It's not about me," Rennie said on Thursday.

"I've got no regrets. I got to work with some really good people, people I've a lot of time for.

"It's part of a game we're involved in."

World.title: She's finally beaten Ledecky, now Pallister wants Olympic gold
World.content:
Swimming superstar Lani Pallister wasn't meant to be a distance swimmer.

At the beginning of her career, she was focused on the butterfly events.

It was only when Pallister mistakenly selected the 800 metres freestyle on a race program (instead of the 100m butterfly) that her career path would change.

"I ended up swimming it [800m freestyle], qualified for my first junior team, and now I'm on the senior team, and short course world record holder for the event," Pallister told ABC Sport at the Australian Short Course Championships earlier this month.

It's been a packed year for the 24-year-old, but a satisfying one.

Lani Pallister had a breakthrough in August, finally beating Katie Ledecky in the women's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Sean M. Haffey)

Her success at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, where she won gold in the 400m, 800m and 1,500m, saw her become the first woman at the Games to complete the treble.

But her performance at this year's Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in August, less than two weeks after the Glasgow Games, was her most remarkable breakthrough, beating United States powerhouse Katie Ledecky for the first time in the long course 800m freestyle.

"When you achieve a feat like that, you don't believe it until your hands are on the wall," Pallister said.

"It's not as much about just beating the one person in particular, but I think when you have someone as monumental as Katie, that definitely plays into the feelings and the sense of achievement off the back of it."

Pallister puts this success down to a change in coaching, making the shift from Michael Bohl to Dean Boxall over a year ago.

Lani Pallister has switched to legendary coach Dean Boxall, seeing results already in the pool. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"The past 18-month journey with [Dean] has been unbelievable, and I've achieved things in swim times I didn't think possible for myself," Pallister said.

It is a change that could take her to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, earning redemption for the heartbreak she has experienced in the past few years.

Rebuilding after Paris

It hasn't been an easy journey for Pallister, with illness and mental health taking a toll on her swimming career.

In 2021, she developed an eating disorder and a series of illnesses that saw her miss qualification for the Tokyo Olympics.

After seeing improvement in her times in the lead-up to the Paris Olympics in 2024, COVID struck, causing Pallister to pull out of the 1,500 and 400m races and finish sixth in the 800 metres.

She thought her swimming career could be over at 22.

Katie Ledecky was incredibly supportive of Lani Pallister gold in the women's 800m freestyle at the Pan Pacs. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

But after changing coaches, breaking world records in short course events, and finally claiming her win over Ledecky, Pallister is excited for the future and focusing on LA.

If everything goes right, an individual Olympic medal could finally be on the cards.

"I really wanted to focus on staying humble," Pallister said.

"There's a lot of work and a lot of things that are going to happen between now and the LA Olympics and I think that week over in LA in 2028 is going to be about consistency, repeat performance and just preparing."

Pallister will be 26 years old by the time the LA Games arrive, and 30 when Brisbane rolls around.

Age doesn't worry her though; moving to Boxall's squad has given her a fresh perspective.

"Female distance swimmers are slowly getting a little bit older," Pallister said, referring to Ledecky, who broke her own 800m world record at 28.

Lani Pallister believes the future for women's distance swimming is bright, with new talent Molly Walker rising through the ranks. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Any thought of retirement is far from Pallister's mind, and with a home Games in Brisbane in sight, it is tempting to hold on.

"At the end of the day, swimming's one of those sports, when you know you're done, you'll be done," Pallister said.

"With friends and family, in a city that I grew up swimming [in], it's probably the perfect way to end, and I think there's a lot of athletes that are in my age group that are kind of thinking the same thing."

Defending her title

Before the LA and Brisbane Games, however, Pallister will be continuing her busy year, having qualified for the 2026 World Aquatic Championships in December.

The championships will be held in China, with Pallister returning as the defending champion and short course 800m world record holder.

Lani Pallister is looking to defend her 800m title at the Short Course World Aquatics Championships in Beijing in December. (Getty Images: Mondadori Portfolio)

At the Australian Short Course Championships, she claimed victory in the 200, 400, 800, and 1,500 metres, meaning her World Championships will be busy.

"The biggest goal for me this year is going back to a World Championships and defending my back-to-back title in the 800," Pallister said.

"When you have the opportunity to race on the international stage and get more race practice under the belt, particularly before the next two years going into LA, it is something that's really important."

World.title: Germany too strong for Matildas with late goals in Karlsruhe
World.content:
The Matildas have been dealt a reality check as they ramp up their 2027 Women's World Cup preparations, suffering a 4-2 defeat to an understrength Germany.

With limited international windows remaining before next year's global showpiece event in Brazil, the clash against the world No.3 in Karlsruhe was crucial.

Headlines before the game were dominated by the absence of Manchester City star Mary Fowler for personal reasons, while coach Joe Montemurro spoke of the next generation coming through.

Germany scored the opening two goals, before captain Sam Kerr's had a header on the stroke of half-time to help the visitors close the deficit before the home team's Camilla Kuver scored in the 83rd minute.

Striker Holly McNamara did find a late consolation goal for the Matildas, but Chelsea midfielder Sjoeke Nusken made sure the Europeans dealt the last blow.

For Germany, the victory came despite the two-time world champions missing a plethora of stars, including captain Giulia Gwinn (ankle) and Liverpool forward Vivien Endemann (calf).

The error-prone Australia, however, will rue the missed opportunity to capitalise on their opponents' outs as a win would have helped them remain firmly in pot two out of four for the World Cup draw, meaning a mathematically better chance for a more favourable draw.

Despite the result, the Matildas will have something to celebrate as defender Tori Tumeth made her debut off the bench in the second half.

She was one of six second-half changes Montemurro made, with Tumeth coming in the final five minutes.

AAP
